Our work builds upon this foundation by applying a state-of-the-art model, the Long Short-term Memory network, to the study of oscillatory events during feeding behavior in Caenorhabditis Elegans. Our experiment demonstrates that the proposed temporal regression model is more effective at modeling neural activity than a traditional approach centered around probability distributions. Furthermore, a variant of this model, in its simplified version known as SRNN, can be adapted into a viable method for dimensionality reduction in the study of neural systems. Our findings emphasize the practical advantages of using RNN models in the study of brain function and encourage the continued development of novel machine learning approaches for understanding the complex dynamics of neural systems. We offer a new proof that displays the minimal equation of $\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{d}\right)$ within the equation of Chebyshev polynomials, and then use this insight to factor certain variants of these polynomials. Additionally, we identify a connection between the Galois groups of $\sin(x)$ and $\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)$, and reveal the origins of previous attempts to factor Chebyshev polynomials that were based on the wrong minimal equation. These attempts involved $x^2-\cos(2x)$ and resulted in an inseparable polynomial. Our method also allows us to factor $\sin(x)$, and we conclude by explaining the rational behind the incorrect previous approaches. Our analysis showcases the power of understanding the algebraic nature of transcendental functions like $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ and highlights the importance of correctly identifying minimal polynomial equations for such functions. Finally, it is acknowledged that further research is needed to factor other variants of Chebyshev polynomials.

Specifically, we demonstrate that any subgroup of index $n$ in an RF group $G$ will also have its subgroups of the same index in $G$, and these form an RF group, thereby extending a previous finding by Harald Schlichting. We then utilize this result to prove that certain lattices in $A_4$ and $SD$, featuring non-adjacent shells, possess the RF deviation of order $n$. The dissipation factor of high-quality sapphire is crucial in solid-state cavity quantum electrodynamics research due to its potential for limiting superconducting qubit coherence. Although sapphire's dissipation factor has been extensively measured, its impact on very low Q values, characteristic of many-state qubits, remains unclear. To address this gap, we measured sapphire's dissipation factor across a wide temperature range using a versatile bridge, enhancing our sensitivity to Q changes. Specifically, we were able to detect Q variations as small as 0.1% at temperatures around 0.35 K, translating to a 300-million-fold improvement in the measurement of the dielectric loss tangent. Our study found that the dissipation factor exhibits a well-documented increase with temperature but, surprisingly, we observe minimal frequency-dependent loss at very low Q values. Conversely, the dissipation factor's quality varies significantly at higher Q values, as evidenced by the establishment of two groups based on the dielectric material's origin. Furthermore, the dissipation factor exhibits a pronounced peak at 30.7 K, consistent with previously reported results, as well as the observation that the dissipation factor's magnitude varies by a factor of 20 across the 0.35-0.6 K temperature range, coinciding with the predicted minimum. Based on our findings, we calculate that the dielectric loss limit of the 4K sapphire is around 50 MHz. While our study focuses on the 0.6 K to 35 K temperature regime, we believe that the application of our high-sensitivity measurement method could lead to the detection of the dielectric loss mechanism operating below 0.6 K, as well as a more in-depth measurement of the dielectric loss mechanism operating above 35 K. In recent times, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been successfully applied to diverse real-world domains, driving research into their inherent generalizability. This study investigates the application of various GNN architectures and learning strategies for transfer knowledge in analogous domains. Our findings show that the choice of GNN model and learning method significantly affects transfer performance, with ConvGNN and GraphSAGE encountering difficulties on more complex tasks, whereas GNNP performing better on less complex tasks. Additionally, our examination reveals that using a baseline for evaluation and employing stochastic training strategy can help improve transfer performance. Notably, introducing dropout as a stochastic approach not only enhances transfer performance but also improves model performance on seen data. This research seeks to contribute to the understanding of GNNs by providing insight into the transfer learning process and we make our code available at https://github.com/dxw1995/gnn-transfer-learning. Online interactive learning is a type of collaborative learning where humans work alongside artificial intelligence models. This form of learning requires significant input from humans, typically provided in the form of feedback or suggestions. We investigated the AI's perspective in human-AI collaboration through the use of suggestion models. Unlike previous research which focused on the human perspective, we explored the benefits of such models from the AI's standpoint. We analyzed the dual roles the AI takes, namely, generating hypotheses and making suggestions based on new information it receives, and keeping track of the history of human feedback to update its internal models accordingly. From a machine learning perspective, we viewed the suggestions made by the AI as noisy versions of the human feedback, aiming to correct the AI's internal models through self-improvement. Employing a Dual Feature Distribution Model, we developed a method that is effective in maintaining a consistent flow of information between the AI and human feedback. Our experimental results confirm that this method enhances the AI's self-improvement capabilities. Additionally, we found that the AI's ability to provide accurate suggestions improved, and it was able to keep track of the history of human feedback accurately. We evaluated our approach through various metrics, including precision, recall, F1-score, and the Matthews correlation coefficient. We conducted two experiments, one focusing on an image classification task and the other on a software debugging task, demonstrating the practical applications of our innovative model in realistic online interactive learning settings. Our paper provides an in-depth analysis of the AI's self-improvement capabilities, offering valuable insights for experts in the field of semantic representation learning. Our innovative DFD model sets a new standard for researchers and practitioners, opening up new avenues for collaborative learning between humans and AI models. Our project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/biondii/DFDModel. Further details on the historical data learning can be found at https://github.com/biondii/DFDModel/blob/main/historyLearning.pdf. The group of complex numbers that satisfies the equation $f^q(Z) = Z$ for a given positive integer q is referred to as the platform group of the iteration of $f$. We, however, present a characterization of the platform group by focusing instead on the group of complex monic polynomials that satisfy the equation $f^q(Z) = Z$, where we call this the stabilized platform group. Our main result shows that this stabilized platform group has a maximum size of $q^3$ and that this value can be achieved. To prove this, we first show that a stabilized root free function of degree $d$ has at most $d$ iterations that yield a fixed point, a result that applies regardless of the coefficients. We utilize this result along with the properties of symmetric functions and Chevalley's theorem to reach our conclusion of the maximum group size. We also make use of the theory of Newton iterations and the action of the symmetric group to further illustrate the characterization of the stabilized platform group. These tools, however, do not seem to be effective in determining the platform group of iterations of univariate rational functions. We conclude by considering bicritical functions of higher dimension and providing a characterization of the group of linear transformations that satisfy the equation $f^q(X_1,...,X_n) = X_i$ for a given positive integer q and 1 ≤ i ≤ n, where we call this group the platform group of the iteration of $f$ at the jth coordinate. Our results in this section show that this platform group has a maximum size of $q^3$ and that this value can be achieved. We, however, do not have a characterization of the platform group that applies universally, as it does not necessarily consist of linear transformations over the field of complex numbers. Our characterization does, however, demonstrate that the platform group is contained within a subgroup of the wreath product of the symmetric group of degree $n$ and the multiplicative group of the field of complex numbers. We investigate two variants of this approximation: one employing a C^0 smooth boundary and the other with a C^1 smooth boundary. Our analysis involves calculating the differences in perturbative factors and surface elevations to assess the accuracy of each approximation method. We also introduce and adapt existing tools from approximation theory to facilitate this comparison. Our findings indicate that utilizing C^1 smooth boundaries yields sufficiently precise results, supplanting the need for even smoother boundaries. We further demonstrate that applying C^2 smoothness does not yield a substantial improvement but does result in increased computational demands. Ultimately, we recommend adopting the C^1 smooth boundary variant as the standard approach. We back up our findings with precise measures of accuracy, specifically error norms and breakdown thresholds for relevant relevant singular integral operators. We support these results by conducting a thorough numerical investigation. Our motivation stems from simplifying molecular simulations by leveraging the steady-state solution of a gas dynamics model that assumes a collision probability. This probability is expressed via the Boltzmann or other weak collision models in the rarefied regime of gas dynamics. By extracting macroscopic variables from the simplified model, which is computationally intensive, researchers aim to reduce the required processing time. This research is focused on validating theoretically derived steady-state solutions for particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of gas dynamics, including an extended version of the Debye-Hellmann model that accounts for the electron number density. We applied an iterative method to derive solutions for the PIC simulations. These solutions, along with the simplified model equations, were implemented in a parallel code based on PETSc and MPI for the PIC simulations and solution verification. Our experiments showed that the derived solutions for the PIC simulations converge within dozens of cycles, despite initial significant discrepancies. These solutions have been successfully validated against direct simulations and experimental results. They have also been integrated into the existing PIC code used in plasma simulations at the University of Michigan, with plans to integrate them into the existing codes used in plasma simulations worldwide. This study focuses on the transcendence of measures of degeneration for Siegel modular functions, specifically those associated with the Hecke operator. We also investigate the divisibility of specialized Sturmian constants, an area previously explored by Cantor, Cai, Dyson, and others. While our findings align with theirs, the approach and setting for study are distinct. Moreover, we establish a convergence rate for the "rate of geometric distribution" in the context of modular forms. This rate is analogous to a theorem attributed to Erdos, Ives, and Koblitz. Finally, the work presented provides a framework for the general case involving even-degree polynomials, building upon the work of Bergé, La Breteche, Miller, and Veitch. This research can be seen as a mathematical illustration of the notion of "freedom of choice" in the field of number theory. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the modular forms of weight one and degree two encompass all possible geometric distributions. This result has implications for future studies on transcendence of measures of degeneration in the context of modular forms. In addition to the theoretical conclusions, the study provides explicit examples of modular functions that validate the "freedom of choice" concept. Moreover, the study satisfies the transcendence conjecture of La Breteche for all polynomials of the form $x^2 + ax + b$ over fields of odd prime orders or orders six, in addition to the work of Bergé, La Breteche, Miller, and Veitch which validated the conjecture for quadratic extensions of rational numbers and infinite fields of algebraic type. This research validates the conjecture for all cases excluding quadratic extensions of rational numbers. Finally, the study provides an example validating a hypothesis proposed by La Breteche. This work validates the conjecture through a different approach, setting it apart from the initial study by La Breteche. This framework allows us to analytically compute flat bands at integer fillings within a non-relativistic description. Notably, we identify a reentrant flat chiral Fermi state arising from valency changes between $n=2$ and $n=3$, which is consistent with recent experimental observations. Our work also explores the boundary between the non-relativistic and relativistic regimes of the effective field theory, with implications for the moiré quantum wells' strong correlation physics. Moreover, the effective field theory provides a universal model for the emergence of non-Abelian Chern insulators in three-dimensional and topological hedgehog systems. This correspondence is expected to be generally applicable to low energy descriptions of twisted bilayer graphene and other moiré systems characterized by $2\pi$ flux variability. Our research explores high-current electron and ion currents produced at the plasma surface when intersecting a highly intense laser beam, which undergoes shockwave formation. By utilizing one-dimensional simulations of nonrelativistic plasma, we examine how varying plasma density profiles and, specifically, linear versus nonlinear polarization, affects these current signals. These simulations reveal that linear polarization leads to the greatest peak current, followed by elliptical polarization, and lastly circular polarization. This phenomenon is a direct result of the simultaneous plasma density gradient and laser's transverse electric field that triggers seed electron emission. Furthermore, we find that linear and elliptical polarization generate currents of nearly identical magnitude while circular polarization yields the lowest but still significant currents. This difference in current output arises from the distinct electron emission mechanisms triggered by linear, elliptical, and circular polarizations. Linear and elliptical polarization generate large seed electrons via a process of thermally driven emittance, whereas circular polarization produces an electron current via a photoionization driven by the laser's transverse electric field. Additionally, we find that linear and elliptical polarization generate large forward boosting currents due to the enhanced electron acceleration by the highly intense laser current, which overcomes the electron emittance limitations. In contrast, the electron current generated by circular polarization is too small to be boosted in a similar manner. Overall, our research highlights the previously underappreciated significance of nonlinear polarization in plasma and its crucial role in boosting high-current electron injections and serves as a valuable consideration for plasma based acceleration experiments. This work could have far reaching impacts if plasma based acceleration were to be used in charged particle guns for future particle collider facilities. Furthermore, we believe these findings may also have implications for a possible future fusion approach involving plasma and high energy lasers. A key colorization challenge lies in capturing color consistency across different images of the same scene, particularly when captured by cameras with varying specifications and positions. In the context of street-view surveillance, street lighting changes over time and can significantly affect the color representation of images captured by cameras in the same area, making it challenging to ensure consistency across their colorized results. In order to address this issue, we introduce Cross-Camera Profound Colorization, a novel colorization framework designed for multiple cameras. This framework utilizes a self-attention mechanism to synchronize the colorization process across cameras, as well as a self-adaptation module to rapidly minimize the discrepancy in color distribution, thereby achieving consistent colorized outcomes across the cameras, as verified by the results of our extensive experiments. Additionally, we created a comprehensive dataset, known as CityCity, consisting of 180,000 street-level images captured by 5 cameras, along with their corresponding colorized results, which are available for download on our website. Our proposed framework has consistently outperformed other baseline methods, with the time required for training it ranging from several hours to two days, while our approach can also be effectively applied to other domains, such as single-camera colorization, where it has outperformed other competing methods. Furthermore, our model exhibits exceptional performance even under extreme lighting conditions. Overall, our cross-camera colorization framework is capable of accurately predicting consistent colorized results for multiple cameras, while its adaptability allows it to be seamlessly extended to other domains, such as the colorization of a single image captured by a camera. In competitive internet gaming, players often stop playing online games suddenly, and their reasons for doing so are unrelated to their skill level. This study uses a novel dataset that tracks real-time behavioral changes in players who are newly paired in games for short periods. It investigates how quickly these pairings end and uses predictive models to identify factors that contribute to these pairings' demise. By examining data from nearly 300,000 game sessions involving over 100,000 unique players, this research provides an in-depth analysis of the early stages of social interactions in online gaming, focusing on how solo players's behaviors change when paired with others and how those changes affect the length of time they play together. Ultimately, this study aims to develop an advanced machine learning model capable of accurately predicting which pairings will end early based on this initial information. Our findings illustrate that early interactions are associated with significant social and behavioral consequences, and we show that our model can enhance game experiences by helping developers implement personalized matchmaking strategies. An implementation of this system could lead to an overall increase of up to 11% in players' average game session lengths. This research makes a significant contribution to the field of online gaming research by combining methods from behavioral economics, social science, and machine learning, and provides valuable insights into the early stages of social interactions in online gaming. In particular, our results show that multi-component-based predictive models can help overcome the challenges of measuring attrition in the early stages of social interactions. Moreover, our findings have implications for behavioral economics theories, such as the notion that being in a'suspense mode' for a short period is an essential aspect of social interactions, and that providing public feedback can play a crucial role in lengthening gaming sessions. Finally, our results highlight the potential of using social skills and cooperation as key factors in predicting which pairings will continue playing together. Our analysis suggests that supplementing skill-based predictors with model-based social variables can lead to substantial improvements in predicting solo-player pairings' longevity. An implementation of our model in a large online shooting game led to an increase of up to 11% in players' average game session lengths. Our results have also motivated game developers to modify their matchmaking strategies based on our recommendations, leading to a significant reduction in the frequency of short game sessions. The substantial expansion of cycling has led to increased concerns about cyclist safety in automotive collisions. A key consideration in auto manufacturers' Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and Vehicle-to-Everything communication technologies should be the priority of cyclist well-being in urban environments. The design of Urban Vehicle-to-Everything safety systems needs to be particularly alert for hard-to-detect cyclists in contexts where infrastructure is lacking.

This study introduces a real-time Cyclist Risk Identifier that utilizes video footage captured by auto-mounted cameras, with the aim of prioritizing cyclist safety in urban environments through the use of Driver Assistance Systems. The Identifier's design considers various urban environment factors that contribute to collision risk, including the visibility of cyclists due to reflective gear, as well as their motion in multiple dimensions. The proposed Identifier achieves real-time performance by leveraging a combined multi-sensor information-based system, which combines the processing of video data with the use of additional urban environment sensor information. A thorough evaluation of the approach was conducted using a dataset of approximately 2000 manually annotated video clips from urban environments, which showed the system's ability to accurately identify cyclists at a high frames per second rate. The resulting identified risks are categorized into three levels: high, moderate, and low. The corresponding code for this work has been made publicly available. The authors also report the results of a user study, participants of which were cyclists, in a related paper. In this study, a similar Clifford-algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann map is formulated and demonstrated to be isomorphic to the Taylor transformation.  The latter transforms Clifford-algebra-valued polynomial functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ to Clifford-algebra-valued homogeneous elements in the Clifford algebra of the Fock space of $\mathbb{R}^d$.  A key step in establishing this isomorphism was the discovery of a new monomial representation of the Clifford algebra in terms of elements of the Fock space of $\mathbb{R}^d$.  This new representation of the Clifford algebra is denoted the $\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}$-representation.  The $\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}$-representation extends the conventional Fock representation of the Clifford algebra and facilitates the extension of Clifford-algebra-valued functions from the classical domain to a larger domain.  The relationship between these representations of the Clifford algebra and points on a paraboloid in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ in a coordinate-independent (sheaf-theoretic) way is also investigated.  This relationship is denoted the paraboloid sheaf $\mathcal{P}$.  The Clifford-algebra-valued functions on the paraboloid are related to elements in a specific quotient of the Clifford algebra. The notion of pathwise conditioning of a Gaussian field $G$ given another Gaussian field $F$ originates from the real-line case where the Gaussian distribution $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ can be expressed as a conditioning operation for another Gaussian distribution $N(\mu',\sigma'^2)$. This results in the conditional distribution $N(\mu,\sigma^2)|F=\mu'+\sigma'\zeta)$ being standard normal for any real $\zeta$. In the context of Gaussian fields, the conditioning of a Gaussian process by a Gaussian field based on the underlying space of $G$ is explored. This is framed within the context of the existing theory of irregular operator ideals, specifically with regard to the ideal of transversal operators, known as $[\perp]$. For Gaussian fields $G$ with specific properties related to sample mean square integrability and separability, the existence of pathwise conditionings by other Gaussian fields $F$ is demonstrated, including cases where the underlying space of $G$ is a Banach or Hilbert space. This work also provides conditions under which unique pathwise conditioning by Gaussian fields is ensured and investigates the question of whether pathwise conditioning by a Gaussian field is a unique feature among Gaussian field conditions. Additionally, the field of $G$ being a Banach space is used as a case study to demonstrate these conclusions. Finally, the method of operator ideals is used to establish a connection between pathwise conditioning and the concept of irreducibility, specifically with regard to the properties of $(\alpha,\beta)$-cocoherent operators. This is in addition to the investigation of conditions under the sole influence of mean square integrability, without requiring separability. Moreover, the underlying space of $G$ can be any locally convex space, thus broadening the scope of these findings. Following this, an examination is made of the significant differences between the sample integrability requirements for conditioning on the real line versus the underlying space of a Gaussian field, highlighting a notable gap in the literature. This work is split into two self-contained parts, the first focusing on the scope of sample integrability in the underlying space of $G$ and making significant contributions to the literature, specifically [CS91], [CS95], and [Sz00]. Many real-world applications such as pedestrian and vehicle collision prevention, where in the past researchers used optical flow, now use deep learning-based optical flow algorithms. However, these algorithms hide important dynamic details like the movement of specific objects or whether a moving object is actually moving, in their output maps of optical flow. This motion information can be crucial in predicting potential collisions. Our work focuses on developing methods to extract hidden optical flow details, using the representation of motion in the three-dimensional space, specifically along the z-axis, first by redefining the fundamental equation of optical flow to include this dimension and then developing algorithms based on this new definition. Our analysis shows that using the proposed three-dimensional motion representation improves the accuracy of optical flow and significantly enhances the performance of collision avoidance systems, using the predictions made by a pedestrian tracker model. In addition to this, using the proposed three-dimensional motion representation also allows for the detection of moving objects and the estimation of their states, utilizing a technique called set prediction. Our set prediction approach using the proposed three-dimensional motion representation achieves state-of-the-art performance and outperforms existing techniques such as object graph-based methods, especially in predicting the actions of pedestrians and vehicles. The proposed three-dimensional motion representation is also used to estimate the intentions of other actors in a collision, utilizing a intention recognition model. Additionally, it's discovered that the most critical factor determining the nonlinearity of this system within a certain time frame is not the size of the initial values, but rather their interaction. This work also explores the possibility of reducing the growth of the difference between the two solutions by employing a specific type of global symmetry in the periodic system and demonstrates that such symmetries can indeed lead to more conservative growth patterns of the difference. However, these results are highly abstract and likely won't be directly applicable to practical problems in fluid dynamics. As a result, the field of quantum software testing is increasingly being explored to provide tailored approaches for validating quantum calculations. This research aims to develop and validate a general testing framework for quantum operations lasting a linear duration. The proposed model, LND-QC, is a classical imitation of the quantum system and is used to generate test cases based on specific coverage criteria. The effectiveness of the test cases is then evaluated using fault-based testing methods. This research introduces a new model, provides an evaluation technique, and offers an early perspective on applying quantum software testing principles. The conclusions are based on a two-part evaluation: a technical assessment, which examines the practicality of the testing approach, and a philosophical analysis, which considers the ethical implications of the resulting test cases. The findings indicate that the initially proposed model fails to accurately represent the quantum system, but a revised version is then suggested. This revised model aims to provide a more suitable classical equivalent for quantum operations with linear duration. The corresponding test cases were able to identify previously unsolved faults in the tested quantum programs. This research marks a significant step in validating quantum calculations based on classical testing principles. The study's results can serve as a foundation and inspiration for future testing endeavors. Recently, implicit neural representations have garnered significant attention within the computational biology community for modeling complex cell shapes. Unlike traditional mesh-based approaches, implicit methods enable efficient processing of cells with arbitrary shapes, suppressing unwanted details and allowing easier integration of biological knowledge. Nevertheless, existing implicit representation techniques frequently produce unrealistic outcomes and struggle with shape reconstruction. To address these limitations, we introduce novel techniques for the explicit manipulation and visualization of cell shapes. Our approach involves generating a compact network that represents the cell's surface, using it as input to an implicit model, and subsequently leveraging gradient-based optimization for detailed part addition. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our pipeline in generating structurally and visually accurate cell shapes, particularly in scenarios involving generating cells with specific biological signatures or altering existing cells for novel structures. The implementation details can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/mjchavchan/CelGen. Exoplanet researchers using transit spectroscopy to investigate exoplanet atmospheres are faced with several behavioral issues from the host stars. Variations in the host star's activity, spectral shape, and surface motion affect the spectroscopic analysis, especially for low-resolution datasets. This project assesses the impact of stellar behavior on both low and high-resolution transit spectroscopy datasets. A synthetic analysis model, ASTEP, was created to simulate these effects, combined with real-world data from the Teatro strain and the ADAS software analysis of Teatro, WASP-19, and HAT-P-7's transmission spectra. This research reveals that stellar activity has a significant effect on the synthesis of exoplanet features, especially in low-resolution datasets. Active regions in the host star can produce false negative or positive exoplanet signals, or alter existing features' directions or strengths. High-resolution transit spectroscopy provides a better understanding and weaker constraints on the synthetic signals, allowing researchers to analyze the atmosphere's composition more effectively. By analyzing high-resolution data, scientists can rule out false signals caused by stellar activity or interpret these effects as atmospheric features, depending on the specific planet. By combining the JEnhance algorithm and magnetic field analysis, researchers can identify the source of synthetic features, such as magnetic activity or other atmospheric elements, in greater detail. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive assessment of stellar activity effects on exoplanet transmission spectroscopy, offering recommendations for future missions and experiments. Additionally, it proposes high-resolution transit spectroscopy as an improved method for accurately interpreting exoplanet atmospheres while minimizing stellar activity's influence. During walking on land, it exhibits a more conventional type of gaits including the primary triplex and quadruplex movements found in other centipedes. In addition to the three-legged gait, another unusual walking style called the pivot turn was also observed. Key differences between its gaits at the water's surface and on land were found, possibly due to changes in its leg interactions and in-air movements. Additionally, it was discovered that the three-legged gait provides optimal stability and movement at the water's surface, but when walking on land, multi-legged gaits offer more benefits. A theoretical model of its walking movements was developed, classifying its gaits according to their patterns and regularities. The ultimate goal of this research is to create a realistic simulation of a global ocean tsunami sparked by an asteroid impact, which could serve as a starting point for apocalyptic scenario simulations in virtual games. To begin, a comprehensive review is conducted on asteroid impacts, tsunami waves, and their potential effects on society, as well as existing models used to simulate these events. A step-by-step process is outlined to develop an accurate tsunami simulation, commencing with preliminary asteroid orbit calculations to determine the likelihood and frequency of impacts. A probabilistic approach is utilized to calculate the force and velocity of the resulting impact, taking into account variables such as asteroid shape and the energies involved in the collision. To simulate tsunami waves, a damped wave equation is applied, with the linear model assuming that the ocean's density is fixed and uniform, while incorporating the effects of tidal forces due to the asteroid's size and the distance of the collision. To visualize the asteroid's path and the resulting tsunami waves, a basic 3D rendering system is established within the simulation code, which is written in Python and served as a valuable educational experience in coding for an undergraduate student. In various data classification tasks, incorporating expert knowledge can be beneficial. Expansion learning, which uses this knowledge, involves transforming negative samples into positive samples to facilitate learning. Traditional hyperbolic deposition learning methods have primarily focused on image recognition and have not been applied to classification expansion learning. Our new approach, HyperExpan, uses hyperbolic deposition learning to maintain the hierarchical structure of taxonomies and incorporates a new loss function that allows for precise geometric representation and improved learning results. Additionally, HyperExpan's ability to adaptably learn from various data sets makes it a versatile method. When tested against alternative methods on multiple classification expansion datasets, HyperExpan demonstrated superior performance. The code for HyperExpan is available on the GitHub platform.

The performance of density functional theory combining specific functionals is evaluated for calculating electric field effects on interaction energies of molecular dimers from the S66 test set, which focuses on non-covalent interactions. The following functional combinations are examined: 25 set-ups involving meta-GGA and hybrid functionals. The influence of further corrections for dispersion and exchange defects on the calculated electric field effects is also explored. The results indicate that a particular functional, PBE0+D2, provides the most accurate predictions among the examined combinations. The calculated electric field effects show varying dependences on the distance between molecular components. The analysis suggests that electric field effects in molecular dimers mainly result from changes in permanent multipole moments and molecular polarizabilities. The calculated electric field effects are found to be in line with experimental data from spectroscopy. This study demonstrates the potential of density functional theory with the PBE0+D2 approach for predicting electric field effects in complex chemical systems. The calculations were performed with the ONETOP version of the range-separated hybrid exchange-correlation functional. The augmented version of the basis set with additional atomic functions for better description of intermolecular interactions was used in the calculations. The geometry of the molecular dimers was optimised without constraints on the interaction distance, resulting in a minor deviation from the experimental distance between the molecular components. The second-order property response theory was used in the calculations. The property density corresponding to the molecular dimers was calculated with the basis set including a triple excitation for accurate results. The calculations were performed with the quantum chemistry program package TURBOMOLE. The Thole model was employed to describe the indirect effects of dispersion in the molecular dimers. The model assumes that the effects of transient attractions between molecular components are caused by temporary dipoles induced in neighbouring molecules. These dipoles are centred at the positions of the outer atomic components. The effect on the molecular interaction of the electric field due to these transient attractions is calculated using the local response theory for density. In the absence of explicit wavefunction variation, this theory provides an approximation that is comparable to a coupled perturbation theory with the electron-electron interaction. The model has a small effect on the electric field effect, with an effect size of about 25 millielectronvolts per atomic unit of distance, which is equivalent to a 0.08 picometer change in distance for an electric field intensity of 10 inverse square roots of a millimeter. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly enhanced supply networks and logistics visibility, enabling the capture of real-time data from the production and logistics systems. This enables the creation of complex models that aid in making data-driven decisions. Despite the advancements, uncertainty management in scheduling remains a complex challenge within Industry 4.0 systems. Existing literature often omits the representation of processing machine uncertainty, relying instead on a limited range of probability distributions, including uniform and truncated normal distributions. This study contributes to the development of methods for representing uncertainty in scheduling systems and contributes towards the integration of probabilistic logic in Industry 4.0 planning. We focus specifically on the enhancement of constraint networking representation by incorporating the lognormal distribution, often neglected in previous research. This work aims to provide industry practitioners and researchers with practical guidance on representing uncertainty in scheduling systems and promoting the adoption of probabilistic logic in Industry 4.0 planning. We highlight the need for further research into uncertainty representation, processing uncertainty, and distribution selection in scheduling systems. Additionally, in real-world manufacturing settings, enhanced representation methods can lead to increased system efficiency and flexibility, ultimately affecting the overall cost efficiency and resource utilization. We demonstrate the applicability of our work in scheduling solutions provided by Industry 4.0 software such as Planko. This study is an extension of an original publication in the proceedings of the 2021 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence. We have obtained a related patent as of September 2022 (EP3775238A) We are also in the process of obtaining a second related patent as of September 2022 (AT20K0002). Further research is required to integrate the enhanced representation of uncertainty into planning and scheduling solutions for the Industry 4.0 sector via AI methods. Such research could lead to the development of an uncertainty model library for Industry 4.0 scheduling systems, ultimately enabling users to quickly select an appropriate distribution for their specific needs. We also recommend integrating the enhanced representation methods of uncertainty into widely-used Industry 4.0 software platforms and enabling planning and scheduling solutions to take uncertainty into account through weighted graphs and network flow algorithms. We also recommend enabling constraint networking representation by incorporating uncertainty and demonstating the feasibility of integrating probabilistic logic in Industry 4.0 planning and scheduling systems. This could be achieved through the development of a constraint networking language that allows for uncertainty in scheduling systems and can be incorporated into planning and scheduling solutions. We also aim to enable the integration of uncertainty in production systems and the integration of probabilistic logic in Industry 4.0 supply chain management

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust designs that can withstand unexpected disruptions while ensuring predetermined behaviors.  Past research has presented various concepts of robustness although a unified framework has yet to be developed.  To address this gap, we introduce a novel formulation for robustness based on Time-Relative Logic, which views a system's behavior as robust if it remains consistent despite disturbances that do not violate its temporal properties.  Our approach, centered around a weighted automaton model, enables us to define and evaluate robustness in cyber-physical systems in a straightforward manner.  Furthermore, we expand our framework to encompass multi-aspect robustness, encompassing multiple properties described by STL formulas.  A decision-making algorithm and an efficient, automated design method for generating robust control policies are also presented.  The effectiveness of our approach has been demonstrated through case studies involving common control design problems.  Compared to existing methods, our research offers a fundamental understanding of robustness, flexibility in dealing with diverse properties, and automated design capabilities.  A formal explanation of the underlying concepts can be found in our published research.  The source code for our framework has been made publicly available on GitHub, facilitating its practical application.  Additionally, a tool allowing users to define and evaluate robustness for multi-asymmetric properties has been developed and is available at withinycors.github.io/lab/ tools.  Our research has significant implications for the development of formal requirements in cyber-physical systems and could also be applied to other fields of interest.  The results of our study have been thoroughly documented in a dissertation titled "A Formal Framework of Robustness: From Temporal Logic to Control" at https://doi.org/10.26179/7051419. This study explores the second-order accuracy of a semidiscrete approximation to a nonlinear diffusion equation on a comprehensive Riemannian manifold. The equation in question is loosely related to the gradient flow of an energy consisting of a combination of a nonlinear diffusion process and potential interaction between elements. The numerical solution in question is based on a standard Galerkin approach using piecewise linear elements on a geodesic mesh. The corresponding semidiscrete equation is analyzed, and its approximate solutions are shown to converge, where convergence rates are determined by spatial mesh sizes and a time stepping factor. Specifically, in the case of interest, this corresponds to a convergence rate of $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{p}$ in time, and an optimal spatial convergence rate of $p$. To verify these claims, this study shows that numerical solutions to the semidiscrete equation are stable and prove that they replicate the behavior of the continuous solution when approximating potential interaction between elements. Furthermore, this study's findings are extended to include approximate calculations of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange derivative. The results presented in this study are novel as they address second-order accuracy on a geodesic mesh, and correspond to the first such case in a geodesic setting. Previous research on this subject by the author utilized finite element methods on a mesh influenced by Eulerian mechanics. Notably, this study's findings are extended to include the Euler-Lagrange derivative, and its practical applications in the study of particle systems on a Riemannian manifold are also explored. A corresponding algorithm is provided, and its efficiency is analyzed. The results presented in this study show that numerical solutions to the semidiscrete equation are efficient and accurate in the study of interacting particle systems on a Riemannian manifold. The study's findings also address second-order accuracy in the context of fundamental equations on a geodesic mesh, and its results are novel in this subject area. The results presented in this study and its associated references demonstrate that numerical solutions to the semidiscrete equation are widely applicable in the study of Eulerian mechanics and geodesic settings. The study's findings also have the potential to be extended to include the study of fluid dynamics and biological modeling. Our approach is presented in an abstract and abstracted framework that reflects the inherent properties of Markov models while isolating those that are specific to CMCs. This allows us to distinguish these models from traditional Markov models and explore their relationship in a principled manner. Our reasoning is facilitated by the use of a specific conceptual framework that combines the ideas of actions and effects as expressed through the concept of a monad, thereby providing a unifying structure for the treatment of CMCs and related topics in the literature. Our work also provides a systematic review of the existing research on the topic, and as such, it offers a solid foundation for the continued development of the theory and methods associated with CMCs. We investigate the relationship between dynamic consistency and statistical nonlocality in the context of structural analysis.  Despite a lack of clear definition regarding these terms in the literature, we endeavor to provide a thorough explanation and demonstrate their interconnection.  Initially, we review the criteria for dynamic consistency proposed in the research by Kierkegaard et al. within the IASSAR workshop proceedings, based on their theoretical framework.  Subsequently, we highlight the need for consistent definition of statistical nonlocality within the literature.  Having established these foundational concepts, we delve into the evidence suggesting that certain instances of statistical nonlocality are, in fact, a consequence of requiring dynamic consistency.  This association raises the possibility that models labeled as nonlocal due to their inherent nonlocal characteristics might actually be equivalent to dynamically consistent models of conventional local models, encompassing a broader category of structures.  This distinction has significant consequences; for instance, it potentially alleviates the burden of proving positive definiteness for certain classes of nonlocal models used in applications, as they might actually be equivalent to regular local models.  Furthermore, we propose a systematic method for converting a dynamically consistent nonlocal model into an equivalent standard local model, thereby simplifying the computational process.  This methodology can be used to transfer various nonlocal models into well-established local models through the use of the Multiple Level Summation Method.  In doing so, we demonstrate that the widely employed Averaged Nonlocal Integrodifferential Equation is equivalent to a standard local model, thereby facilitating computations.  In addition to theoretical contributions, we also aim to promote the development of a unified understanding of dynamic consistency and statistical nonlocality.  Ultimately, the purpose of this paper is to foster a deeper appreciation for the relationship between these concepts and the potential implications on the design and analysis of nonlocal models in the field of structural mechanics.  In particular, the paper aims to encourage continued research on the fundamental theory of nonlocal models as well as the development of effective computational methods.  In the process, the paper also explores potential applications for Nonlocal Elasticity.  In the end, the paper seeks to advance the field of Nonlocal Elasticity.  In the process, the paper also explores various classes of nonlocal models and the possibility of establishing a more systematic approach to categorizing the extensive range of models within the literature which includes Positive Definite Quadrature Methods, the Multiple Level Summation Method, the Variational Message Passing framework, and others. To address this issue, we have developed a location tracking privacy metric based on the expectation principle. This measure assesses the difference between the actual probability of a location history happening and the probability of the same event under a distorted history, obtained through a variational distance transformation. Furthermore, we have also obtained crucial lower bounds on the minimum possible distortion levels. Recent years have seen an enormous increase in code-mixed content across social media platforms, which presents a significant challenge to NLP models. The field of code-mixed model research has largely been hindered by a lack of suitable approaches for handling code-mixed data. This study proposes the Transition Point Embedding Technique for Output Codes (PESTO) to address the representation of code-mixed words and words transitioning between languages. PESTO achieves this by embedding words at different language stages (initial, transition, and outcome) in a unified framework. Furthermore, a relative position representation submodule is incorporated to capture inter- language transition patterns. The proposed model is evaluated on code-mixed datasets from three languages: Hindi-English, Urdu-English, and Sri Lankan Varieties of English. Experimental results show that PESTO outperforms baseline methods in accuracy, achieving impressive results with an overall char-level accuracy of 99.7%. The model's success lays the groundwork for further exploration of code-mixed language models. The proposed approach further fosters multidisciplinary research into the understanding of code-mixed languages and may lead to the development of more comprehensive linguistic models. A major challenge in localizing a camera spatially and temporally is the initial phase, especially in real-time operation for advanced features. Many methods collect point cloud data using 3D lidar or stereo cameras but struggle with predicting 3D geometry from depth maps efficiently. This paper introduces an offline surface mapping approach using a pre-trained point detector and tracker to identify and match static surface features online. Unlike conventional methods, our surface map is not purely geometric, providing 3D context and color information to guide feature matching, thus improving the accuracy of pose estimation. Additionally, our approach exploits kinematic constraints and employs temporal feature matching to filter out low-quality matches, ensuring real-time performance on mobile platforms. We have tested the method on a mobile phone platform with geotagged images from the KITTI dataset, achieving a 97% success rate with a 5-meter accuracy. This method has been successfully used in an autonomous helicopter project at the EU FP7 project CHORUS. Video demonstrations are available online. The source code is available upon request.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic or structural phase transition. Some studies have hinted at the existence of nematic fluctuations and a nematic superconducting state in LiFeAs, but recent findings from this study indicate that pristine LiFeAs, along with LiFeAs doped with low levels of Co and V, lack instability at the Q-nematic wavevector, contradicting the hypothesis of nematic fluctuations and the nematic-superconducting scenario in this material. Instead, the study attributes the perceived nematic-like behaviour in LiFeAs to an orbital-dependent electronic response on the Li sites caused by ionization. Furthermore, Co and V doping in LiFeAs exhibits first-order structural phase transitions and magnetic behaviour, respectively, and Co doping shows a magnetic order parameter proportionate to the amount of Co, and shows proportional spin susceptibility on the Co d-orbital, supporting the idea that these transitions in LiFeAs are due to the absence of charge transfer or molecular orbital effects. As such, the absence of nematic instability and the unique characteristics of the underlying electronic structure in liFeAs supports the simple electron-phonon coupling as a mechanism for superconductivity in this material. These findings reject the nematic-superconducting scenario in LiFeAs, and suggest that liFeAs represents a particularly unique and interesting superconducting compound. We studied a two-Higgs-doublet model with a globally adjusted parameter space, 
taking into account the effects of multiple new particles on various physical processes.
Our analysis started by evaluating the impact of four standard measurements: the mass of the Higgs boson, the charged current coupling, the electroweak vector boson mass, and the rate of B to Xs, Xd decays. For each measurement, we adapted our model to find the best fit values for the entire parameter space. 
Next, we determined the allowed range of parameters based on each individual measurement and found that different standards have varying restrictions. While the mass of the Higgs boson imposes the most stringent conditions, the rate of B to Xs, Xd decays has the widest limitations. 
We also identified regions of parameter space that could potentially be ruled out by future measurements at LHC, SHHC, and electroweak precision experiments. 
Our conclusions were confirmed by verifying that our model can effectively explain and complement existing and future experiments within the framework of renormalisation, confirming that two-Higgs-doublet structures are viable candidates. 
Our study has been made available to public as an open-source tool that allows for the incorporation of new measurements and predictions from experiments and theoretical calculations, facilitating the integration of new results in the future. 
This tool was used to demonstrate that two-Higgs-doublet structures remain viable across a wide range of parameters and remain viable even under stricter conditions than currently allowed by existing measurements, suggesting that they may ultimately be ruled out by precision experiments at SHHC and collider experiments in the future. 
Our study was finalized by evaluating the performance of global fitting and sensitivity analysis in the presence of correlated and heterogeneous data and was compared to results obtained from simplified models, demonstrating the following key findings. 
Where previous analyses focused on a single standard or multiple standards with independent constraints, our comprehensive global analysis with the incorporation of correlated and heterogeneous data reveals a more stringent scenario where two-Higgs-doublet structures are largely constrained but remain viable even under more stringent conditions than currently allowed by existing measurements, suggesting that they may ultimately be ruled out by precision experiments at SHHC and collider experiments in the future. 
Our results have been compared to a simplified model analysis and reveal a more restrictive scenario than expected, indicating a notable difference between the allowed range of parameters in the two models.

We've introduced a groundbreaking training method that leverages neuroevolution to prepare topological units (particles with fixed connections) and the processes governing their structural arrangements in a scalable system. As a result, the system's constituent parts and the processes themselves are optimized in tandem, yielding adaptive systems with the capacity to reach self-assembled states from diverse initial conditions with reduced entropy. In contrast to conventional simulations where processes are predetermined, our novel framework enables scenarios where the processes are designed and manipulated during simulations, enabling the systematic exploration of various system configurations. Furthermore, this approach allows us to explore complex temporal models and explore novel research directions for the development of adaptive systems. The proposed solution is applicable to a wide range of problems in physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering. We demonstrate its capabilities through adaptive heat transport and the creation of superconducting loops. The accompanying source code is available on GitHub, providing users with the flexibility to modulate its behavior. Moreover, we have formulated a set of open challenges for the field of self-assembling adaptive systems. By advancing the understanding of the underlying processes at a system-level, we aim to lay the groundwork for the design of adaptive systems with optimized properties, thereby paving the way for the creation of functional materials with the capacity to regulate their own evolution. We introduce Dict-BERT, an enhanced pre-training method for BERT that utilizes a
glossary to capture word meanings and improve model performance. The main issue
with traditional BERT models lies in their tendency to prioritize word
appearances over actual word meanings. To counter this limitation, we merge
word meanings from a dictionary and add this integrated glossary to the BERT
model during pre-training. By doing so, the Dict-BERT model is encouraged to
learn representations that amplify word meanings. Theoretical analyses validate
the effectiveness of the Dict-BERT model, which achieves better results in
downstream NLP tasks and exhibits more nuanced word meaning representations. 
Empirical evaluations conducted on 8 datasets demonstrate that Dict-BERT
outperforms the standard BERT model in 6 out of 8 benchmarks. The code used for
these experiments can be found at the address https://github.com/dulucas/Dict-BERT.

This rate is first established in the energy scale of B-meson decay, and then used to determine the branching fraction and direct CP violation ratio for B-meson decay into a proton and a lambda antibarion. This process has been shown to be the most likely way for B-meson decay to produce isospin breaking and CP violation in hadronic baryon decays. This assumption led to the establishment of lower mass limits of 0.06 and 0.15 GeV for a dark photon mediating dark matter interactions, and a mass range of 0.38 to 0.42 GeV for a dark photon not mediated by any force. In response to escalating threats from highly skilled and distributed cyber attackers, modern cities are being equipped with an intelligent layer of cyber protection. This protection is critical not only because of the potential financial costs but also because of the risk of harm to human lives. To address this challenge, an innovative game called Urban Defense has been developed as a simulation tool to explore strategies for coordinating defenses against massive, distributed attacks. Building on this concept, the Urban Defense game has been extended to focus on the management of limited resources within the city's cyber infrastructure. This version of the game, Tactical Resource Administration during Urban Defense (TRAUdC), requires players to effectively manage battery power, compute capacity, and network accessibility across the city's infrastructure. Scenarios in TRAUdC probed the ability of human players and artificial intelligence (AgentC) to collaborate effectively in responding to extreme stressors, including widespread attacks and limited time frames to implement a defense strategy. The simulation revealed critical insights into human and artificial collaboration, including the emergence of a leader, reduced communication transactions, and, ultimately, failure in both human and artificial groups to execute effective responses. The findings from TRAUdC highlight crucial requirements for the development of intelligent, automated systems capable of assisting and informing human decision-making in complex, high-stress cyber environments. These include incorporating psychological influences on human behavior, incorporating varied skill sets of human players, and developing more sophisticated artificial decision-making systems. By filling a critical knowledge gap in the field of socio-technical cyber defense, the Urban Defense and TRAUdC framework offers a valuable research framework for exploring strategies of human-AI collaboration in highly stressful cyber assault scenarios. This framework has significant potential for application in a range of critical domains, including urban defense, medical device protection, and election integrity. Future research will delve into the development of TRAUdC's artificial intelligence component, grounded in Multi-Agent Collaborative Learning (MACL), with potential implications for a broader range of cyber systems. This work represents the initial implementation of the Urban Defense and TRAUdC framework, offering a foundation for the development of more sophisticated models and intelligent systems in the future. Ultimately, the Urban Defense and TRAUdC framework has the potential to contribute to the creation of a robust, automated cyber defense system that is equally effective in preventing financial losses and saving human lives. By using the Einstein-aether model's boundary conditions, we demonstrated the model's ability to describe a thin black hole shell. Furthermore, we discovered that for a specific case with reflective boundary conditions, the temperature of the shell can become negative, indicative of a more complex phase transition. Lastly, we explored the thermodynamic limits of the black holes within the Einstein-aether model. Our findings suggest that the presence of the ambient space has a profound impact on the thermodynamic properties of the black stars. We were able to identify four distinct phases: a black hole phase, a black hole with a crust phase, a vestige of the thermal radiation cloud phase, and a vestige of the thermal radiation cloud with a black hole crust phase. All of these phases were found to be analogous to the black hole and radiation phase and the blackening of the black hole phase observed in a confined environment. Moreover, we were able to determine the mass ranges for each of the different phases within the ambient space and also found that the mass of the black hole and a crust are not dependent on the ambient space parameters. Graph neural networks have achieved significant improvements in domain-agnostic tasks such as link prediction and node classification. Previous research has shown that semi-supervised learning can be effective for large graph classification tasks using a small number of labelled nodes. However, when it comes to predicting edges or nodes, having limited node labels can be a major constraint. To address this challenge, we introduce a global optimization method that enhances semi-supervised learning for edge and node prediction tasks by mimicking supervised node prediction. Our approach works by optimizing edge and node weights in a unified framework, providing insights into the predicted edges and nodes. This mechanism can be seen as a pseudo-tagging process that assigns importance weights to graph nodes and edges. As a result, it offers performance guarantees and can be used as a standalone component or as a regularization method for existing graph models. Our experiments with the Northwind, Wikipedia, and Twitter graphs demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. An implementation of this method is available on the GitHub platform. Betatrons are optionally integrated into contemporary particle accelerator experiments to produce a range of short-lived radionuclides through interactions between particle beams and thin foils. A comprehensive computational model has been developed to study radiation processes occurring when charged particles collide with targets, triggering the emission of relativistic betatrons as a result of electron-degenerate plasma excitations. This model has been applied to the AWAKE experiment, where a high-energy wakefield awakened by an injected proton beam interacts with surrounding plasma components. Our research examines the generation and propagation of excited plasma waves within the wakefield, triggered by the injection of a seed particle, as well as the emission of betatrons resulting from interactions between the beam particles and targets. A key aspect of this model is its integration of fully nonlinear governing equations, enabling the simulation of intricate radiation processes and their intricately interconnected physical mechanisms. This model has been utilized in a series of simulations of the Betatron-like Radiation (BBR) experiment, a proposed complement to the AWAKE 2 research initiative, aiming to optimize parameter settings for maximizing betatron yield. Specifically, our simulations explored the emission of betatrons produced by beam collisions with separate, individual foils. Upon optimizing the spacing between these foils, we achieved an approximately 60-fold increase in total betatron yield, with a notably high peak betatron yield observed in this optimized configuration. This model and our accompanying simulations offer valuable tools for optimizing experimental settings in similar betatron-based radiation experiments. Future research will involve refining our computational model to enable the simulation of an alternative, external radiation source. The resulting optimized setup is anticipated to serve as a valuable starting point for future experimental collaborations involving optimized betatron production in experiments. This optimization strategy could potentially be transferred to other experiments, offering a valuable approach for achieving enhanced research results. Notably, our simulations of optimized experiment settings have yielded very high yields of a range of short-lived isotopes, offering new possibilities for their creation and study. The resulting optimization strategy could be applied in a wide range of applications and contribute to the advancement of future experimental research in this area. A future goal of this project will involve investigating the feasibility of using the betatrons produced in this experiment as an injection source for other research initiatives, offering a novel pathway to optimizing particle accelerator performance and advancing scientific research in this area. This future research will examine the technical requirements and implementations necessary for making this strategy a reality. Preliminary results indicate that this sort of future optimization strategy could be highly beneficial for a variety of particle accelerator experiments

The requirement for data confidentiality in large-scale data analysis has increased exponentially as massive datasets are continuously collected from various sources. Despite the data's anonymity, it contains sensitive information about the data contributors, which is known as differential privacy. Our research focuses on achieving this privacy without compromising data analysis accuracy. In this study, a new, expandable framework for learning decision trees from distributed data is presented. The framework's key components are fully explained algorithms for tree node choice and tree growth, both of which meet strict differential privacy requirements. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithms' precision using existing synthetic datasets from decision tree learning experiments. The results show that the algorithms can effectively learn up to 99.8% of a base tree's nodes while maintaining an error rate very close to the base tree's, with error rates consistently under 0.7%. The framework's simplicity and fully explainable results make it a reliable choice for confidential data analysis. The algorithms's high accuracy and our ability to apply them equally to data from any source make them suitable for a wide range of applications, from research to more commercial interests. The main contribution of this research is the development of a new, expandable framework for differentially private distributed decision tree learning. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to learn decision trees from distributed data while adhering to strict differential privacy requirements. The research also makes a methodological contribution by adapting a private algorithm from the literature to a new context and demonstrating its precision using a combination of known techniques. Finally, a publicly accessible implementation of the framework is available at https://github.com/szli13/differentially-private-distributed-decision-tree-learning. Though the R\'enyi distance can be utilized in optimization processes, its non-convex nature leads to the absence of proximal gradients in the traditional sense, and this paper presents two methods to circumvent this issue. The initial approach converts Bregman distortion into a convective surrogate by taking the derivative of its argument, resulting in a proximal gradient algorithm. The second method, incorporating a Bregman relaxation, enables the creation of a self-updating algorithm. Both algorithms are applied to the problem of linking R\'enyi distances between empirical and target densities, with a combination of these methods ultimately providing the most accurate results. This research develops and presents a Bayesian framework for selecting the most effective chain event networks using real-world event data. The proposed method employs the markov model to simulate network dynamics and utilizes the product space of parameter sets to calculate the Bayesian posterior probability distribution. The approach clusters parameter sets with similar log-likelihood values and applies the Markov chain Monte Carlo method for an efficient exchange rate estimation process. The method achieves Bayesian MAP inference by choosing the largest cluster with the highest prior probability. The empirical results show that the proposed method can effectively select the best chain event networks and improve predictive accuracy in network dynamics forecasting. The methodology does not require any parameter optimization and efficiently handles large networks with numerous parameter sets. The method has been validated using event data from terrorist and river flooding events in different regions, demonstrating its reliability and practicality. The research also highlights the limitations of the original parameter space search method in Bayesian Networks and suggests possible improvements. The study utilizes the NETCONVERT network conversion tool to convert networks from various formats, including an updated version of the tool to handle large network files with multiple node groups. The method has significant implications for future research, including the development of efficient search algorithms for selecting effective network models with challenging parameters. The approach opens up opportunities for practical applications, such as using the method in conjunction with genetic algorithms to improve network dynamics forecasting and practical optimization. The study also sheds light on the future research directions and potential extensions, including the development of an automated tool for selecting the most effective chain event networks and integrating the Bayesian framework with genetic algorithms for future applications in different fields. The results of the search method have been applied to real-world event data across various domains, including an analysis of the effectiveness of law enforcement agencies in preventing terrorist attacks in the United States using the FBI's Law Enforcement Intelligence Primers event data. The method demonstrates the significance of event network topology and parameter values in predicting future events and reveals valuable insights from the empirical results. The study utilizes the t-test to compare the predictive accuracy of the selected networks with and without the event parameter p1, and confirms that the event parameter p1 has a statistically significant effect on the accuracy of the predicted networks. The approach can be extended to other domains, such as natural disaster risk assessment, with potential applications to real-world systems like networks and biological systems. The study also explores the development of efficient search algorithms for different problem types, including set cover and graph partition problems. As a preemptive measure against potential security threats, installations such as the Pinhole Camera System at the Swiss Transport Museum are equipped with barriers that can be moved. This project involves designing a robot capable of navigating around these obstacles with ease. The robot's trajectory is analyzed using Predictive Path Planning, an algorithm originally developed for semi-supervised learning. Determining the barrier's adhesion is a critical component of this pathfinding process. The robot's navigation system is capable of estimating if the barrier is being adhered to consistently during the approaching phase and can trigger a change in the barrier's position if necessary. The robot's controller utilizes Multi-Dimensional Perception-Hierarchical Dynamic Modeling (MDP-HDM), which facilitates a soft switching mechanism on the barrier's position, ensuring smooth transitions on the z-axis. The robot's ability to adapt to non-linear shifts in the barrier's position is also explored in the study. The curvature-based motion, specifically growth processes driven by curvature, has been studied through mathematical models that capture the essence of crystalline and faceted pinning interactions from a collective behavior perspective. This survey aims to provide an in-depth examination of the mathematical framework behind these models and their associated analysis, emphasizing novel developments since 2016. It will also explore connections with other growth processes and future research directions that emerge naturally from the discussed outcomes. Key concepts covered will include the mathematical formulation of the models, their associated challenges, initial conditions, uniqueness and regularity of solutions, long-term behavior, uniform estimates, and precise analysis of the solution regime. Additionally, this study will delve into the challenges associated with obtaining precise estimates of the solution. Finally, this work will cover the outcomes of various pinning model variations and discuss open questions and potential future research avenues. This research presents an innovative method for producing unique plant shapes in three dimensions by leveraging algorithms that mimic the processes of plant growth. A novel strategy, referred to as Plant Growth Growth, enables the creation of intricate stalk structures and can be applied to a wide range of plant models through simple and adjustable rules. High-quality visual representations are generated from these stalks using a scanning technique that incorporates random fluctuations, providing a foundation for diverse applications such as 3D printing, sculpture, and even supporting actual plant growth. Additionally, this method allows for the creation of realistic plant images using a painting algorithm, and our sculpture platform, GrowSpace, facilitates user-generated and user-controlled unique plant sculptures. Finally, this study explores the potential for supporting real plant growth using these generated stalks and discusses how this method can contribute to advancements in evolutionary algorithms and plant biology. Ultimately, we hope that our research enables novel interactions between plants, people, and technology. A video illustrating the method's capabilities and an interactive website where readers can create unique stalks and 3D sculptures are available at growspace.org. A related demonstration of this method was presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH 2021 Conference in Virtual Reality, contributing valuable insights to the interactions between plants, people, and technology. A forthcoming paper will delve into the details of our growth approach and can be found at arxiv.org/abs/2110.13880. A unified normalization technique for imaging would streamline cross-modal and cross-subject comparisons, facilitate the sharing of derived anatomical and physiological measurements, and ensure consistent image interpretation.

This process involves reverse-engineering the normalization used in image processing and reversing it to make the data more comparable. This approach was tested using MRI scans from different parts of the body and demonstrated successful standardization across various modalities.

A recent shift in research emphasis from standardized test scores to a more comprehensive understanding of students' academic journeys has been observed. In this paper, we explore the application of data mining techniques to a large dataset collected by the New York City Department of Education through their NYC Public School Dataset project. This dataset contains detailed student information, including demography, standardized test performance, and school affiliation. Utilizing latent variable models, we develop a methodology to accurately predict students' academic backgrounds and school affiliations. Our methodological approach is validated by comparing the predicted outcomes with actual student trajectories. Following the validation phase, we divide the dataset into two segments. One portion is used to train the models, while the remaining dataset is employed to test the accuracy of our models. Our results reveal notable levels of both predictive and explanatory accuracy, achieving explanation rates of approximately 70% and prediction rates of around 60% for models predicting school affiliations and demography respectively.
