This is in line with findings that show similar models with real alterations to have a leading order eigenvalue spectrum described by a Gaussian model, despite the presence of non-Hermitian properties. In this context, we focus on the statistical properties of a single eigenvalue and propose that, for large bandwidth $W$ and size of the alterations $L$, the distribution of the difference between this eigenvalue and its model-predicted value is given by a Poisson distribution with a parameter proportional to $L^2/(W^3)$. This provides the basis for the development of an estimation method for $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric band matrices, where we apply this method to compute the Hamiltonian of a system describing the coupling of two Bose-Einstein condensates in a double-well potential. A core capability for conversational systems is grasping the meaning of dialogues. Although some models can excel in dialogue processing without learning this skill, it is crucial for systems that interact with humans on a semantic level. In this study, we teach models to understand dialogue semantics through our proposed 'Meaning Enriched Conversation Pre-training' (MECP). Our MECP combines a cutting-edge conversation pre-training model with one that develops sentence meaning from large text collections, using this merged model in dialogue response generation. Our experiments show that MECP yields superior results in the Hotpot Extension and OpenBook Knowledge networks and comparable outcomes in the Gigaword when compared with conventional conversation pre-training methods. Furthermore, we validate that MECP teaches models to process dialogues more effectively in a semantic context and to detect relationships between sentences more accurately. The resources and codes related to this research are available on our public GitHub repository. They contribute to the growing body of natural language processing research code and can be accessed at https://github.com/autonomouslam/MECP. Additionally, we have released an enhanced version of the Meaning Grapher used in this research at https://www.github.com/autonomouslam/meaning-grapher-2.0. With this research, we argue that teaching models to process dialogues at a meaning-bearing level has significant potential to elevate the semantic capability of conversational models. Our work is the first of its kind in incorporating meaning-based learning in conversation pre-training, and it is backed by thorough experimental analysis. In particular, we have tested the robustness of the models to various semantic reasoning tasks and found the patterns of model performance at different levels of semantic processing. Consequently, this research opens doors for future work in integrating meaning-based learning in conversational models and teaches models to process dialogues more semantically. An online review platform of the paper, Discussion on Meaning-based Learning for Conversation, is accessible at https://www.imedusa.com/dl-for-conversation/. Our team has also launched a platform to enrich text collections with meaning, at https://www.imedusa.com/meaningify. The resulting text collections possess a deeper semantic structure, enriching the pool of data for language model pre-training and fine-tuning. To ensure that explainable AI promotes interpretability, we must first clearly define and assess it. By analyzing various machine learning algorithms from a cognitive perspective, we identify key factors that contribute to interpretability and understand how various algorithms work. Our comprehensive, scientifically grounded approach evaluates algorithms based on their clarity, simplicity, and consistency in providing easy-to-interpret explanations. We have developed a method to calculate the Cognitive Complexity of an algorithm using a set of formal rules, and we are using this metric to compare the interpretability of popular gradient-boosting algorithms. By learning how a machine learns (i.e., algorithmic interpretability) and imposing strict requirements (i.e., rules), we can ensure that AI explanations facilitate meaningful human understanding. With this metric, we can identify and improve inefficient learning processes and optimize the clarity of AI models for better decision-making. Our research offers a groundbreaking, practical framework for understanding and assessing the interpretability of AI algorithms through human cognition. Anomaly detection is a crucial task that identifies data points significantly different from the rest. One of the anomalies can be found in Time Series Data where an outlier occurs unexpectedly. Typically, anomaly detection is either supervised or unsupervised, but a semi-supervised approach can also be applied. Given the time series properties of data, anomaly detection is often handled by one-class models or by converting time series data into more manageable forms like images. Either way, there's an inherent problem of limited label availability. Thus, a loosely supervised approach is adopted. In this paper, we introduce four strategies to adapt the Isolation Forest model for time series by leveraging time series data's visual characteristics and reducing the input time series data into a more manageable format, specifically a 1-D signal. Our method can also be applied across various platforms, including devices with limited resources. The effectiveness of our approach and model is evaluated using accuracy and F1-score metrics on seven datasets from the Time Series Data Repository. Our findings demonstrate that the semi-supervised Isolation Forest model outperforms the traditional one by overcoming the limitations of limited label availability. Moreover, our implementation of the model in Python is accessible via the following repository https://github.com/andre-cs/Loosely-Supervised-Isolation-Forest. This model can also be deployed using TensorFlow Quantum, enabling the creation of quantum speedup protocols as described in the following study https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7549158. Our method can also be accessed via the following repository https://github.com/Andre-CS/Quantum-Speedup-Isolation-Forest. Finally, the source code for our loosely and tiny supervised implementation of the Isolation Forest model is available at the following repository https://github.com/Andre-CS/TiWS-iForest. Our implementation of the model also earned the first place in time series anomaly detection track of Data Science Competition at InSITE2022. The prize money award was $1500. The competition details are available at the following link https://insiteu.github.io/2022/competition/anomaly_detection/. The code for our model can also be deployed on IoT platforms as described in the following study https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-23149-1_11. The source code of the model is available at the following repository https://github.com/Andre-CS/iForest-deployed-on-IoT. Our goal is to precisely determine properties of the metal-rich globular cluster NGC 2808, focusing on its metallicity, heating history, and age. We analyzed 20 bright red giant stars with the help of FLAMES/ESO VLT data, incorporating 18 unique FeII lines and 25 specific Scrabec2 lines to determine carbon abundances. The initial step involved refining a standard atmospheric model in a 1D photogravity diagram to confirm stellar characteristics. We then used the scaled-solar abundance distribution from the GS98 model to determine the cluster's metallicity, finding a precise value of [Fe/H] = -1.35 ± 0.03 (statistic error) ± 0.01 (systematic error). A close inspection of carbon levels revealed a roughly 0.3 dex spread of carbon abundances, further indicating a diverse composition within the cluster. We note that both the metallicity spread and temperature increase at the cluster's core are expected outcomes driven by the dynamic interaction between stars. A subsequent comparison with the M68 cluster, sharing a similar metallicity but featuring less internal movement, was conducted. Our findings were then compared to the theoretical models for stellar movement and rotation. Lastly, a calculation of the cluster's horizontal movement was made and found to be 0.60 ± 0.16 km/s, resulting in a rough estimate of 13 billion years old for the cluster's age. The calculation was based on model tables from Gennaro Giacconi, featuring mixed-element movements. The estimated movement values were found to be in rough agreement with the movement generated by the dynamic interaction of stars. A secondary finding was that both temperature and movement levels at the cluster's core were lower than in the M68 cluster. Urgent message transmission often necessitates an immediate quantization of the encoded information, typically using a uniform quantizer, which lacks knowledge of the channel noise. Since the receiver is unaware of this quantization, this can lead to an undetected attack in which an imposter claims to have transmitted a valid message. To counteract this vulnerability, we explore the application of authentication codes that require minimal data storage and can detect false transmissions, even when communicating through noisy Gaussian channels. We investigate the performance limits of such codes and implement a straightforward, rate-limited search for these codes, which results in superior performance compared to a previously established approach. Notably, at high signal-to-noise ratios, our method achieves a search time that is virtually indistinguishable from that of the optimal search. Furthermore, the methods we develop can be easily adapted for secure communication within secret key-based cryptographic systems that employ noisy channels. We outline potential methods for obtaining secure keys in settings that involve trusted intermediaries or error correction, which may be utilized independently or in conjunction with the authentication and authentication-limiting techniques described above. We also provide additional insight and analysis in the companion paper titled "On the Impossibility of Superseding Traditional Keyless Authentication". \cite{impossibility}

The continuous expansion of data in cloud environments poses a significant challenge for virtualization technologies. Effective virtualization relies heavily on high-quality interfaces, but standard interfaces are insufficient for managing large datasets due to substantial load times and memory requirements. This paper presents a new interface, the prepartition interface, which enables fast and efficient virtualization of data by distributing load across virtual machines and reducing dependency on physical data structures. Furthermore, we provide a concrete implementation of this interface using Apache Spark, which combines ease of use, scalability, and fault-tolerance. This approach allows users to choose between two load distribution methods: a method that creates and manages green threads internally, reducing reliance on external mechanisms; or a method that leverages existing allocators and decouplers to minimize overhead. We evaluate the performance of this interface using two load distribution methods against traditional interfaces on large datasets, and our experimental results demonstrate superior performance under stringent time constraints. Additionally, we showcase the real-world application of this interface in supporting parallel training for a machine learning model. In modeling real-world scenarios as games, considering multiple possible solution types beyond equilibria is crucial. While many practical situations are best captured by discrete games with multiple pure or mixed equilibria, most predictive models are built using continuous games and focus solely on predicting pure equilibria. This study breaks this tunnel vision by introducing a novel approach for predicting both pure and mixed equilibria using a flexible, adaptable framework. This framework, known as Fixed Point Networks (FPN), leverages a variant of the projected gradient descent algorithm and is the basis for a trainable model. In developing FPN, the authors tackle challenges associated with its regression task, which previously lacked clear criteria for optimization. By establishing a mathematical framework for these problems, the authors derive specialized stochastic algorithms for optimizing FPN, leading to superior results in various game simulations and a notable improvement in predicting both pure and mixed equilibria in the game of Three-Player Rock-Paper-Scissors. FPN's success also extends to the problem of predicting pure equilibria in high-dimensional games. This study explores ways to measure exponential causality with precision in noisy situations. Our findings set bounds on how explicit causes can influence an information source, even when that source has a large number of attributes. We apply these bounds to establish strict limitations on an information source being influenced by multiple explicit causes. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that modifies the conventional FDR control strategy by incorporating information about data dependence. Additionally, we develop an assessment tool to quantify the dependence of different variables in various settings, as model-based approaches often break down in real-world applications, including clinical trials and intervention analysis. Our empirical analysis reveals that controlling conditional FDR, factoring in data dependence, significantly reduces the actual FDR rate. This finding motivates the development of a new framework for inferring intervention impact through a combination of FDR and the proposed dependence metric. Our approach is versatile, applicable to diverse intervention models and distributions, and can be adapted for online experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method's performance exceeds that of the unconditional FDR and negative control principle methods in various simulated data scenarios. Lastly, we verify the efficacy of our approach using actual data from a Google-kitted plane study and a NIDDK-funded study, supporting the use of dependence-adjusted FDR control as a reliable tool for inferring intervention impact. Most current action parsing methods are based on a strong assumption that ground truth labels are readily available for training. However, defining comprehensive action categories is often a challenging task as customizing action labels to specific video datasets can be quite laborious. This study addresses the previously neglected but crucial problem of unsupervised action category partitioning from a limited set of action categories. To this end, we propose a novel, unsupervised learning approach for action category partitioning in videos, facilitated by deep neural networks, and can be coupled with existing two-stage action parsing methods without requiring any manual adjustment of action categories. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets (Kinetics-400 and ActivityNet-20) demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in achieving better overall performance and more robust diversity in action categories compared to other competitive methods. Additionally, our method reports a remarkable performance with an inter-ratio of 87.8/94.7 for Part-Arc v2 on ActivityNet v1.3, and an inter-ratio of 83.7/93.7 for Part-Arc v2 on ActivityNet v2 without using external tools. The code for our approach is available at this link: https://github.com/fiveai/SSCAP-Parcing. A related project can be found here: Multi-modal Autonomous Activity Detector. 

For the generation of action category words, we draw inspiration from existing human action datasets and word frequency analyses. Human action datasets, such as the Human Action Bible and Human Action Categorization, provide insights into general human action categories, while statistical word frequency analyses, as found in the Corpus of Historic English, help to identify commonly used action verbs. Once action category words are defined, we employ a clustering-based method to perform unsupervised action category partitioning. Specifically, we use a self-supervised co-occurrence modeling approach to learn the probability distributions of multiple dense temporal segments in videos. Then, we leverage a neural network to derive a compact and structured partition of action categories from these learned probability distributions, where the partition size is equal to the predefined number of action categories. Notably, this partitioning method can be coupled with existing action parsing methods without modifying the predefined action categories. As a result, the proposed self-supervised action partitioning method can be seamlessly integrated with the high-performance two-stage action parsing method Part-Arc v2, where it improves the overall performance with an inter-ratio of 87.7/94.7 for ActivityNet v1.3 and 83.7/93.7

Following the launch of EXOPLINES, several line lists were created and uploaded, including the LUXPOP line list for SiO, and the HARPS-N solar-irradiated exoplanet line list containing 25 molecules, which was generated using the VRT program. These line lists, along with the repository, aim to support the development of modeling and observational studies for giant exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. A demonstration of the potential impact of ExoPlines on future research was performed during the selection process of the line list for the James Webb Space Telescope's General Observer Program, where Harps-N line list was chosen as one of the three finalists.

Answer set programming has reached a level of maturity that enables it to be applied in a broad range of domains including real-world settings. Yet, the existing formalizations for many practical problems lack precision or else rely on incomplete solutions. An essential aspect of addressing this issue involves developing efficient and accurate implementations. This work establishes a new perspective on interpreting logic programs by adopting a semantic approach grounded in set theory. This approach serves as a foundation for an improved algorithm to compute answer sets and also facilitates the creation of grounded transformations for ASP solvers. Furthermore, our method allows for an alternative interpretation of programs with variably typed variables. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing solutions in terms of execution speed. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of this technique beyond the scope of this paper. Non-classical properties of quantum systems and their associated quantum resources (QRs) have been exploited for significant enhancements in quantum tasks. In the context of quantum computation, understanding QRs and their behavior under specific conditions is of utmost importance. One such condition is the quantum Fisher information (QFI), which is concerned with the presence of quantum mechanisms (QMs) allowing for the collection and potential exploitation of QRs. This study investigates how QFIs and QMs affect the generation and utilization of QRs prior to a quantum information transfer, essentially providing a theoretical basis for the generation of QRs. Upon deriving a relevant quantity, called quantum superpotential, the research reveals its critical role in modeling the behavior of QFIs and QMs. This approach not only complements existing theories but can also serve as a potential framework for identifying novel mechanisms for the creation and manipulation of QRs. In addition, the results show that QMs and QFIs can be viewed as interconnected components of a larger theoretical framework. This understanding has significant implications for a comprehensive theoretical model incorporating diverse quantum information properties. Such a model could facilitate a deeper analysis of quantum information and its numerous applications. The proposed framework, grounded in Euler-Lagrange equation, can help identify novel mechanisms for generating and utilizing QRs, while also enabling a unified understanding of QFIs and QMs through an integrated theoretical structure. The versatility of this approach is reflected in its applicability to diverse quantum systems, as demonstrated by its analysis of complex systems such as multimode nonlinear cavity and double-slit experiments. This study introduces a novel framework for the creation and exploitation of QRs, while also providing valuable insights into the understanding and development of quantum information and its numerous applications. The approach can serve as a potential tool for quantum computing and other related tasks. One of the significant outcomes of this research is the suggestion that QMs and QFIs form an interconnected and holistic unit, contributing to our understanding of quantum information and its numerous applications. The results of this investigation position the questioned initial principle at the core of quantum information and provide significant implications for quantum computing and other related tasks. The analysis reveals that the presence of QRs, represented by QFIs, necessarily implies the presence of QMs, allowing for the collection and exploitation of QRs. In addition, QMs play a pivotal role in the creation and exploitation of QRs, while the bound relationship between QMs and QFIs forms the core of quantum information and its numerous applications. A new, non-parametric statistical approach focuses on estimating key features of a unknown probability distribution for a finite set of data. By examining the coefficients of a power series that represents the characteristic function of this distribution, this method determines the central moments of the distribution. Furthermore, this technique is expanded to consider cases where the data is subject to errors. The study defines two measures of error, one affecting the probability distribution and the other influencing the data itself, resulting in two corresponding correction methods. By analyzing these two types of errors, the technique is shown to be capable of handling cases of both biased and skewed data. Moreover, when the data is generated from a selection of a larger dataset, the technique is able to estimate the characteristics of the original dataset. The method's performance is evaluated through simulations and is also used in three real-world applications. Lastly, a tool has been developed that enables researchers to use this method to analyze datasets online. This study introduces a method for analyzing non-stationary, multi-dimensional time series that are influenced by specific types of noise. We develop this framework to generalize the findings of Kaufman and Calabrese (2017), who discovered that in a particular setup, performing equal calculations in three dimensions is optimal. Our solution applies to scenarios with "robust-tail" noise and encompasses "long memory" systems. We demonstrate the performance of the new estimator through an analysis of multi-dimensional white noise, fractal noise, and two real-world applications - the financial and electricity markets. Our findings show that the new estimator produces accurate results and is capable of handling up to six dimensions without requiring complex calculations. We further reveal that in some scenarios, our estimator outperances the standard alternatives. We demonstrate the practical utility of our estimator through a real-world example of the financial market of South Korea. Our results show a strong correlation between the properties of the estimator and the characteristics of the financial market. Our work provides a new perspective on the behavior of the financial market and can be applied to other multi-dimensional time series data. We make our code available for other researchers to use. By applying linear duration codes, which combine sparse quantum operators with conventional LDPC codes, it has been demonstrated that quantum LDPC codes can be optimized, resulting in significant reductions of both quantum and classical error rates when subjected to parallel random quantum noise models. Moreover, this study has introduced a novel perspective on quantum LDPC codes, which has further solidified their position as the most versatile quantum error-correcting codes to date. Finally, this work has laid the groundwork for applying classical LDPC code optimization techniques to their quantum counterparts, offering an exciting area for future investigation. This research has been accompanied by the provision of open-source code and corresponding graphical illustrations to facilitate future exploration. The study also speculates on future directions for improving quantum error-correcting codes through LDPC code optimization. In this paper, we explore the concept of a distance-$r$ dominating set in a graph and propose a novel high-performance distributed algorithm for creating a corresponding subset. Unlike traditional set-covering problems, our variant considers faster message exchanges and stricter synchronization in a distributed setting. We establish the equivalence of the concept to a specific type of set-covering problem known as the UAMC problem, and show how solving this problem yields a approximation ratio of $\CalC_{r+1} \ln n$. We provide a distributed solution to the UAMC problem with a significant improvement over existing algorithms, achieving a better approximation ratio in $O(\log^2 n)$ time for large sparse graphs with a high-girth property, thereby resulting in a quality output near optimal. We also apply the technique to create a distributed $r$-distance dominating set, providing an output with a limited increase in size but still outperforming existing solutions with a better approximation ratio in $O(\log n)$ time. We support our claims with comprehensive numerical analysis and graph experiments. Furthermore, we apply the technique to create a distributed algorithm for minimum-weight $r$-distance dominating set in $O(\log^2 n)$ time and provide an energy-efficient solution for wireless sensor networks with significant improvements in performance. Numerical experiments and real experiments on up to $160$ processes are provided to show the technique's effectiveness. We also compare our output with the results of recent centralized algorithms for a distance-1 dominating set in a similar setting. While the technique doesn't apply to the specific problem, it highlights the significant improvements in output quality, in particular with a factor of ratio $O(\log n)$ better than state-of-the-art solutions, thereby nearing optimal output with a limited increase in size. We also provide an extensive test bed and experimentation section to show the technique's effectiveness and robustness in a parallel setting. We support our claims with various numerical experiments and real experiments on large, sparse graphs with a high-girth property, thereby ensuring the technique's distributional efficiency and robustness. We also provide a section on potential extensions with the technique likely applicable to other graph-based problems in a distributed setting. Moreover, our analysis with the technique highlights a new distributed ensemble, thereby contributing to the body of knowledge in graph algorithms with a distributed approach. Finally, our experiments and results demonstrate the significant improvements in output quality, thereby surpassing state-of-the-art algorithms in a distributed setting. We also provide an implementation guide for the technique and support our claims with numerous figures

Recent deep learning methods have significantly elevated the intricacy of neural networks employed in neural rendering, integrating variables such as view, material, and geometry into a unified representation. Central to most neural rendering schemes is the encoding of lighting information, typically approached through traditional pixel basis methods limiting detailed spatial lighting representation. This paper proposes an advanced lighting representation, referred to as Brightness Fields, comprising a patchwork of small, highly detailed lighting patches with spatial coherence. This novel representation, implemented using neural networks, attains a high level of quality, particularly in rendering fine spatial variations in lighting across large scenes. Additionally, the proposed system combines lighting information with scene geometry and material information, thereby unifying the rendering process and eliminating the need for separate lighting maps in fields. This methodology has far-reaching implications, enabling the creation of highly realistic, spatially distinct lighting effects in scenes, even when reference lighting information is limited to a single image, not only accelerating but also simplifying the rendering process. This approach has been extensively tested and demonstrated novel rendering capabilities on a variety of challenging examples, incorporating complex materials, geometry, and lighting effects. Furthermore, the method's adaptability is underscored by its successful application to both synthetic and real-world video and photography domains, effectively augmenting existing rendering techniques with advanced brightness information. This addition has the further result of enabling a seamless transition from neutral rendering approaches to the incorporation of highly realistic, richness and depth in rendering effects. Using the proposed method, the creation of multiple photorealistic rendering effects is shown to be greatly simplified, reducing the complexity of the rendering process. This is because the main challenge in rendering is resolved by the use of the brightness field map, precomputed not through the rendering process but rather through analyzing reference images of the scene. This approach is thus in accordance with the fundamental principle of rendering, namely that rendering = imaging. Analysts of the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) 171-A data set have identified jet-driven piston signatures in the form of rapid loop evolution and rapid changes in loop shape. To observe the associated whistler-mode radio waves, researchers utilized the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) to capture 30-second images of 3.0 GHz and 6.0 GHz loops at 2 s intervals. As these jets moved inward, they caused the loops to appear brighter at the source of the jet and grow more diffuse at the ends of the loop, indicating an increase in emission. Furthermore, researchers have observed the formation of LOFAR bright regions accompanied by rapid changes in EUV-I magnetar field observations and found that the 3.0 GHz and 6.0 GHz radio waves have similar patterns of emission. Two possible explanations for the LoFAR observations exist: the presence of two plasma regions with 100 % electron ionization and neutral gas or semi-turbulent plasma with electron gas ionized at the jet boundary. Researchers also proposed an experiment designed to measure the entanglement present in the entire state vector of a boson sampling device. Reinforcement learning, a method of opting for the optimal course of action by evaluating predicted outcomes, is typically used in scenarios where environments are fully understandable but not always visible. We expand upon this concept by investigating a scenario where environmental perceptions are sometimes blocked. Our study introduces novel architectures for recurrent networks that can adapt to these unpredictable scenarios, focusing specifically on scenarios involving the learning of beliefs about hidden states. We develop three architectures for this scenario: (a) a self-referential recurrent model that directly creates its own predictions about the hidden states; (b) a recurrent network that incorporates an additional 'belief' layer which adjusts according to its own perception of the hidden states; (c) a recurrent network that combines the 'value of being right' with its own perception of the hidden states, through a module called the 'conviction' module. Our investigation of these architectures demonstrates that the 'conviction' module, which relies solely on the model's perception of the hidden states, is capable of achieving the same level of accuracy as the other architectures, in multiple scenarios. Our analysis suggests that the 'conviction' module can be seen as a form of'stochastic mirror' that reflects the uncertainty associated with the hidden states. We discovered that our recurrent architectures are able to learn robust strategies in scenarios involving the generation of epistemic uncertainty, thanks to the use of a precise mathematical analysis of the uncertainty. Our analysis by Backward Induction also confirms that these strategies can be considered optimal. Our study highlights the importance of the 'conviction' module as a potential architectural template for addressing challenging uncertainty problems in machine learning. Our code is publicly available at github.com/constantin-hofs/Recurrent-inferences-in-RL. Our work is also related to theories in cognitive psychology, in particular the theoretical framework of Epistemic-Cognitive Dynamics, which explores the interplay between the mental states of knowledge, uncertainty, and attention. Our investigation sheds light on the practical implications of the ECD framework when individuals are forced to make do with limited perceptual resources. Lastly, our work contributes to the ongoing debate in the field of AI decision-making as to what constitutes reliable conviction for decision-making purposes. Our unique architectures, along with our contributions to the understanding of the interactions between the mental states of knowledge, uncertainty, and attention, open up novel avenues of investigation in both AI and cognitive psychology. Ultimately, our study offers a comprehensive theoretical framework for addressing the wide range of uncertainty problems found in both artificial and human intelligence. This research focuses on the theoretical analysis of stochastic models that describe materials with significant flaws, as modeled by a Schrödinger-type equation. First, we investigate the limit behavior of a family of degenerate elliptic operators under periodic and random conditions. Second, we examine the dynamics of a degenerate diffusion process with periodic jumps. Both problems are closely related, as a stochastic process can be represented by the solution of a degenerate parabolic equation. Therefore, we approach these topics by analyzing various perturbed parabolic equations, taking into account boundary conditions, which in turn enables us to explore the limit set of these degenerate operators. Furthermore, this study involves a detailed investigation of boundary value problems, including a priori estimates, vanishing small parameters, and high-frequency perturbations. Ultimately, we use this analysis to determine the limit operator in homogenization theories for both elliptic and parabolic equations, as well as stochastic models. A significant aspect of this research is the role that boundary node problems play in the limit operator, which is particularly important in stochastic models with periodic and random jumps. Furthermore, this study has a range of practical applications, including a mathematical model for a biological system with fast and slow components. In this case, the limit behavior can be understood by analyzing node problems at the singular point of the model. Additionally, this research is relevant to a variety of physical systems that can be modeled using relaxation models, including systems with periodic and random imperfections. In these cases, the node problems play a crucial role in the limit behavior, which in turn enables scientists to observe new physical effects at the microscopic level through numerical simulations. For instance, this research confirms that random imperfections may reduce the strength of fluctuation effects, which is relevant to experimental studies in the field of superconductivity. Finally, this study is related to a mathematical model for the behavior of particles in a system with periodic walls, where the limit behavior can be understood by analyzing node problems at the periodic boundaries. In this case, the limit behavior is understood by averaging the boundary conditions of node problems along the periodic cycle. Our research involved employing the linear organizational form of correlated wave function (LOCV) to study the effect of intense magnetic fields on diamond and silicon dioxides' nuclear substances. We utilized the Jastrow-type ansatz for factorized ground state of correlated electrons, and our findings indicate that the second-order correction to the energy is sufficiently small compared to the ground state energy for both diamond and silicon dioxides. Consequently, the ground state energy's first-order approximation is adequate. Additionally, in the presence of intense magnetic fields, the nuclear substance of both diamond and silicon dioxides exhibits gradual increases. Furthermore, the increases are directly proportional to the strength of the magnetic fields, the ground state energy, and the spin parameter, while being inversely proportional to the kinetic energy parameter. We observed that the rates of the increases in the nuclear substance are substantially lower in silicon dioxide than in diamond. Finally, we analyzed the effects of electron-electron correlations on the nuclear substance by comparing the calculations from the LOCV approach with those from the local density approximation (LDA) and obtained significantly lesser values in the presence of intense magnetic fields. In particular, the electron-electron correlations give rise to a substantial enhancement in the nuclear substance of diamond and a less pronounced increase in the nuclear substance of silicon dioxide. The computed nuclear substance of diamond and silicon dioxide at specific magnetic field intensities with varying spin parameters was also presented. The computational method employed to determine the organizational form of correlated wave function (LOCV) and the specified results provide valuable insights into the effects of strong magnetic fields on the properties of matter. The increasing nuclear substance with magnetic field intensity suggests that the increased spin parameter (gyromagnetic ratio) leads to a more substantial increase in the nuclear substance. The substantial increase in the nuclear substance of diamond and the less pronounced increase in the nuclear substance of silicon dioxide further confirm that the electron-electron correlations play a critical role in determining the properties of systems under intense magnetic fields. The widely used mirror learning in remote educational settings can be vulnerable to information security threats. Recent advancements in secure machine learning have introduced trusted execution environments, providing robust adversarial defense in mirror learning. Nevertheless, current solutions often overlook the communication aspect, which can lead to excessive data exchange and expose sensitive information. We introduce DP-REC, an optimized framework for secure machine learning in remote educational settings, achieving two key goals: first, it reduces data transmission by limiting model exchanges between clients and servers; second, it protects students' and teachers' privacy from the server. DP-REC integrates reversible encryption, noise management, and flexible encryption schemes to achieve these objectives. In line with these requirements, our research focuses on developing a concrete implementation of reversible encryption using LASSO, which is followed by a detailed analysis of noise management and a comprehensive evaluation of DP-REC's effectiveness in achieving these goals. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DP-REC in reducing data transmission by 54%, preventing the server from guessing the label with only a 2% chance, and comparing favorably with the latest secure machine learning frameworks in both goals. Additionally, we evaluate the trade-off between the model accuracy loss and the effectiveness of DP-REC in reducing data transmission and preventing the server's guesswork. The source code of DP-REC is publicly available, and our research is supplemented with in-depth video demonstrations. The framework has potential applications in both educational and general federated learning settings, and we anticipate its extension to other non-educational settings as well. We also compare DP-REC with the latest secure machine learning frameworks, including SecML and FHE, which is another contribution of this research. A comprehensive far-ultraviolet light map has been created by combining data from the far-ultraviolet channel of the Pan-STARRS-5 filter camera located at the Haleakala Observatory across the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga region. This UV image covers 3000 square degrees andencompasses the entire region. Photometric data from the UV image have been analyzed for 300,000 sources with high precision, spanning a range of 1500 to 3200 Angstrom wavelength. In addition, a detailed spectroscopic analysis was conducted on 1500 sources within the region using the HST COS instrument, which revealed the true nature of these sources. These observations have provided new insights into the characteristics of young stars based on their birth place and properties. It's also been discovered that hot stars emit specific chemical signals into their surroundings. This effect is most noticeable in molecular clouds where this signal is absorbed and in turn, influences the observed color and brightness of the stars. This phenomenon of absorption and emission affects a third of the sources in the sample, primarily due to their relatively low temperature. This systematic pattern of absorption and emission has enabled the determination of the overall scale factors for the UV spectral types. Moreover, our dataset has provided key information about the distribution and variation of the UV spectral types across the region. This information has also allowed us to make a precise age chart. To explain a slight disparity between the distribution of B/Y ratios (a result of absorption) and the star cluster ages across the region, we propose that 40% of the stars in the sample have their surface coated with a layer of dust. This effect is found to be prevalent in denser areas. This finding has also shown to have notable implications for our understanding of the star formation process as a whole. It's also been discovered that external layers only affect the environment around very young stars. This precise knowledge of the overall scale factors and distribution of the UV spectral types across the region has also helped researchers study and understand magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and red noise patterns at a local cosmic scale. These patterns of absorption and emission also prove challenging for researchers to accurately map the overall 3D distribution of the stars within the region. This challenge is also compounded by the fact that some of the sources possess planets or are part of binary star systems. Future research could further refine the understanding of the environment and the physics of the stars within the region by incorporating additional data. This could also help researchers quantify the overall scale factors and distribution of the UV spectral types

A table's semantic description is vital in summarizing document content and facilitates understanding, and in large collections of documents, such as databases and archives, identifying the most relevant tables based on content is a key task called table retrieval. We present an advanced table search system that integrates graph neural networks, including a new model, E2EN, which uses learning to map table content and a structured indexing technique that efficiently encodes table content with a simplified graph neural network. Our experiments show that this system surpasses the current best methods in retrieving tables from PDF documents. Additionally, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation to analyze the influence of various factors on table retrieval, and our results indicate that more data and better indexing can significantly improve this task. Our study's findings are expected to open new avenues for improving table search in the future. The code and models for our work are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/uni-rehberg/GNN4TabRetrieval. Malaria elimination initiatives heavily rely on accurate population data coverage to assess risk and create targeted strategies for high-transmission areas. Population distribution is often measured through surveys, but administering these surveys domestically can be a significant financial burden, making external organizations necessary to obtain these vital data points. To address this challenge, our external team alongside the National Institute of Public Health in Mozambique collaborated to develop a cost-effective and efficient population mapping approach. By leveraging international funding, we conducted extensive population surveys across Mozambique, yielding data on 305 million individuals. Following these surveys, we developed and released an open-source platform that uses population data to inform sustainable and efficient population forecasting. Trained local agents can utilize this technology to provide up-to-date population data to the government, ensuring it remains domestic-driven and financially sustainable. As a result, we anticipate reduced external costs associated with conducting and funding these surveys. Furthermore, our approach increases the internal autonomy of the government in data collection, allowing for more effective decision-making and tailored prevention and intervention efforts against malaria transmission. We are now working to integrate our technology with the health sector to assess malaria risk and adjust transmission mitigation strategies accordingly. Given that Mozambique's population data are still in the early stages of development, our approach focuses on cost-efficient methods for continuous data updating and expansion. For instance, utilizing our technology on a single GPS-enabled motorcycle, we can collect data for 80-160 sq km daily, yielding 380,000 to 480,000 individual density estimates per acre. Training a small team of agents can significantly enhance data collection, potentially up to 50 times more efficient. To ensure domestic-driven data collection, we are promoting local training for 30-40 agents, enabling the Mozambique government to collect data independently and efficiently. By doing so, we are creating a network of informed and empowered local agents who are equipped to handle data collection and population forecasting, ultimately benefiting the Mozambique health and malaria elimination efforts. We are currently implementing a network-optimized training program for domestic-driven data collection and population mapping, which is set to enhance data updating and expansion efficiency. By providing agents with data visualization and analysis training, we are empowering them to identify and prioritize areas for targeted data collection and population mapping. Over the past 20 years, the growth in data has outpaced the advancement in processing capacity, resulting in a significant ratio increase by a factor of 25. This surge presents difficulties in data analysis systems that rely on set operations because existing methods employ algorithms with a high false positive rate, which become less efficient as data sets grow larger. As a result, there is a need for new algorithms that minimize false positives, especially in applications that utilize frequent membership queries. We introduce a new collection known as the DP-col, which addresses this issue by leveraging droplet physics and exploiting the relationship between fluid and matter. The DP-col offers an inclusive membership filtering capability and can be utilized as a pre-processing step to mitigate the impact of false positives in data processing applications. Furthermore, the DP-col allows its construction and query operations to be distributed across multiple platforms, which can be utilized for redundancy and fault-tolerance. Our experiments demonstrate significant performance improvement in data processing applications that involve the DP-col, with some exhibiting up to 5 times faster results. Notably, the DP-col has the potential to apply to a broad range of problems, which can significantly benefit from a decrease in false positives. One such example is genomic data processing. Genomic data is typically large in size and frequently subjected to membership queries. By employing the DP-col, we can reduce the false positive rate and, as a result, lower the genomic sequence retrieval time. With modern, high-performance genomic data storage systems, it is now feasible to achieve near-real time retrieval of genomic sequences using the DP-col. This innovation has the potential to significantly accelerate genomic data processing across a variety of crucial applications, such as the computation of the genomic edit distance. We can achieve a substantial speed-up of the genomic edit distance computation using the DP-col, with results showing up to 3 times faster than previously possible. Our experiments also suggest that the DP-col can be applied to other problems, such as the processing of location data in sensor networks and data compression. Our contribution in these areas marks an important step towards developing new algorithms with a low false positive rate, which can lead to a significant improvement in data processing efficiency. Ultimately, the DP-col has the potential to contribute to a more efficient utilization of data processing resources, which can otherwise be overwhelmed by the large amounts of data being created. Our work also raises important implications for research on the emerging trend of edge computing, which aims to minimize data transmission delays by shifting data processing to the edge of the network

However, developing interaction models for highly nonlinear and deformable bodies with complex multi-phase fluid dynamics poses significant challenges. To address these issues, a novel smoothed particle hydrodatics (SPH) framework has been developed, incorporating a multi-scale approach and an enhanced wall boundary condition to simulate turbulent Flows. This multi-body framework allows for the simulation of unique flow behaviors around deformable bodies under diverse boundary conditions, in addition to a novel method for detecting and handling contact between bodies. To mitigate computational expense, a model of homogeneous isotropic turbulence has been developed and integrated into the framework, offering an alternative to simulating turbulent fluid flows. This SPH framework has been successfully applied to the simulation of ocean currents and their impact on a deformable submarine, showcasing its capabilities in multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. Furthermore, this approach has been used in modeling complex wind effects on off-shore turbines, highlighting its potential in simulating turbulent and deformable multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. This work aims to demonstrate the adaptability and versatility of the SPH framework, opening up new possibilities for modeling various engineering applications. In order to create efficient quantum information processors for machine learning, two key algorithms - the Quantum Associative Memory and the Quantum Layered Artificial Neural Network - have been developed and optimized for superconducting quantum devices. These algorithms can function either independently, without needing results comparisons, or by receiving intermediate results and comparing them, and have been optimized for the New QuAntum Inspector (NQi) processor. Our study shows that the optimized Quantum Associative Memory has the same efficiency as its classical equivalent, while the optimized Quantum Layered Artificial Neural Network outperforms its classical version in terms of performance to training ratio, and surpasses the classical machine learning approach in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, the optimized quantum algorithms have been successfully adapted for use in a multi-qubit quantum system, without relying on additional pre-training and initialization procedures. Our findings also reveal that the quantum algorithms perform better as the number of training steps increases, without the need for re-training, and without being affected by noise levels up to a specific limit, but their performance degrades beyond that point. Overall, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of the quantum-classical hybrid machines that can learn and perform automatically. In particular, the proposed quantum-classical hybrid machines have the capacity to overcome some common limitations of classical deep neural networks, such as requiring extensive training and being fragile to thermal noise. Our study sets the ground work for developing efficient quantum information processors for machine learning and related applications. It also opens a new chapter in the development of quantum-classical hybrid machines that can learn and perform automatically. Moreover, the proposed quantum-classical hybrid machines can be easily adapted for use in a multitude of applications, such as drug discovery, astronomy, medicine, chemistry, linguistics, mathematics, economics, finance, logistics, transportation, etc. Our study facilitates a major breakthrough in the field of machine learning and related applications, and it lays the foundation for a new generation of machine learning and quantum computing advancements. In summary, our study reveals that the proposed quantum-classical hybrid machines can efficiently learn and perform a variety of complex tasks and operations. Future studies should focus on developing and adapting the proposed quantum-classical hybrid machines to different application domains. It is also desirable to develop and suggest additional methods for comparing the performance of quantum and classical algorithms in real-world settings. Our study can be easily replicated by researchers who have access to the NQi processor and the necessary software tools and is supported

Developing more natural-sounding text-to-speech (TTS) models is an ongoing priority, particularly in speech synthesis where even minor imperfections can be distracting. Augmentation is being explored as a way to enhance model performance in speech synthesis. This paper presents an innovative application of speech augmentation to the Tunesbench challenge, which involves transforming input audio signals to match designated pitch labels while preserving their timbre. This approach is implemented through an advanced version of the FastPitch model enhanced with a timbre matching module. Key components of the method include a timbre matching loss function and a semi-supervised pitch augmentation technique. The results demonstrate the benefits of timbre-preserving pitch augmentation in speech synthesis, with the augmented dataset resulting in a higher Tunesbench ranking. Specifically, the augmented version achieved 0.848 MOS, a 0.004 point improvement over the standard Tunesbench dataset. This gain is consistent with the findings of previous work using pitch augmentation with a different model. However, when combined with the TimbreTrack dataset, the augmented dataset performance improves to 0.862 MOS, a 0.019 point improvement over the standard Tunesbench dataset. This result reveals that the value of the augmented dataset is even more pronounced when used with a dataset that includes timbre information. Moreover, the results show that the timbre matching loss has a regulatory effect on the pitch augmentation process, reducing its tendency to produce extreme pitch transformations during training. This phenomenon is in contrast to previous studies of pitch augmentation, which identified the following: (1) pitch augmentation can produce high fidelity transformations in both unison and multitone audio signals, (2) pitch augmentation is equivalent in performance to the TimbreTrack dataset, (3) pitch augmentation is shown to generalize to unseen speech for speakers who speak quickly, (4) pitch augmentation is shown to work in combination with the standard Tunesbench dataset as well as a larger, extended version of the standard Tunesbench dataset. All of these findings hold true for speaker speeds of normal speech rate. Finally, the results of the challenge demonstrate that the proposed method is superior to the standard Tunesbench dataset in terms of speech synthesis performance, with the standard Tunesbench dataset ranking 1st out of 7 in the challenge. This paper introduces Hopper, a multi-hop framework for spatiotemporal forecasting that leverages the strength of transformers combined with cyclic constraints. As a novel, highly parallelizable method, Hopper is well-suited for large-scale prediction tasks. We thoroughly evaluate Hopper's performance using two widely used datasets that encompass a range of difficulties. Experimental results demonstrate that Hopper surpasses state-of-the-art performance, achieving significant improvements of up to 20.6% for the sea surface temperature dataset and up to 4.2% for the USCNN dataset. Furthermore, an exploration of the model's parallelizability and scalability is conducted, including a discussion on strategies for enhancing the model's interpretability. As a response to the growing environmental concerns, there is now an increased focus on developing climate models that are both effective and sustainable. In line with this goal, we find that Hopper is not only environmentally friendly but also, in large part, transferable to other prediction tasks, thus reducing the need for new, resource-intensive training. Hopper's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexk41/Hopper. 

Key words: transformer, spatiotemporal forecasting, multi-step prediction, deep learning, energy efficiency. There's no consensus yet on a standard forecasting method among data scientists. This confusion may stem from the vast array of models and techniques available. This paper aims to introduce a group of Bayesian hierarchical linear forecasting models that incorporate key time series characteristics and provide a comprehensive framework for modeling. These models can be thought of as a combination of two primary models: the Bayesian Vector Autoregression model, which establishes a forward-looking relationship between random variables and accounts for their inherent correlations, and the BEAST model, which identifies and prioritizes influential time series. We'll provide a straightforward approach to implementing these models numerically and offer guidance on incorporating additional time series characteristics and dependent noise. We'll also highlight the models' advantages in accurately predicting non-linear patterns and outliers, and illustrate their effectiveness on real-world datasets including airpassengers and shareprice with comparison to popular non-parametric forecasting models like ARIMA and LSTM. Furthermore, we'll show the feasibility of using model selection to determine the optimal forecasting configuration. Lastly, we'll discuss the models' potential applications and expansions in diverse fields. These models can be found in the BayesianForecastingModels package on Python's PyPI. This investigation into planet formation centers on the impact of gas gathering around a pair of massive planets simultaneously. Simulating planet formation using a detailed model, we explore how the unique circumstances of planets developing in tandem affect their long-term growth. Our analysis reveals that when planets form in close proximity to one another in a circular orbit, they eventually reach similar masses at 1000 AU, whether or not they develop in tandem. Notably, when both planets form from the same initial mass range, their combined mass falls within the range of massive planets observed. Conversely, when each planet develops from a wide range of initial masses, only the more massive planet achieves the same level of growth in tandem, indicating that the less massive planet at birth has little influence on their shared disk. When planets form in close proximity to one another in an eccentric orbit, their long-term gas accumulation rates vary, however, and are influenced by this orbital configuration. Our analysis further indicates that when planets develop in tandem, their combined mass pushes the transition from type-I to type-II planetesimal drift further into the planetary system. Finally, when planets form in close proximity to one another in an eccentric orbit, disk evolution, and the spread of surface density (α-disk model), have varying outcomes depending on α and the planets' orbital eccentricity. As a result, when planets form in tandem with α = 10^-3 and 0.1, their orbital separation increases to 100 AU and 20 AU, respectively, before being dispersed. These findings imply that when planets develop in tandem, their long-term growth interacts and is influenced by one another's effects on their shared protoplanetary disk. Additionally, when planets form in close proximity to one another in an eccentric orbit, their concurrent gas gathering around them may be associated with a reduced efficiency in producing massive planets in the outer planets zone and, consequently, fewer giant planets might be produced in the planet population. This could, in turn, contribute to a planet population characterized by the presence of terrestrial planets in particular regions of their orbits (hot super-Earths, warm mini-Neptunes) through core migration, and explaining the formation of massive planets in the outer planets zone through gas giant core instability. This work is part of a larger series of plan formation investigations aimed at simulating the diverse origins of planets in our solar system and other celestial bodies. Theoretical models predict that carbon nanotubes should exhibit conducting properties, but experiments have shown that isolated nanotubes are typically insulating or conducting at extremely low temperatures. By exploring the thermal dependence of conducting films composed of armchair carbon nanotubes, our research aims to understand the relationship between the film's macroscopic properties and the individual nanotubes' electronic behaviors. Our findings demonstrate that the film's conducting properties are influenced by the temperature, suggesting the presence of conducting channels supported by the vibrational movements of the atoms at low temperatures. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the movement of energy through the lattice, known as the Franck-Condon effect, is crucial in explaining the conducting properties of the film, leading to the conclusion that the film's conducting properties are a collective effect resulting from the individual nanotubes' conducting channels being coupled with the vibrational movements of the atoms. This study provides direct visual evidence of conducting channels between adjacent nanotubes, thereby advancing our understanding of the individual carbon nanotubes' electronic properties. By extending the concept of energy transport to the macroscopic level, our research opens up new avenues in the study of the collective electronic properties of conducting nanomaterials. Ultimately, our analysis of the film's conducting properties reveals that the movement of energy through the lattice is a critical factor in understanding the electronic properties of the individual carbon nanotubes and their collective effect on the macroscopic film. Our research sets the stage for exploring other electronic and thermal properties of the collective electronic systems formed from the individual nanomaterials. It is anticipated that the understanding of the intricate relationship between the individual materials' electronic properties and the resulting collective electronic properties of the macroscopic film will lead to novel nanoscale electronic materials and devices. Such an exploration not only contributes to the development of nanoscale electronic materials but also sheds light on the fundamental principles of the movement of energy through the lattice, potentially uncovering unforeseen and intriguing aspects of the Franck-Condon effect. The importance of achieving a thorough understanding of the individual materials' electronic properties and their collective effect on the macroscopic film has far-reaching implications in the context of the bottom-up assembly of nanoscale electronic materials and devices. Such an exploration may very well uncover novel phenomena associated with the movement of energy through the lattice, thereby advancing our understanding of the individual materials and their collective effect on the macroscopic film. Ultimately, our analysis of the film's conducting properties is a crucial step towards uncovering the intricate relationship between the individual nanotubes and their collective effect

In many scientific fields including data mining, computer science, engineering, and physics, clustering is a crucial task. The underlying principle of clustering is to group data objects based on their similarity. Various fuzzy clustering algorithms have been developed to tackle noise and group similar objects together. The selection of meaningful clusters depends on the choice of weights assigned to similar features. There are two primary approaches for weight determination: variable weighting and equal weighting. The variable weighting approach is self-learning and dynamically determines the weights based on the cluster variance. This research introduces a new method, entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (EFWFKM), which combines self-learning and dynamic weight adaptation with the fuzzy k-means algorithm. The EFWFKM method works by relabeling features using entropy to identify the optimal number of clusters. The real-world performance of EFWFKM was evaluated using equal weighted fuzzy k-means (EFK) and variable weighted fuzzy k-means (VFK) for comparison. The results show that EFWFKM surpasses EFK and VFK in terms of robustness and adaptability. The method has been successfully applied to diagnose acute leukemia using equal weighted fuzzy k-means (EFK) and variable weighted fuzzy k-means (VFK) for comparison. The results of the analysis using EFWFKM, EFK, and VFK are consistent with the ground-truth data provided by the University of California, Santa Barbara. The data include 479 samples with 799 features from three types of leukemia: acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphatic leukemia (ALL), and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). The performance of the three algorithms was evaluated using the Tau index, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and Average Shift Measure (AASM) as the key performance metrics. The results show that AML and ALL samples have the highest similarity, followed by CML samples. The performance of the three algorithms was evaluated using real-world datasets including cancer cell data, gene expression datasets, and high-dimensional data. The results show that EFWFK is the best performer in terms of accuracy, robustness, and adaptability. The code for EFWFK is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AhsanulHaq/Entropy-driven-Variable-Feature-Weighted-Fuzzy-k-Means. In the context of deep learning, a topic's transferability refers to how well information is retained across a series of models. Research has revealed two apparent truths: initially, highly similar models exhibit high transferability; and, secondly, compact models tend to have higher transferability. These findings may seem significant, however our research shows they are built on flawed foundations. Through an in-depth analysis of a representation learning challenge, we determined these theories are incorrect and instead discovered the transferability of models is heavily influenced by the quality of the models' representations, which can be better captured by measuring the challenge's data independence using the Mean Squared Cross Correlation. Conversely, the theories are supported by data independence that diminishes over time. Furthermore, using the MSCC allows us to predict the challenge's data independence and provides new insights into the nature of transferability, leading to the development of an innovative method for creating compact models that has proven successful in tasks such as low-shot learning in NLP and Computer Vision. This method has achieved results comparable to other model pruning techniques in several areas and significantly outperformed other methods in others. Moreover, as expected, the MSCC effectively captures the topic's data independence and accurately reflects the transferability of models. Finally, an examination of the challenge's data independence through an entropic lens has allowed us to establish a link between transferability and the challenge's data independence time evolution, thus providing a comprehensive understanding of the topic's transferability. In recent years, AI models have begun to appear in real-world healthcare settings, initially as supplementary tools for healthcare professionals. The integration of these models however comes with challenges, notably a lack of understanding of how they will perform in actual situations and how to evaluate their performance accurately when there is a significant difference between the data used to train and test these models. To address these concerns, we have developed and tested a novel method for evaluating the performance of AI models trained on data that may not accurately represent real-world situations. The conformal prediction framework, a formal method for evaluating predictive models, is often used in practical scenarios due to its ability to be easily customized; however, this traditional framework requires the use of identical training and testing data - a constraint that does not apply to our proposed method. The proposed method is based on a new framework, one that only leverages data from the training set, allowing for direct and intuitive interpretation of the results. The method is then tested on trained models in two distinct healthcare scenarios and the ability to estimate performance in real-world situations is compared with traditional evaluation methods for predictive models. The results show that our proposed method achieves significantly better accuracy and stronger generalization of the model's performance in real-world situations for AI models in healthcare settings. The full source code for this study is publicly available on a collaborative platform. The study also includes a accompanying paper on a related topic that provides further detail on the importance of accurate evaluation of the models performance in real-world situations and offers a relevant dataset for researchers working with deep learning models in healthcare. The dataset includes a collection of 200,000 images representing two distinct healthcare conditions and is intended to support research in healthcare analytics. Molecular dynamics simulations, used extensively for predicting properties, require task-specific setups that involve choosing between various options, such as representation, force fields, and sampling techniques. One critical decision is representing the DNA's solid support, with models implying different physical interactions for the DNA chain ends. We developed a new, mathematically rigorous way to model the interaction between the DNA and its solid support, drawing from theoretical concepts of flexible interfaces and rigid foundations. This support model influences non-bonded interactions, thus affecting the dynamics of the DNA chain ends. We tested our model with two DNA structures, a tetranucleotide dimer and a 20-base pair fragment, examining the effect of different representations and force fields on their conformational dynamics. We found that representing the support as a rigid foundation enhances the discovery of low-energy states in molecular systems. This advancement is expected to have a significant impact on the simulation of large, biological systems. We also suggest that representing the support as a surface with flexible properties, such as a flexible foundation, can help maintain the balance between energetic and entropic forces in system design. This study provides a framework for choosing the most suitable representation and force fields for exploring the conformational dynamics of DNA and similar polymers. We apply this framework to the problem of designing sequences with selected properties, such as a non-branching sequence or a sequence with a specific melting temperature. We used the flexible foundation model to develop a sequence design method based on the concept of return path free energy (RPF energy). The RPF energy is a family of free energy surfaces that represents the DNA's conformational space and includes all low-energy states in the thermal sample. This sequence design method is general and can be applied to any system for which thermodynamic properties are easily calculated at zero pressure. We demonstrate its application in the simulation of DNA systems. The use of the rigid foundation model in the DNA/titania system enables the calculation of its mechanical properties, such as its Young's modulus. We re-interpret the results of the mechanical properties measurement of a similar system, such as the DNA/nanoclay, in terms of the weak flexibility model. This system is expected to have a significant impact on the simulation of materials with polymers, such as the calculation of mechanical properties, for example, yield strength, for systems in which the conformational dynamics is important for their behavior in thermal environments. Finally, the concepts developed in this study are applied to the simulation of cell biology systems, such as the simulation of actin

The Active Number Compression method, developed as an efficient entropy encoding technique, takes advantage of intra-frame correlations in video and color data, leveraging local contexts to reduce bit rates. Similar to other context-based compressors, its performance heavily relies on well-chosen codebook entries. However, existing research has failed to thoroughly examine the characteristics of local patterns. In response, our study investigates the properties of local patterns by analyzing the one-bit decisions made during the ANS encoding process. Our experimental results reveal that these decisions exhibit distinct non-stationary patterns. Consequently, we have proposed a novel approach to dynamic codebook adjustment, aimed at improving the effectiveness of local pattern representation. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach can significantly enhance the quality of compressed images, particularly in regions with intricate details. The impact of this improvement is more pronounced in high-compression settings. In specific instances, our method has achieved a 0.3 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) improvement over standard entropy encoding under an extremely low bit rate of 20.5 bits/pixel, resulting in a corresponding 0.3 dB loss in image quality. Our research suggests that local patterns can serve as reliable indicators of image quality, enabling developers to tailor their applications and tailor their applications accordingly. With this setup, it is possible to generate results that closely mirror our studies under stringent bit rate constraints, ultimately leading to improved bit rate reductions in real-world applications. This project's underlying philosophy is rooted in the early 19th century publication 'Institutiones Calculi Differentialis' by Augustin Grassmann. Our work differs from the approach presented in his work, which involves a contrasting combinatorial and algebraic viewpoint that we find highly innovative and versatile. This result generalizes a previous finding from Jost and Langforst for the case of negative curvature (k<=0). For the case of a square metric on a torus, we demonstrate that a harmonic map from this surface to another torus with a hyperbolic metric does not always exist. However, we show that in situations where this map does exist, the harmonic function on the boundary remains consistent with the original metric, leading to a harmonic branched cover from the original surface to the target surface. This harmonic branched cover leads to a conformal map from the original surface to a Riemann surface of genus one, with values in the group of real numbers. This values form a Malcev neighborhood of the original uniformization map from the original surface to a hyperbolic surface. This result, in combination with previous findings from Kahn and Wood, leads to a formula for the homotopy invariance theorem for harmonic functions on boundaries of surfaces with hyperbolic metrics, the case of negative curvature having been solved by the second author in a previous study. This homotopy invariance theorem, in combination with findings from Dubrode and the first author on harmonic functions on boundaries of surfaces with hyperbolic metrics and mild obstacles, leads to a new result on the homotopy invariance theorem for the case of positive curvature (k<8). Notably, our study discovered that a specific mechanism involving the resonance of Polder interactions and the conversion of plasma waves can trigger the release of intense X-ray beams. Our research, however, indicated that a plasma wave cannot be maintained in the absence of a critical residual background magnetic field. This study explores the conversion of data formatted according to RDF standards
from a relational database management system to RDF, with a focus on incorporating
shape expressions to ensure data integrity during the conversion process. The research
evaluates common data integrity constraints in relational databases and discusses their
corresponding representations within the RDF data model. Furthermore, the study introduces
a shape expression framework that formalizes this mapping, and then examines how this
constrained conversions affect query results, using the RDF query language SPARQL. The
research also presents an approach to partially constraining an RDF shape expression and
outlines a method for incorporating this constraint into an SPARQL query, resulting in a
query that only yields results conforming to the specified constraint. The conversion of
relational data to RDF, specifically when enforced by data constraints, is an area with few
established guidelines, making this research a significant contribution to the scientific community. The analysis revealed notable differences in query results, with some queries having up to a 21 times greater number of results when enforced by data constraints.
