In the machine learning field, few-example analysis is a significant challenge, largely due to the difficulty in acquiring labeled data. We explore the possibility of leveraging pre-trained language models to conduct thorough analyses using minimal data examples, without requiring additional annotations. Our experiment involves using the BERT model to perform causal analysis, and our results demonstrate promising outcomes. Our innovative method allows the model to perform few-example analysis by incorporating three key components: 1) utilizing natural language inference to identify relevant knowledge and incorporate unmonitored data; 2) inferring analysis results from few data examples by generating explanation-based representations; 3) iteratively refining model performance via explanation-based representation and incorporating unmonitored data. Our approach significantly improves causal analysis performance, especially with limited data, and we found that through self-supervised learning, our method can generalize to out-of-distribution causes, even with no training on a particular cause class. Our research reveals the potential of utilizing pre-trained language models to conduct thorough analyses using minimal data examples, and paves the way for future research to tackle the few-example analysis challenge. Our code is publicly available at github.com/ranqiu/UEF. Furthermore, the causal analysis dataset we developed is also publicly available at uiqc.stanford.edu/fewexample-c4. Additionally, the data used in our research, including link prediction and explanation-based representation datasets, is also publicly available at uiqc.stanford.edu/fewexample-link-prediction-and-explanation. According to our results, our method outperforms state-of-the-art models, including the proven-link predictor WN18RR, ELMo, BERT, and Alon's Causal Discovery Algorithm. Our research reveals the potential for large language models to conduct thorough analyses using minimal data examples, and our findings could contribute to various real-world applications, such as medicine, astronomy, computer vision, and others. Our research also has far-reaching implications and could potentially lead to breakthroughs in data-efficient optimization of both computer vision and machine learning models, and may even open up opportunities for leveraging large language models in various machine learning tasks through the development of new interfaces. To enhance screen reader accessibility, inverse text standardization is a crucial process of converting normalized text back into its original, readable form. This is typically applied to standardized text obtained through automatic identification processes, such as OCR or speech recognition. The quality of inverse text standardization directly impacts the accessibility of the resulting text, prompting the development of various methods and algorithms. Despite these efforts, significant room for improvement remains, particularly in areas where conventional training data may not be sufficient. To address this limitation, we investigated the integration of data enhancement techniques, which allow for the creation of new, customized training data tailored to specific tasks. By applying this approach to a state-of-the-art neural network model, we were able to achieve notable performance enhancements, both in terms of overall accuracy and, more significantly, our ability to maintain correct predictions across the full spectrum of possible outputs. Our improved framework has been successfully applied to a variety of real-world applications, including a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of speech-to-text services for users of accessibility features in Google Chrome. Our research provides valuable insights and methodologies for the development of other accessibility projects in a similar domain. The code and associated models for our study are publicly available at https://github.com/mattkoe/ITS. Our model, which has been integrated into the Google Chrome browser for enhanced screen reader accessibility, can be accessed via chrome.google.com/accessibility/aidassistant. An associated demo illustrating the importance of our proposed data enhancement approach can be found at https://mattkoe.github.io/ITS-data-enhancement. Furthermore, we have successfully applied the concepts underlying our model to significant real-world applications, including the creation of a neural network capable of predicting the emotional impact of audio materials for users of Google Chrome's accessibility features at https://github.com/googleaudio/EmoWise. To the best of our knowledge, our model represents a pioneering effort in this domain and has yielded impressive results in a wide array of practical situations. Ultimately, our research has been motivated by our fundamental belief in the importance of accessibility and digital inclusivity, which we hope our contributions and insights may inspire in the readership of this community. The presented model serves as an initial step towards the development of highly robust, sophisticated models for real-world applications, even in cases where the available training data may be limited or characterized by exceptional variability. This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue

specific attention to the operator's isoperimetric nature. In addition, a 
sharp inequality is also provided in terms of the volume and surface area. 
Previous research by Frank and Heidenreich was crucial in achieving these 
results, which further established the isoperimetric nature of the first 
eigenvalue under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. Here, a more 
general and challenging scenario of Robin boundary conditions was selected, 
as it presents a condition of sign indefiniteness. To resolve this issue, a 
careful examination of the limit of the exterior (or exterior part) of the 
given open set was necessary. Furthermore, the problem was complex due to the 
lack of knowledge about the isoperimetric nature of the first eigenvalue. 
Therefore, a crucial step involved proving the isoperimetric nature of the 
first eigenvalue, which was, in turn, essential for obtaining the sharpness of 
the inequality. Another contribution of this research lies in the new asymptotic 
behavior near the ball and the comparison with the classical Faber-Krahn inequality. 
Finally, a method involving the Euler-Lagrange equation and a suitable constant 
method was utilized to resolve the problem.

Our research reveals that interactions diminish one-dimensional non-Hermitian point-gap topology and create topological features along resonant interactions, including extended edge states, in addition to analyzing the associated Hamiltonians of the system using the Landau theory of phase transitions. gender, and attitude. Although prior research focused on producing realistic

on the naturalness of synthetic speech using the mean opinion score (MOS) 
as a measure. We reveal a significant interaction effect between trait pairs

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become the preferred choice for controlling complex systems due to their flexibility and ability to learn from experience. However, their reliance on a broad understanding of system behavior leaves them susceptible to unpredictable failures in critical applications like autonomous vehicles. Despite this vulnerability, there is currently no model-driven approach that can teach DNN-based controllers how to adapt to unexpected disruptions during operation. This paper presents a new method called RESCUE, designed to enhance the resilience of DNN controllers by integrating a model of the system into a policy-learning process. This model provides a theoretical framework for determining the controller's parameters and can be used to identify and prioritize potential system failure modes. By simulating failures and estimating the resulting system state, RESCUE can generate a range of hypothetical failure modes. During training, the controller is challenged with these hypothetical failures, calculated using a combination of the model and a measure of desired resilience. This approach prioritizes the most severe failure modes, enabling the controller to adapt to new failure modes as it becomes available. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of RESCUE in controlling two complex systems, including an unsealed fueling system and a twin-jet aircraft. This work marks a significant step towards improving the resilience of DNN-based controllers through a model-driven policy-learning approach. The proposed method can be used in various complex control applications, including those that involve human risk-takers, as well as in systems with multiple controllers. However, the model used in RESCUE requires significant system knowledge and may not be able to identify all potential failure modes, especially subtle ones. Future work aims to develop an enhanced version of RESCUE that can also identify and prioritize system failure modes that are not anticipated by the model. This requires a deeper understanding of the relationship between model confidence and actual system failure modes, as well as the development of a method to teach the DNN controller how to adapt to unexpected failure modes not predicted by the model. The proposed enhancement aims to ensure that the controller is prepared for unexpected failure modes, enabling it to safely navigate uncharted system behavior. By integrating failure mode identification and controller adaptation, RESCUE can teach the controller how to adapt to unexpected failure modes not predicted by the model, representing a significant improvement in system reliability. In deep learning, especially in audio applications such as speech recognition and sound pattern learning, deep neural networks are increasingly used. However, these networks typically operate within real-valued domains. Therefore, it's necessary to determine whether complex-valued networks, which better model some audio characteristics, can be transformed into equivalent real-valued ones. This paper introduces a new concept called co-domain equivalence, which means two networks, one complex-valued and the other real-valued, yield the same output for the same input. By restricting the complex-valued network to output within a specific range, we can ensure its co-domain equivalence to a real-valued network. This idea is rooted in complex-valued arithmetic. We can implement this concept using a simple function after verifying its presence in deep learning systems. This paper discusses the co-domain equivalence in deep learning and verifies its relevance to audio applications. Additionally, we provide evidence that this equivalence is useful in audio tasks by conducting experiments on two audio datasets. The results show that two complex-valued and real-valued networks with restricted co-domains exhibit similar performance on speech recognition and sound pattern learning tasks. This finding implies that using complex-valued networks is unnecessary as long as we can ensure the co-domain equivalence in real-valued networks. Moreover, we found that using complex-valued networks can also lead to overfitting, which may hinder performance. Producing full-sky cosmic microwave background (CMB) maps is an essential task that has critical applications for studying cosmology and galaxy/AGN interactions. These maps are used to analyze CMB data from observations, forecast future projects, and generate simulated data. We employed the XCAM code to create full-sky CMB job lists for three specific purposes: studying lensing effects, simulation, and data analysis. To achieve high accuracy in estimating B-mode polarization through gravitational lensing effects, it's necessary to generate high-order job lists for a large number of pixels. This requires computing the square of polarization angles and a curvature matrix for each pixel, a computationally demanding task. We also generated full-sky maps of lensing effects and temperature, used to analyze Planck data and forecast future projects like LiteBIRD and Euclid, as well as simulated data for testing delensing techniques and studying galaxy/AGN interactions. These full-sky maps are based on the SMICA map, which incorporates foreground removal via multi-frequency cleaning. We selected a maximum probability sky to minimize computational effects, as in Euclid's foreground cleaning code, to bypass problems with map cleaning. We generated 102 job lists for polarization and 34 for temperature, each containing pixel-specific curvature information for computational efficiency. Curvature matrices are stored in file headers, which also indicate the SMICA map used for processing, a crucial detail for analyzing results. We presented our full-sky job lists, available online, and confirmed their accuracy by studying the properties of curvature matrices. These lists have been integrated into the Cosmological Simulation Package (CSPSID) code, which generates cosmic microwave background (CMB) job lists for analysis and simulation purposes. Natural language instructions used in reinforcement learning often contain ambiguities stemming from word meanings and sentence structure. We explore methods to mitigate interpretation uncertainty through reinforcement learning techniques. Initially, we develop a technique to isolate interpretation ambiguity by learning a task-neutral vector representing a specific instruction and its desired reward, with the understanding that this vector itself may be open to interpretation. We demonstrate that constraining the task-neutral vector within a predefined boundary yields a reliable and robust indicator for reinforcement learning. We apply this approach to the training of goal-conditioned reinforcement learning agents, using the instruction as both environment feedback and reward signal. We present a novel evaluation technique to assess agent performance on instructions with varying levels of ambiguity, and show that agents trained using the proposed method achieve more consistent performance across diverse instructions, outperforming those trained without the proposed method. This research contributes to overcoming interpretation ambiguities in through reinforcement learning, making task implementation via natural language instructions both more autonomous and versatile. An investigation of the nanodots' electronic properties via conductive atomic force microscopy confirmed that their conductance patterns are consistent with the presence of Sc2TbN@C80 molecular nanodots, and the observed changes in morphology at varying temperatures can be attributed to the flexibility of the molecules' shell structure. The Internet of Things, comprising of various devices like sensors, is part of the larger Internet, consisting of a mass of connections, allowing these items to be in constant communication. A key requirement for IoT cryptography is for encryption methods to support low energy usage, minimal energy consumption, and limited computational requirements. 

Cryptographic algorithms used in the IoT typically face three principal challenges: first, the need to minimize computational effort; second, the need to be energy-efficient; third, the need to prevent data theft during transmissions, known as side-channel attacks. 

A specific issue within the IoT is a potential side-channel attack called the Low Energy Critical Application (LECA) problem, occurring when a device sends a data packet but provides an unauthorized party with information about the device's internal processes, often through additional data packets sent as part of the communication process. 

A recent study on LECA attacks has focused its efforts on lightweight algorithms such as the Light Light Weight Cryptography (LLWC) and the Low Power Data Encryption (LPDE) algorithms. 

Performance analysis of the LLWC algorithms under different conditions using the AVISCAR evaluation framework shows that out of seven evaluated algorithms only one is considered secure against LECA attacks and meets the required speed and energy efficiency standards.

Letifos performance analysis under various conditions using the AVISCAR framework shows that this algorithm only requires 55-65 million cycles and 2.8-3.4 milliwatts of energy to complete an encryption or decryption transaction, and offers a secure option for IoT applications.

Researchers are highly enthusiastic about the future of quantum computing. A promising approach called the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) has shown great potential in near-term computing for molecular ground state calculations. The main challenge with current VQE implementations is error accumulation due to repeated measurements, which restricts its efficiency. Our innovative adaptive VQE (AVQE) tackles this limitation by dynamically adjusting circuit depth based on excitation levels after each evaluation, thereby optimizing circuit complexity and reducing circuit length, without compromising circuit accuracy. Through simulation studies, we observed significant reductions in circuit length, averaging around 30%, at varying excitation levels. Furthermore, we reduced circuit depth by at least an average of 51(± 21%) in homogenous Simon's problem variants. Our prototype implementation based on IBM quantum experience shows great promise and we believe our approach has broad applicability to various quantum algorithms. Our results indicate that the AVQE protocol is an effective strategy to mitigate measurement errors and make the VQE more suitable for near-term computing applications. Two pivotal signs of inflationary cosmology are extremely high-frequency gravitational waves and cosmic density fluctuations. Gravitational waves leave an imprint on gravitational wave frequencies and amplitudes in the early universe, while the cosmic density fluctuations are observed in large-scale cosmic structures and the cosmic microwave background. A problem arises when interpreting LIGO-Virgo and Planck data because the large-scale structures are dominated by a background from inflationary gravitational waves which is much larger than the stochastic primary gravitational waves expected from inflation. A similar issue occurs when trying to estimate the Hubble constant from low-l BAO data due to inflationary gravitational waves. Recently, the NANOGrav data released provided further evidence for inflationary gravitational waves, further solidifying the problem. A possible solution is to look for direct signs of inflation such as non-Gaussianity in the cosmic microwave background data or models that postulate a transition from inflationary to a secondary gravitational wave background. If this transition occurs at the GUT scale it could provide an alternative explanation for the 1.8d frequency and amplitude of the NANOGrav foreground also resolving the tension between strong first-order cosmological principles and the NANOGrav data. A similar effect of "rigid amplification" of gravitational waves also occurs in models where gravitational wave production during inflation is not the primary source and rather the primordial stochastic gravitational waves are amplified by a "cosmic foreground" within the sensitivity range of the NANOGrav collaboration. Radiation from new light species or cosmic strings could serve as this "cosmic foreground" which amplifies the primordial gravitational waves. A new model extending the standard model of particle physics by including a "cosmic string" network as the "cosmic foreground" which amplifies the primordial gravitational waves is also presented in this study. This "cosmic string" model can serve as an extension of the standard model of particle physics and is connected to the standard model through a "Higgs portal" interaction. This model along with the "rigid-amplified gravitational wave backdrop from inflation" provides a new and significant constraint on the primordial gravitational waves and the "Higgs portal" interaction, specifically the model and constraints are discussed in relation to the NANOGrav data and the 2020 Planck data release on the tensor-to-scalar ratio. A new approach to cosmological modeling which correctly predicts the large-scale cosmic density fluctuations and the cosmic microwave background data including the primordial gravitational waves is proposed in this study. Most effective approaches train these models together from large amounts of labeled data, a costly and complex process. Inspired by the efficiency of the autoencoder, we propose a simplified and efficient unsupervised framework in this paper that separates the two models and eliminates the need for aligned data, reducing both costs. Additionally, we present a new acoustic model formula that simplifies the acoustic component and makes the system more feasible. Experimental results on a Chinese dataset reveal a high level of speech quality and significantly lower computation requirements. Furthermore, we achieve quality comparable to the current state-of-the-art using a training dataset size of 12.6 GB, while the next model paper requires 5 TB of aligned data. Multi-objective energy-related optimization problems often involve both continuous and discrete variables with constraints that cannot be easily expressed in a quadratic form. This makes it difficult to use approximate linear or quadratic approximations, necessitating the utilization of non-convex models, which typically lack efficient algorithms for multi-objective optimization. In such scenarios, multi-criteria branch and bound methods present themselves as a promising strategy. However, their effectiveness in solving real-world problems is often hindered by issues like excessive computational complexity in full branch and bound processes and inadequate convergence in approximation-based methods. In response, this paper presents an innovative approach that integrates NSGA-II into multi-criteria branch and bound algorithms for efficient problem solving. In order to minimize computational overhead, population-driven bounds and efficiency metrics for approximation-based iterations are implemented. This improved algorithm is then tested on a complex energy optimization problem involving a multi-story building and a micro-community in a desert environment subject to multiple constraints, including weather and energy distribution. Results demonstrate that this method can successfully tackle demanding MO MINLBO challenges, including those with non-convex and non-smooth objective functions, while yielding high-quality Pareto front solutions. This method is implemented in a publicly available open-source software framework. Our numerical experiments reveal that this novel strategy outperforms conventional single objective optimization algorithms in terms of Pareto optimal solutions, while also significantly reducing computational complexity through population-driven bounds and efficiency metrics for approximation-based iterations. Further research is recommended to enhance the scalability of this method to even more complex optimization challenges across a broader range of applications. This work has the potential to significantly contribute to the advancement of multi-objective energy optimization algorithms in the field of building energy recovery. Its applications and implications extend beyond the scope of this specific paper, however further research is needed to expand its reach to other domains and use cases. In this study, traditional Lie theory is reinterpreted through the lens of synthetic differential geometry, offering a deeper understanding of classical concepts. Specifically, this research explores the generalization of Lie groups, Lie groupoids, pseudogroups, and local Lie groups within the framework of synthetic geometry. We find that in this context, linked Lie groupoids are inherently linked and complete. It is also demonstrated that1.1: links between two groupoids exist if and only if their path prolongations are equivalent; and 2.2: local Lie groups are fully equivalent to their path prolongations. This research combines elements of differential geometry and algebraic topology with the synthetic approach to differential geometry developed by Kock and the uniform approach by Spivak, while building upon the foundation of a sheaf-theoretic approach by Berline and Serre. A critical conceptual layer of this work involves the use of group-valued functors on the sheaf category, treated as a category with morphisms defined by étale maps. Following the initial chapters on sheaf foundations and geometry, the later chapters delve into the application of product sheaves to address these questions. It is shown that1.1: links between two groupoids exist if and only if their product sheaf extensions are equivalent; and 2.2: local Lie groups are fully equivalent to their product sheaf extensions. It is hoped that this new perspective on linked Lie groupoids may lay groundwork for further research in the future. It is also demonstrated that1.1: links between two groupoids are inherently connected; and 2.2: local Lie groups are fully complete. This is done by showing that1.1: links between two groupoids are equivalent to germs at a 2-point set; and 2.2: local Lie groups are fully equivalent to germs at a 2-point set. It is also observed that the sheaf of 2-point germs is a formal sheaf, and that the sheaf of semicharacteristic germs is a formal sheaf as well, although the former has a formal subsheaf that is integral, while the latter does not. This sheaf-theoretic interpretation of local Lie groups and groupoids offers a connection to formal schemes in algebraic geometry, and may hold potential for further advancements in the future. Various fields in life sciences rely heavily on computational methods such as modeling, simulations, and analysis. Although numerous databases provide access to relevant data, user interfaces typically consist of basic web search tools and crude query builders, hindering broad user engagement. As a result, users may prefer to manually input data, even if it leads to errors, or create their own datasets from scratch. Furthermore, the need for significant data downloading and manual management often deters individuals. To address these issues, we propose a cutting-edge cyberinfrastructure portal that enables users to easily input and format relevant data, facilitating data exchange between users, biomedical databases, and computational tools. Our portal, designed for pharmacokinetic parameter analysis, allows users to analyze simulation results, make comparisons across groups, calculate statistical values, and publish studies with interactive visualizations. By providing an intuitive and in-depth understanding of computation is beneficial. Our research focuses on developing an innovative cyberinfrastructure to enhance user experience and facilitate data exchange between various biomolecular simulation and analysis tools, databases, and visualization platforms. As an example of the potential of this cyberinfrastructure, we show that it is now possible to easily run extremely computationally intensive analyses, such as the automatic calculation of 100,000+ structures for protein-ligand systems using evolutionary optimization. This research highlights the importance of designing cyberphysical systems and interfaces that facilitate data exchange, computation, and collaboration among users, researchers, and analysis/visualization tools. In the future, we plan to expand our cyberinfrastructure to include more bioinformatics tools, databases, and analysis/visualization platforms, providing a comprehensive platform for the next-generation of bioinformaticists and life science researchers to facilitate efficient and in-depth explorations of systems biology, the functions of biomolecules, and associated events. Our cyberphysical platform is available online at http://cmodeller.cs.uow.edu.au, http://analysedatabase.cs.uow.edu.au, http://analysedisplay.cs.uow.edu.au. Strengthened by the integration of visual imagery, multimodal representation learning has become a top priority in the development of multilingual models capable of understanding language preferences.  Despite significant progress in multilingual sentiment analysis, particularly in terms of identifying sentiment aspects and sentiment labels, there is still a significant knowledge gap regarding the extraction of underlying emotions associated with those sentiment aspects.  To bridge this knowledge gap, we developed a novel approach to extracting underlying emotions from text images or visual descriptions.  This involved a novel contrastive pre-training method that utilizes both positive and negative guidance to develop a sensitive emotion extractor that can accurately operate in low-resolution multimodal environments.  By pre-training the emotion extractor with a contrastive learning method, we can effectively train the emotion extractor to ignore irrelevant text descriptions and focus only on the underlying emotions expressed through facial expressions and body language.  Moreover, we developed a novel supervised fine-tuning method that incorporates two key objectives: first, we encourage the emotion extractor to accurately identify emotion labels while aligning the emotion representations with the corresponding sentiment aspects.  Second, we incorporate a relevance loss function to ensure that the emotion extractor can accurately operate in low-resolution multimodal environments by ignoring irrelevant descriptions.  Experimental evaluations were conducted using four publicly available datasets including MOSEI, VASWAXI, ESW, and Sentimix.  Results indicate that our approach demonstrates significant superiority over existing multilingual sentiment analysis models capable of identifying sentiment aspects and sentiment labels.  Moreover, our approach demonstrates significant ability to accurately extract underlying emotions from text images or visual descriptions across a variety of application domains including 5, 000 movies, 20,000 hotel reviews, an extensive Wikipedia corpus with 200 languages, and 20 other multilingual datasets. A convex optimization problem is proposed to achieve maximum network throughput under a secure threshold, and its solution yields the optimal phase shift values. Notably, the solution does not require the exact calculation of the channel state information at the transmitter, thanks to the constraints being expressed in an algebraic form. In the field of artificial general intelligence through learning, creating tools to enhance cognitive tools, like decision-making systems, is being explored. This paper examines the value of two fundamental cognitive tools, resampling and renaming, which are foundational aspects of executive function. By examining their role in probabilistic inference tasks, we find that they serve as complementary instruments for processing distinct forms of information. A decision-making agent valuing these tools as tools has the potential to lead to more effective, principled decision-making. The study highlights the significance of considering artificial general intelligence learning in a collaborative setting, where tools are used to facilitate learning and problem-solving. A mathematical model of the flow of information within this setting, which we call hindsight summarization, provides insight into the nature of cognitive tools and their role in collaborative learning. This analysis suggests that leveraging resampling and renaming requires more than just technical capabilities; rather, it demands an understanding of the broader collaborative learning context in which they are applied. This understanding may involve incorporating various mental representations and perspectives, which in turn may demand the use of additional cognitive tools, including modeling and metacognition. A decision-making agent able to utilize resampling and renaming effectively is one that is capable of adapting to a variety of mental representations and learning strategies, suggesting that external and internal tools, like reevaluation and reflection, are essential components of collaborative learning. A more general theory of cognitive tool usage and its application in collaborative learning remains an area for further research. This theory should enable artificial general intelligence learning systems to integrate resampling, renaming, and other tools in a more systematic and effective manner, which in turn will enable them to facilitate and reflect human cognition. A collaborative learning system, whether human-only or human-AI, should be designed with the goal of enhancing human decision-making through the utilization of internal and external tools, which in turn will enable the discovery of useful patterns and rules at multiple levels, including the AI-level. This goal should lead to the discovery of meta-learning strategies that optimize tool usage in different contexts, which in turn will enable the discovery of the underlying psychological and philosophical principles driving cognitive tool development. Ultimately, this goal should lead to the discovery of the nature of intelligence, whether human or artificial, and the importance of collaborative learning and tool discovery in its realization. One promising meta-learning strategy for achieving this goal is to integrate tool discovery into the learning process, which in turn will enable the discovery of the usefulness of tools, including resampling and renaming, and leading to more effective, principaled decision-making. We utilize a dataset from the solar proton trip line sensor on the Parker Solar Probe to investigate the characteristics of the solar wind within 0.67 to 1.2 AU of the Sun's equator. The data reveal how the energy densities of low-energy and high-energy protons are correlated with the solar wind speed, displaying distinct slopes at different energy levels. A non-relativistic energy range sees a 30% increase in its energy gradient, whereas the high-energy realm exhibits only a 7% variation. To understand these discrepancies, we consider how they relate to the characteristics of interplanetary space, the energy distributions of low-energy and high-energy protons, and the mechanisms that produce these energy gradients. As a result, we propose that the solar wind's energy development is influenced not only by its age but also by its birthplace, suggesting variations in the solar wind's energy along different latitudes. These differences could be attributed to the uneven distribution of magnetic fields in the low solar atmosphere, which may be influenced by activity belts similar to those found at low latitudes during solar maximum, leading to anisotropic energy flows from the low atmosphere to interplanetary space. Such internal solar sources of energy gradients could be an alternative explanation for the separate energy profiles observed within the solar wind, which are otherwise attributed to interplanetary space observations, the solar wind speed, and the Sun's coronal temperature. By recognizing these solar wind energy disparities as indicators of different birth latitudes and ages of the solar wind, we gain a deeper understanding of its formation processes. Moreover, its distinct energy gradients provide a measurable effect on particle acceleration at the bow shock, the electron and proton heating rates, and compositional differences between species, which can be used as metrics to monitor solar wind advancements and comparisons with coronal models. We're investigating the potential for language models to incorporate visual knowledge in generating human-language outputs, like descriptions, within a visual context. Our primary focus lies on text generation tasks where visual inputs are crucial. To evaluate the effectiveness of visual knowledge in language modeling, we developed a task-specific evaluation battery to assess visual understanding and utilisation in generated outputs. This evaluation battery guides the design of our proposed framework, called Leo, a visual language model that combines visual and language libraries to generate visual and text descriptions concurrently. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of two components: an innovative Blinded Message Verification technique and an encoded cumulative product hash algorithm.
Leaving the ring signature method utilized in RingCT unchanged, our research demonstrates that incorporating Blinded Message Verification, along with Delegated RingCT's first transaction participant blindification process, reduces transaction sizes by approximately two-thirds. Furthermore, our Delegated RingCT implementation offers a time complexity proportional to n, where n is the length of the public key list, along with a proportionate increase in transaction size. In contrast, standard RingCT transactions exhibit a quadratic time complexity and cubic relation to transaction size.
While Delegated RingCT's ring signature method resists forgery, it can be compromised via the find collision problem. This trade-off may be tolerable in a non-open network, but could be catastrophic if a quantum computer were to pose a threat. Nonetheless, this compromise is acceptable within the RingCT framework as previously proposed by Chen et al. In our Delegated RingCT implementation, the Blinded Message Verification technique also compiles with these findings. Moreover, our Delegated RingCT model can be applied to the Blinded Non-Interactive Attestation scheme, along with other models possessing similar characteristics to RingCT. As a result, the proposed Delegated RingCT model can be seamlessly integrated into various RingCT-based schemes, while the Blinded Non-Interactive Attestation model is distinct from other RingCT-based schemes. 
Lastly, our Delegated RingCT model outperforms the RingCT transactions in terms of size and computation requirements. Notably, the proposed Delegated RingCT can be utilized alongside Shamir's Secret Sharing, along with the recent MMS Homomorphic Signatures introduction, to perfectly execute the Private Set Operations protocol. This perfect execution of the Private Set Operations protocol, along with the other schemes, may potentially be achieved in future research. Nonetheless, the proposed Delegated RingCT model fails to safeguard against the circulation ratio attack, a threat that should be further studied in the future. 
In addition to the proposed Delegated RingCT model, our future research will also expand from the current findings in order to develop an even more efficient RingCT-based model.

Our experiments, however, reveal significant retrieval bias when employing disintegration in these fact-based verification tasks. In response, we introduce the Fact Identification Challenge under Retrieval-rich Settings (FICRRS), aiming to thoroughly evaluate disintegration's application and retrieval-based approaches in general. Our analysis also explores multiple strategies to mitigate retrieval bias, and ultimately find that a well-known retrieval model, T5, is the most resilient to bias. Our findings, along with the data, code, and models for FICRRS, have been made publicly available.

Previous studies of the galactic core's fine structure focused on the orientation and spiral patterns of fibers, their distribution, and the search for a consistent underlying structure. This research builds on that foundation by investigating the statistical properties of the distances between fibers within the core. A three-dimensional reconstruction of the core's structure, derived from pulsar data, served as the basis for this analysis. Initial examinations were conducted through one-dimensional and fiber-based models, each incorporating an anisotropic examination of proximity analysis. Upon determining the optimal method for measuring inter-fiber distances, researchers applied the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare the core's distance population with various distributions, including a general and bimodal comparison. A subsequent section explored whether the core's distance distribution could be explained by a uniform planar structure. All of these analyses were grounded in a conservative approach, ensuring that the results remained adaptable to new data. Ultimately, the research revealed that the core's inter-fiber distances are best described by a normal distribution, and the core's distance population does not provide sufficient evidence to support a normal three-dimensional distribution. A subsequent study will delve into additional distribution characteristics. A conservative interpretation of these findings has led to the emergence of some promising hypotheses, which will be explored in depth. Furthermore, the research has implications for understanding the core's microstructure and has generated new hypotheses for future investigation. A comprehensive mathematical analysis and discussion detailing these findings is presented below. A related question concerns the core's distance distribution characteristics, specifically the average distance between neighboring fibers. Initial estimates, derived from a 1998 study by Gilbrecht and Sazhin, suggested an inter-fiber distance of approximately 3.8 fibers. Though this estimate seemed relatively close, neighboring fibers were found to be repelled by approximately 30 degrees, and the resulting statistical results were subject to uncertainty. Consequently, the primary objective of this analysis was to accurately determine the core's inter-fiber distance and distance distribution characteristics. A conservative approach was adopted for these estimates, and the resulting analysis revealed a mean inter-fiber distance of approximately 3.75. Consequently, the repulsive force between neighboring fibers corresponds to a 29.9 degree angle, and the core's distance distribution can be described using a normal distribution with a 1.75 confidence interval ranging from 3.42 to 4.08. A subsequent section discusses the theoretical model developed in this analysis. Research suggests that the core's distance distribution can be explained by a uniform, planar structure. To reduce energy losses in networks and lower operating costs, many electricity distribution companies employ voltage optimization techniques, particularly in low-voltage networks. A prominent method for achieving this is called Ideal Conservation Voltage Diminution (ICVD), which aims to minimize energy losses while maintaining secure and reliable operation. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for the design of parallel and distributed algorithms to solve the ICVD problem across a large number of networks. In the context of decentralized systems, the ICVD problem is reformulated as a decentralized optimization task and solved using the Alternating Direction of Multipliers (ADMM) method. This approach yields two computationally efficient algorithms for tackling the problem: a distributed algorithm leveraging parallel processing and a more streamlined, parallel-conjugate-gradient method. Comprehensive numerical tests validate the efficacy of the proposed solutions in handling complex networks and demonstrate robust performance in the face of heterogeneous system models and mismatch corrections. These innovative algorithms have the potential to be successfully implemented in contemporary smart grids characterized by distributed energy sources and growing demand for low-voltage networks. Moreover, the framework can be extended to address a broader class of decentralized optimization challenges in modern electricity networks. A demonstration project is currently being undertaken to implement these algorithms in a network of over 100 nodes and 300 customers in order to mitigate communication congestion and efficiently manage energy losses. A related demonstration project is also in progress at the University of Science and Technology's (UST) smart grid testing facility in Lanzhou, China, to validate the solutions through hands-on testing. A quick-time animation of the ICVD solution leveraging parallel processing is available on YouTube for the three-node example. A comprehensive framework of the ICVD solution is available on GitHub, complete with the necessary files, including the ICVD solution itself, the Alternating Direction of Multipliers (ADMM) method, and the parallel-conjugate-gradient method. In a nonrandom k-armed bandit setting where each arm has a unique value of at least $\gamma$ with known distribution, we've developed two new algorithms that ensure high probability and conditional probability limits of $\gamma + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln k}{a}}$ and $\gamma + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln k}{\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{1+c\ln i}}}$ respectively, where a denotes the number of times the arm was pulled and c is a new dimensionless parameter. These results hold consequences for nonrandom multi-armed bandit settings and add to the existing knowledge of conditional probability limits in random multi-armed bandit settings. Building upon these results, we extended the work to arm-dependent delays with known distributions, yielding new results, which in turn, lead to improved time and regret bounds for multi-armed bandit settings with arm-dependent delays. More notably, we've obtained a new bound of $O(\gamma t + \sqrt{t \ln t})$ on the expected regret for multi-armed bandit settings, an improvement over previous results in similar scenarios. Furthermore, we've derived an improved bound on the expected regret for multi-armed bandit settings with uniformly distributed arm-delays, yielding $O(\frac{\ln t}{\ln \ln t} + \frac{\sqrt{t \ln t}}{\ln t})$ in previously unexplored territory. These results in turn, lead to new results in the field of conditional spectral efficiency in multi-armed bandits and an improved bound on the expected conditional spectral efficiency, $O(\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{\ln \ln t}})$. Lastly, we've obtained an improved bound on the expected conditional spectral efficiency in multi-armed bandit settings with uniformly distributed arm-delays, $O(T^{-\frac{1}{3}}\ln T + \frac{\sqrt{\ln T}}{\ln \ln T})$. This result surpasses previous results in the field of conditional spectral efficiency in multi-armed bandits as well as the univariate case for multi-armed bandits, an improvement obtained by considering the work of Gabor and Pajor on the central section body of randomly oriented sections in convex bodies as a random multi-armed bandit setting with different arms, an association also demonstrated in the paper, an association which has not been noted in the bandit literature prior to the work. This paper introduces a model architecture to encompass various machine learning approaches to generating natural language through dialogue. By synthesizing these methods, we separate concerns that pertain to reasoning and those involved in generating language. Our approach provides a flexible framework for developing non-native language generations, such as translations and composites of languages. We separate the knowledge required for generatingutterances from the specific language being generated, enabling knowledge to be kept independent of a particular utterance system. This allows for multiple systems to share the same knowledge without duplicating content, thus simplifying the process of integrating new systems. By keeping reasoning and utterance generation separate, we facilitate the evaluation and improvement of these two components independently, thus enhancing the overall system's capabilities. Our architecture is implemented using a modular composition that uses a semantic representation of the state and defines reasoning modules that produce a semantic representation of the response through the application of these modules. Our utterance generation module, LEATHER, produces human-like text by incorporating various techniques such as referring expressions, lexical choice, and syntactic arrangement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture through the creation of a multilingual conversational system that showcases the capabilities of our approach by generating responses in English, French, and Italian based on a shared set of knowledge and underlying reasoning modules. This architecture is further implemented in a real-time system that was used in a hotel setting over a period of 4 months, resulting in a substantial improvement in guest ratings. Our architecture was awarded a silver award in the 2019 LORELEI Competition, while our LEATHER monologues exhibited coherent semantics, earning a score of 6.059 in the 2018 LORELEI SemEval Task, placing our architecture among the top performers in the 2019 LORELEI Competition, supported by experimental results. This paper provides an online demonstration of our architecture at leather.systems. Our architecture is available as an open-source library at github.com/leather-project/leather. Predictive physical modeling and computational simulations of complex offshore wind turbines and their dynamics are intricately linked to quantifying uncertainty. Since detailed models already exist and can be executed, the main objective is to develop an accurate probabilistic proxy model that can effectively capture the uncertainty associated with the stresses experienced by structures under various environmental conditions. By leveraging time series data from high-resolution numerical models and time-varying information from lower-resolution models, a proxy model can be built to inform the analysis of structural reliability and optimize design configurations for advanced offshore wind turbines. We propose a method that utilizes Gaussian Processes to create a proxy model based on the linkage of high-resolution and lower-resolution models. By leveraging data from these models, the proxy model is able to capture both the stresses associated with individual models and the potential interactions and correlations that may occur. The capabilities of this approach are demonstrated through the analysis of offshore wind turbine stresses, with a particular focus on the stresses experienced by the hub, blades, and towers, under a range of environmental conditions. By leveraging the power of high-resolution models, the proxy model is able to accurately capture the stresses associated with complex events, such as typhoons and heavy sea states, while leveraging the efficiency of lower-resolution models it is able to quickly simulate the stresses associated with regular environmental conditions. The results highlight the potential of this approach to greatly improve the efficiency of simulations and analyses, by leveraging the strengths of both models, while minimizing the limitations of each model. As such, the proxy model developed in this research has significant applications in the efficiency and effectiveness of offshore wind turbine design, analysis, and optimization. Future work is suggested to further optimize the models and proxy model integration. In particular, research into the inverse integration of Gaussian Processes has the potential to greatly impact the efficiency of simulations and analyses by directly linking the stresses experienced by turbines in the field to the underlying physical processes. By developing an accurate and efficient model-proxy model framework, the optimization of offshore wind turbines, including their geometry, materials, and placement, can be greatly accelerated, leading to significant reductions in costs and time. For instance, the proxy model and related efforts to quantify modeling uncertainty may be used to develop surrogates of uncertainty analysis methods, such as First Order Design Method, by integrating these methods with surrogate models. Reconstructing dynamic behavior from reverse-time data of physical processes can be difficult, especially in problems with reversed force effects or where motion is highly nonlinear. Our approach involves constructing and optimizing the most likely motion path under given conditions, even when the equation driving the process is unknown and only the initial and final states are known. This method, called Forward-Optimization for Reversing Dynamics (FORD), makes use of static equations and initial conditions to determine a coherent motion path for a wide variety of systems including those with and without constraints. Our technique is flexible enough to incorporate various types of data, static or dynamic, and can also infer missing information about the system without needing a complete understanding of the equation driving the process. Through both controlled simulations and real-world experiments, FORD was shown to accurately and robustly trace the evolution of complex systems in situations where traditional methods failed. Our technique reestablishes consistency between time dimensions in dynamic systems, thereby restoring causality and allowing for efficient and reliable back-in-time data analysis. Our method and associated code are now available for the precise restoration of dynamic behavior in systems with highly nonlinear dynamics. Our results open up the possibility of applying our technique to a wide range of systems that have been thought to be beyond the scope of reversible data analysis. Automated driving technologies, such as self-driving vehicles, heavily rely on scene understanding in unfamiliar environments. Research into this area often utilizes simulated or controlled datasets with standardized settings, but a new self-driving dataset called SceNDD has been developed, focusing on semi-naturalistic settings and semi-synthetic graphics. This dataset is comprised of 7,505 video segments, approximately 170,000 frames, and accompanies each segment with a variety of annotations including semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and post-editing mask annotations. This diverse dataset is designed to facilitate a range of tasks, such as camera-based navigation, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Unlike other datasets, SceNDD is unique due to its extraction methods, diverse contexts, and variations in lighting conditions, offering a more dynamic understanding of real-world driving scenarios and setting a new standard for benchmarking. Additionally, this dataset is distinguished by its large scale and variety of scenarios, as well as being open-source, allowing for community-driven evolution and expansion. Community-driven evolution and expansion of this dataset is encouraged. SceNDD can be applied to multiple tasks and has been found to outperform existing datasets in self-supervised learning, particularly in contexts involving driving scenes and autonomous vehicles. SceNDD is available for public access at: https://github.com/mushop/SceNDD-pytorch. A related project involving self-supervised pre-training of models has been published at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14279. In this research, SceNDD served as a key benchmark and testing ground. Further information and documentation regarding SceNDD can be accessed at: https://mushop.github.com/scednd/. As a result, an alternative method is explored, specifically the Integral Fluctuation Theorem (IFT), which is seemingly less restrictive. However, recent findings reveal that the IFT is also limiting in distinguishing distinct dynamics. Consequently, a new approach is presented here to validate the thermodynamic uncertainty principle (TUP) without necessitating direct access to the thermodynamic parameters of an individual system, thus demonstrating the inapplicability of even this seemingly robust theorem for individual systems as well. A non-equilibrium statistical mechanics framework for electronic circuits is also established in this work. Additionally, another individual energy assessment theorem, the FSdFT, is introduced as a more robust validation of the free energy as a thermodynamic metric. Notably, a non-invasive free energy assessment theorem for a dissipative system is unattainable according to the findings of this work. Importantly, a new measurement technique, the correlation-drift (CD) relation, is proposed, and it is demonstrated that the drift in variations can reveal a system's behavior even when only the fluctuations are apparent. The CD relation enables non-equilibrium dynamics and nonlinear dynamics to be uncovered through a straightforward measurement. A renowned experiment is utilized to validate the CD relation, and it is implemented without any modification to the setup or changing the measured system. As a result, the CD relation has far-reaching implications in fields such as medicine, biology, and materials science. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A nearly G2-structure can be seen as a real 7-dimensional vector bundle, with its connection and curvature forming a 3-form and a 4-form respectively. We define the space of G2-instantons on a nearly G2-manifold as the section of a specific infinite-dimensional vector bundle, with its fiber defined as the linear map of a constant frame. By establishing that the deformation theory of a G2-instanton forms a deformation of curvature, we successfully calculate the obstructions to the deformation of a G2-instanton. We find that the deformation space of a G2-instanton, when it exists, is determined by a specific quadratic form built upon the deformation of curvature, with its rank equal to the deformation degree. This reveals that the deformation of a G2-instanton on a compact manifold is entirely defined by its deformation degree, with its dependence solely on the curvature. Consequently, we establish that the space of G2-instantons on a connected sum of two SU(3)-instanton-carrying manifolds is defined by a quadratic form, with its existence dependent on the topological condition where the sum of the signature of the two manifolds is greater than or equal to 2. This condition highlights the significance of defining a nearly G2-structure in terms of its real 7-dimensional vector bundle and its connection and curvature forming a 3-form and a 4-form respectively. The main results of this paper can be extended to the deformation theory of SU(3)-instantons on nearly SU(3)-structures. This extension allows for the dependence of the deformation degree to be entirely defined by the Nijenhuis tensor of the nearly SU(3)-structure. When this tensor vanishes, the deformation degree is independent of the Nijenhuis tensor, with its dependence solely defined by the connection and curvature of the real 6-dimensional vector bundle and 4-form respectively. Consequently, we successfully establish a version of the Donaldson-Uhlenbeck-Yau theorem, with its application allowing for the resolution of the deformation degree of SU(3)-instantons on nearly SU(3)-structures with its dependence solely defined by the connection and curvature. The widespread COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has led to the suspension of social activities in nearly one hundred countries. Mobile devices' location data, crucial for tracking disease spread, have been voluntarily or involuntarily obtained by governments. Many countries have developed COVID-19 contact tracking apps leveraging users' voluntary self-identification of location. Despite these measures, privacy concerns persist due to data exposure. This study examines the confidentiality of COVID-19 contact tracking apps, particularly the Brazilian government-approved Coronav′irus-SUS app, to evaluate the efficacy of their location-based tracking mechanisms. Our analysis involves a massive dataset containing 1.8 million users' anonymized GPS records, as well as 1,817 GPS trajectories. Our results indicate that the Coronav′irus-SUS app can be located within a 47-meter radius using a single GPS record. Furthermore, we are able to reconstruct a user's true GPS location, combining two weeks of GPS data, and determine their mobile device MAC address with 100% accuracy using a dataset of 2,000 users. These findings highlight the need for national COVID-19 contact tracking programs to disclose users' susceptible status, risking their privacy. In response, we propose a privacy preservation technique, based on hierarchical data aggregation, to expose only necessary data to health organizations, thus preserving users' location privacy. Our proposed method achieves significant data reduction, involving a 99.8% decrease in the transmitted dataset size, while ensuring the privacy of users, as demonstrated by a privacy risk assessment test. The proposed technique is being considered by the Brazilian government to become a required feature of the Coronav′irus-SUS app. Our study is the first to analyze the privacy risks of national COVID-19 contact tracking programs approved in Brazil. In addition to these findings, we provide a set of best practices for national COVID-19 contact tracking programs, aiming to inspire similar research in other countries and contribute to a global discussion on location-based tracking mechanisms. Furthermore, we release our related code and data datasets for public use. The research received significant media coverage, covering 30 news outlets, including prominent publications such as Pessoas and Exame, as well as television programs such as GloboTV and CNN Brasil. Moreover, the research received awards, including a third place finish at the 2021 IFIP WG 9.2-2021 Research Paper Contest and a Best Paper Award at the 2021 ENCORE. Additionally, the research received funding from the CAPES grant APeIF

Recent studies indicate that quantum computations may enhance specific machine learning tasks, yet the underlying principles behind this connection remain ambiguous. This study investigates the key concepts that drive quantum effects in deep neural networks and reveals that the essential quantum characteristics in such models derive from binary input data processing. Although quantum effects in cloud services are currently based on quantum bit states that are not truly binary, advances in quantum hardware will require the adoption of true binary output from quantum devices to validate their applications. Furthermore, the study presents theoretical foundations for quantum-enabled neural networks and demonstrates a novel, quantum-based transformation of logistic functions that utilizes the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. This advancement leads to a creation of quantum gates that represent the basis for true binary output from quantum devices and facilitates the implementation of quantum models that utilize intermediate binary outputs from quantum devices to mitigate errors. A non-signaling quantum mechanism for the classical XOR operation is also presented. The study concludes by discussing forthcoming research opportunities triggered by the findings. algebras in quantum field theory, before exploring how machine learning can be
incorporated to speed up tedious calculations typically encountered in such

homotopy theory and deep neural networks, and propose further research can be

translate physical principles into algebraic topological structures and, more
speculatively, a method for generating topological neural networks directly from
physical networks, thereby facilitating the resolution of intricate problems in

results in physics, with potential applications to validated, reliable, and
efficient computational methods for homotopy theory and related areas. As the

Our research delves into how everyday users, as opposed to an attacker focused on security, interpret passwords and PINs. We surveyed 1000 Signal users, asking them about their reasoning behind choosing their account PINs, and how to recover a lost PIN. The findings reveal that users possess an inadequate grasp of how PINs function in Signal. They primarily choose PINs based on personal preferences rather than considering factors like randomness, as they overcomplicate the importance of randomization. Additionally, users resorting to pattern-based PINs are unaware of these vulnerabilities. Interestingly, users who are not core users of Signal but are casual users, also display a lack of understanding of PINs. Our study underlines the need for simple, intuitive design in security measures and regular communication about security best practices from the application itself. Ultimately, users' Cluelessness Defense is only effective if designers and developers take their security literacy into consideration, and are mindful of the potential risks when relying on this strategy. Moreover, this and previous research suggest that users who are not core users of a security system often exhibit the most straightforward, yet potentially vulnerable, security behaviors and practices. Researchers and engineers often cater designs towards security-savvy users, overlooking or taking for granted less experienced users who may actually rely more heavily on security mechanisms like password managers or PINs. Given the growing users of security applications who are not core users but are casual users, it is crucial to address this core-periphery security gap. Researchers and engineers should expand upon existing security protocols by adapting existing solutions, such as password managers, to accommodate non-core users and integrate easy-to-use security mechanisms that are resistant to exploitation. Achieving this goal will enhance users' overall security and lower their risk of being compromised. One potential approach to bridge this gap is implementing 1-factor authentication, which has already demonstrated success in increasing levels of 2-factor authentication implementation among users. Researchers and engineers should specifically focus on designing simple, intuitive security features that mitigate exploitation from attackers as well as Complacency Attacks that take advantage of users' false sense of security. Researchers and engineers should also explore more generic terms to describe security features so that users can fully benefit from these mechanisms. Ultimately, this gap should be addressed by designers and engineers, rather than leaving it to users to adapt to the core user security protocols. Researchers and engineers should be aware of the potential of the Cluelessness Defense and use this theory to create and maintain more robust security features, especially against exploitation and complacency attacks that compromise user security. The curvature structure in the Gauss-Newton (GN) block diagonal matrix plays a crucial role in the convergence and stability of various optimization algorithms. Analyzing the GN block diagonal matrix requires an understanding of its inherent low-dimensional structure (ILDS) that arises due to linearizations within nonlinear least-squares problems. This paper presents a viirtuality (Vi) criterion to assess the ILDS and categorizes problems based on their virtuality scores to study the GN Hessian's low-dimensional structure. A vivirtual entry (Vi) of the GN Hessian is defined as an entry that does not contribute to the rank of the GN Hessian matrix and is proposed as a key feature of the GN SDP problem's low-dimensional structure. A comprehensive study is conducted using 152 nonlinear least-squares problems from various fields. Problem complexity is measured as the number of virtual entries (Nv) in the GN Hessian, which is compared with the actual dimensions of the GN SDP problem and its numerical dimensions. The results indicate that problems with a limited number of virtual entries can be identified more easily and efficiently than by counting non-zero entries or the numerical dimensions. A connection is established between the virtuality scores and the concept of problem regularity, as well as the concept of source function regularity. A new algorithm, the Vi algorithm, is developed to efficiently locate virtual entries, which is shown to be competitive with the existing algorithm, the ZP algorithm, in terms of performance. A novel cost model is established to measure the computational cost required to locate a virtual entry. The concept of virtuality is further explored in the context of neural networks and is used to develop a framework for analyzing the low-dimensional structure of GN and quasi-Newton matrices. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the GN Hessian's low-dimensional structure can be efficiently identified using the vivirtual entry criterion. The proposed approach is expected to enhance the development of efficient and robust optimization algorithms. This study explores the impact of grammatical gender on word embeddings, specifically looking at languages where nouns are assigned gender. We re-examine the situation in languages classified as 'gender languages' by noting that the connotations associated with these genders vary significantly, often reflecting cultural and social biases present in the language. We utilize and improve upon existing word embeddings, along with a newly created dataset of English and Spanish morphological features, to demonstrate that the gender-associated connotations embedded in word embeddings are a mirror representation of the social and cultural factors at play. We further examine and clarify the distinct influence of grammatical gender on word embeddings, separating it from the impact of biological gender which is often inadvertently influencing these embeddings. We identify methods to isolate and neutralize the influence of biological gender, thereby allowing the grammatical gender to stand alone. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these cleaned word embeddings in applications including replacement word selection and text generation. We further investigate the situation where word embeddings are trained from large datasets of text, revealing that the embedded gender biases can be sustained at relatively low token counts, but also that the biases present in smaller datasets including common word associations can be overridden by more reliable and large-scale sources of information. We further explore the variables that determine the embedded gender biases present in word embeddings which are influenced by a complex interplay of factors including word classification, frequency of use, and connotations, along with the embedded biases present in the name of the dataset, size of the dataset, and the linguistic characteristics of the languages being studied. We further compare and analyze the embedded biases present in word embeddings trained in the US and in Spain, revealing that the biases present in each country reflect the dominant social and cultural factors present at play including historical preferences for the preferred gender. Two key concepts, finiteness and stiffness, are used to study characteristics of discrete subgroups in arithmetic settings.  Finiteness is concerned with a group's size, while stiffness involves the rigidity of translations within that group.  Notably, in many instances, a group exhibiting finiteness automatically demonstrates stiffness.  Following work by Gromov and French/Ardakov, charmbility has been further defined, focusing on COG groups whose geometric actions meet specific criteria, and linked to both finiteness and stiffness through key relationships.  Our research focuses on proving that charmbility is equivalent to both finiteness and stiffness for a broad category of arithmetic groups, including both lattice and non-lattice groups.  Additionally, we establish the conditions under which stiffness or charmbability leads to finiteness or rigidity respectively, for both unitary groups and more generally, COG groups.  Finally, we explore implications of our findings in the context of non-Archimedean local fields and provide key examples of groups falling within or outside these categories.  Notably, while virtually all non-compact lattices in a given dimension are found to be charmbable, this characteristic is no longer naturally extended to non-lattice groups.  This study draws from multiple fields, including my own past work, that of Gromov, Guichardet, Bourgain-Gillam, Vostokov, Parin, Borel-Trees, as well as recent advancements by G. A. Our work involves object position estimation without requiring any training data specific to the categories of objects in question. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the COCO dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach under extreme scenarios where an object category has no corresponding training data. Our results show that our technique can achieve results comparable to state-of-the-art methods even when the object category has no corresponding training data, with results comparable to a strong supervised baseline on the COCO dataset. To address the growing needs of cyberphysical systems, a unified framework for modeling the interaction between a cyber layer and physical layers is developed.
The proposed framework integrates the cyber layer, responsible for data processing and distribution, with three distinct physical layers: one focusing on the coordination of cyber and physical systems through sensorimotor control, another on the interaction with the external environment through perception and adaptation, and the third on the physical system's behavior and performance.
The cyber layer and physical layers are connected by interfaces that facilitate bidirectional data exchange, enabling the dissemination of sensory information and receiving control signals.
A specific instance of this framework is applied to the management of networks of cyberphysical systems, each comprising an intelligent engine, actuator, and sensor.
An illustrative example demonstrates the use of this model for optimizing cyberphysical systems in the management of supply chains and the coordination of school buses. The example highlights the benefits of distributed cooperative algorithms within the cyber layer, while the physical system is managed through sensorimotor control and perception and adaptation mechanisms. The example also shows how the cognitive capabilities of cyberphysical systems can be leveraged for tackling complex problems in social cyberphysical systems. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through the implementation of two practical examples. The first example focuses on the management of school buses within a city, and the second demonstrates the management of a supply chain across multiple stores. Both examples are tested in realistic simulations, and the results are compared with alternative solutions that are constructed manually for the sake of the experiment. The analysis of the results shows that the proposed distributed cooperative algorithm yields a significantly improved outcome when compared to the state-of-the-art control strategies. Furthermore, a comprehensive safety case is developed in accordance with current standards, and the generated code is employed in real-world deployments, including a prototype implementation in the Google Cloud platform and a hardware-based prototype in the Raspberry Pi model B+3 B. The prototyping process highlights several challenges that are encountered when the social cyberphysical system is put into practice. The key findings of this research are finally formalized and published as a new IEEE Standard. The project has been actively contributed to by multiple individuals from the industry and the academia, and the results are expected to contribute to the social cyberphysical systems community. The project resources, including the code and the documentation, are made available for others to use, share, and adapt. According to the Shearer and Biermann theories, this slowdown could significantly impact the calculation of the travel time difference between the north and south poles, thereby necessitating a reconsideration of the rotation profiles derived from helioseismic travel time data. Furthermore, since the underlying physics of the rotation slowdown is still unclear, it also poses challenges for interpreting the travel time differences in terms of the underlying radial velocity. 

In order to model the effect of currents surrounding active regions on helioseismic travel time measurements, we developed a semi-empirical approach for estimating the radial velocity caused by axial differential rotation. We then integrated this radial velocity into the standard Daniel M. Braminghams fast field code, which uses a Fourier representation of azimuthal harmonics to calculate the radial component of the magnetic field's B_x component.

We found that when active regions occupy about ten degrees in diameter and magnetic flux density reaches 50 Gauss at the surface, the required radial velocity at the noise level of the SO/HATI data set amounts to around 50 km per second, which translates to a Taylor series exponent of n=1. We verified numerically that this value of n corresponds to the radial velocity's first-order dependence on B_x's radial derivative, which in turn originates from the fast field code's integration technique. We noticed, however, that when calculating the travel time difference, this radial flow interferes with the shearing flow, which may contribute to the observed rotation slowdown outside magnetic active areas.

In order to assess whether shearing flows outside magnetic active areas also impact the travel time difference, we conducted axisymmetric simulations of shearing regions using a fast field code with a specified surface shear stress. We discovered that shearing regions which cover about ten degrees in diameter and apply a one kilometer per second shear stress at the surface, generate radial velocity at the noise level of the SO/HATI data set. We decided to incorporate both shearing regions and slowed-down rotation from shear stress into the standard Daniel M. The high information dimensionality of light fields necessitates highly efficient compression methods, including linear sub-sampling, LDA compression, and CDArray, that are often time-consuming and inefficient. Recent advancements in deep learning, however, offer a more effective solution. Our research proposes an innovative model that takes into account the distinct directions of directional micro-disparities in a light field and uses a hybrid encoder with an adaptive encoder depth that-enables rapid encoding via skipping redundant calculations. Our results demonstrate the superior quality of our reconstructed light field images, surpassing state-of-the-art deep learning methods like Light-Field CNN and DLF-DAE. Furthermore, our model improves efficiency by combining the substantial preprocessing simplicity of traditional techniques with the high reconstruction quality of deep learning. Our model's source code is publicly available on GitHub. Our model's performance is documented through two practical scenarios: a still scene of a traffic light using 14x14 sub-pixels and a video of a racing car with 7x7 sub-pixels. Our model matches the efficiency of traditional techniques while substantially improving image quality, outperforming state-of-the-art deep learning methods in both scenarios.
