This study investigates and demonstrates the potential advantages of combining interactive and non-interactive approaches for enhancing cross-language image retrieval results. To achieve this, we draw from query reformulation techniques in monolingual image retrieval and adapt them to a cross-language setting, treating it as a form of query translation. This translation is facilitated through a neural alignment model and a generator model, supported by accompanying auxiliary tasks. In contrast to traditional retrieval assessments, we focus on a different metric – the rate of accurate retrievals obtained – rather than the usual precision and recall measures. Our framework is evaluated using the data sets which were previously employed in the CLEF 2021 ImageIR track. According to our findings, the most effective approach combines both interactive and non-interactive methods with a different level of query complexity. Consequently, we propose introducing a new type of retrieval system, dubbed Interactive Augmented Retrieval (IAR), designed to complement traditional methods and aimed at addressing a key challenge of retrieving relevant images even when the query is poorly translated or incomplete. To validate IAR, we conduct a comparison involving a straightforward combination of interactive and non-interactive methods, and uncover contrasting time and accuracy profiles for the system, ultimately demonstrating how IAR can aid non-interactive retrieval results, and pointing out areas where these combined methods could benefit from further optimization. Moreover, our analysis suggests that accuracy times a speed benefit can be expressed as a straightforward variation of the traditional retrieval metric known as mean average precision, and that this metric can be effectively used in various retrieval applications including IAR. To facilitate adoption of IAR, we publicly share its source code in a GitHub repository. This repository includes the framework used for the various tasks listed below: the source code used for query reformulation, the source code used for auxiliary tasks supporting the generator model, the source code used for retrieval model training and testing, and the pre-trained models obtained from the experiments described in this study. To make the experiments more accessible, we also suggest employing a parallel processing framework known as SLURM. Furthermore, our analysis highlights a number of possible extensions to the proposed framework, including incorporating bounding box annotations and using stackers in query reformulation. To validate these possible extensions, we conduct additional experiments described in a companion paper titled "Refined Query Reformulation for Image Retrieval and the Importance of Token Level Accuracy". Consequently, our main conclusion is that combining interactive and non-interactive approaches can yield remarkable results, and our vision is that these combined methods can address a key challenge of translating a monolingual query

When conducting surveys in low and moderate income countries with limited geographic scope, researchers often encounter the issue of dealing with rare events. To address this challenge, they use small area estimation techniques, such as those developed by Bahadur (1975) and Dalen and Langgaard (2009), often emulating randomization through synthetic controls or causal inference algorithms. Small region studies can either be focused on the design (primarily gathering data on the studied region) or model-based (focusing on broader regional trends and their relationships). Our research compares the performance of three leading estimation methods - steel, Bayes, and-eST - in an artificial setting. We also offer suggestions and predictions for future research, potentially including the integration of survey respondents and non-respondents within small region estimation frameworks. This study draws upon knowledge from a range of fields, including statistics, research on survey methodology, geostatistics, computing science, epidemiology, environmental science, international studies and international development. As such, it aims to contribute to this broad and intricate research landscape. Further specific research can be found in the form of supplementary materials.

Exploiting quantum characteristics in decision-making processes can lead to enhanced outcomes over traditional probabilistic approaches. A prominent decision theory, Kelly wagering, has been previously applied to quantum systems relying on continuous variables. However, the initial implementation was plagued by several issues, including inevitable collapse into a single state. To address these shortcomings, we develop a modified Kelly wagering framework tailored to quantum continuous variable systems, avoiding the aforementioned pitfalls. Additionally, we identify and discuss various strategic considerations for this quantum-based Kelly wagering system. By combining quantum principles with decision theory, we are able to achieve greater expected gains compared to a classical decision model. The process of star formation begins with a prestellar core that undergoes a collapse, resulting in a prestellar nucleus. Immediately following this collapse, thermal energy must be generated through other mechanisms because the initial fragmentation of a prestellar nucleus would lead to overproduction of stars. Our study examines the development of a prestellar nucleus that has ruptured through 3D, high-resolution simulations of radiation hydrodynamics. We initially model the nucleus as a spherical core with a representative density and temperature and then apply the ZEUS-2D code, incorporating the Strittmatter & Wilson equation, to study its behavior. Our results show that the ruptured nucleus rapidly increases in mass at the core, forming a dense, hot core surrounded by a cooler, stratified outer shell. This is similar to the observed structure of young stars. As the star forms, mass accretion rates slow and stabilize, and the star eventually cools and becomes stable. We have found that the star formation process from a ruptured prestellar nucleus differs from that of a standard, smoothly collapsing core. Our analysis of these differences reveals that ruptured nuclei form stars more slowly than standard, smoothly collapsing cores and produce stars with lower mass accretion rates. Furthermore, stars formed from ruptured nuclei have cooler and less dense inner cores and larger, cooler outer shells. This is consistent with the observation that very low-mass stars, found in dwarf galaxies, have cooler and less dense inner cores and larger, cooler outer shells. Our simulations provide insight into the star formation process, revealing that the star formation process from a ruptured prestellar nucleus is complete within several years. During observations from surfaces or distances above the atmosphere, various types of scattering phenomena can affect incoming light beams, impacting the position angle by up to 10 radians. To correct for this effect, which measures deformation of the light beam with respect to its original direction, it's necessary to consider time-varying atmospheric conditions. By modeling atmospheric turbulence as an anisotropic random process over a time-scale of about ten seconds, with a characteristic scale of 20 milliradians in angular dispersion, it's possible to accurately simulate scattering effects and thereby develop methods for correcting the position angle without detailed wavefront data. Using a position angle error sensitivity factor, it's possible to determine the required accuracy for this parameter as being tighter by a factor of five than that of the wavefront, with system-specific requirements varying widely. Furthermore, although the position angle error is primarily driven by atmospheric conditions, it's influenced to a small extent by the incoming beam's properties and the capacity of the system to track these variations. Additionally, although the position angle error is typically within the range of milliradians, in extreme cases it can be as large as ten times this value. Such instances can occur, for instance, with ground-based observations using large telescopes under conditions of very intense atmospheric turbulence, or in space-based observations using instruments with a narrow field of view. By considering these varying scenarios, it's possible to develop adaptable strategies for on-dimensions atmospheric correction, tailored to the specific characteristics and requirements of each observational system. By applying these strategies, it's possible to minimize the impact of position angle errors that may arise from atmospheric effects, regardless of whether one relies on ground-based or space-based observations. Moreover, it's possible to also consider wavefront errors arising from atmospheric effects and mitigate their impact using wavefront correction techniques. By combining these strategies for correcting position angle errors with these wavefront correction techniques, it's possible to significantly enhance the overall image quality produced by an observational system, whether one-dimensional or two-dimensional in nature. Ultimately, by considering the various scenarios in which position angle errors may arise from atmospheric effects and by developing adaptable strategies for correcting these errors, it's possible to minimize their impact and achieve the best possible image quality for a given observational system. Such strategies can be applied not only to ground-based observations but also to space-based observations, including those conducted from the ground or from orbital platforms such as LEO, LISA, or any other location in the extensive array of potential observation zones. Given specific charge assignments, this model can seamlessly incorporate dark matter, dark energy, family number violations, and the Higgs mass gaps with only one additional parameter beyond the standard model plus dark sectors. In particular, we find that setting $Q_X(\chi)=0$ yields an exact $Z_2$ symmetry, designating the lightest chiral $SU(2)_L$ doublet and a $U(1)_X$ charged $SU(2)_L$ singlet as stable, functionalised by a right-handed Majorana $B$-invariant mass term for dark matter. Furthermore, this model's strong seesaw mechanism effectively explains the observed hierarchy between the visible and hidden sectors through an extremely light $B$-invariant superfield of mixed $U(1)_X$ charges. Consequently, we obtain a highly massive right-handed Majorana $U(1)_X$ charged scalar, acting as the $U(1)_X$ charged component of the dark sector's lightest $Z_2$ symmetric composite fermion and giving rise to a naturally small dark energy density at the TeV scale. Additionally, we discover that setting the coefficient of the scalar density operator for the $U(1)_X$ gauge sector to approximately $-0.1$ not only produces the correct value of the weak mixing angle but also not only resolves the electroweak hierarchy problem but also yields a heavy gravitino contribution to the Higgs mass to a level that meets the observed Higgs mass. This is made possible by our astoundingly low supergravity scale at approximately 1 TeV, also making TeV-scale hidden chiral matter highly accessible in future high-energy colliders such as HL-LHC and future HEPs. Our work also explores in detail a previously proposed "natural dark matter" theory at the level of elementary particles. We establish a compact theoretical framework for this model by proposing "matter-gauge unification", exemplified by a "natural $U(1)_X$ framework" containing all necessary gauge, flavor, and $CP$ preserving Yukawa interactions. We investigate the underlying underlying unified framework properties and obtain highly constrained but surprisingly modest mass scales in a unified framework extending far beyond the invisible threshold of the standard model plus dark sectors. A new neural network-based approach to control has been developed, using real-world videos as inspiration. By analyzing the motion of experts, this algorithm can learn how to achieve a goal, even when it has no prior knowledge of the environment. All the algorithm needs is a video demonstrating the task, a set of sensory inputs, and a reward structure. This control method succeeds in a wide range of complex simulations, including challenging robotics tasks and optimal flight trajectories. Additionally, the algorithm generates novel and diverse walk and swim movements when given different reward structures in a virtual body, demonstrating its potential for creative problem-solving and artistic expression. The advent of self-supervised pre-training for Natural Language Processing through transformer-based models has revolutionized the field. Their capacity for flat, parallel processing makes them more efficient than recurrent models and enables processing of long sequences in memory without relying on recurrent connections or attention mechanisms. As a result, many NLP tasks can now be framed as sequence-to-sequence tasks, leveraging the power of transformers. This paper reviews recent advancements in transformer-based models for NLP, including key innovations from pre-training to fine-tuning, leveraging external knowledge, and inference procedures. We also survey an array of applications for these models and highlight areas for future research to further harness their potential. Key topics discussed will include handling out-of-vocabulary words, meta-learning for domain adaptation, and lightweight model designs for constrained environments, as well as the ongoing evolution of transformer-based models to incorporate vision and external memory systems for added versatility. As this survey is comprehensive but approachable, we hope it will serve as a benchmark reference for the current state-of-the-art and inspire future advancements in transformer-based models for NLP. Advanced healthcare's key component, risk assessment, relies heavily on actuarial professionals forecasting future mortality rates. Statistical modeling allows for the creation of mortality models that adapt to changing times, considering factors such as past experience and current market conditions. We've developed two statistical models - one with dynamic and another with static connections between time series - for analyzing concurrent data on mortality rates and economic indicators. We've tested the proposed models on simulated data and applied them to actual insurance market observations from the UK. The results indicate that a model with static connections better fits real-world data and offers more accurate mortality predictions. However, mortality models must be viewed as integrated processes, encompassing both inflation and mortality rates. We demonstrate that, in some cases, mortality models can provide significant information in estimating inflation. Ultimately, Mortality Prediction models need to balance statistical associations in order to generate useful forecasts for actual policy decisions. We also explore potential issues when using mortality models for policy decisions at points in time when data is still scarce. In particular, we demonstrate how mortality models can be unreliable and produce irregular predictions during the initial stages of an extraordinary event, such as a pandemic. Neural architecture search (NAS) is an innovative method for automatically discovering the optimal network architecture for a task or dataset within a defined design space. Despite producing results on par with manually designed models on specific datasets, NAS struggles with generalizability due to a significant disruption in performance when adapted to unrelated tasks. In this research, we establish that NAS experience degradation is largely attributed to the varied nature of data distributions rather than differences in model structure. We also investigate techniques to counteract NAS performance decline, focusing on data augmentation methods which can help maintain model accuracy and are easily adaptable to multiple datasets. In particular, a comprehensive study using nine image classification datasets reveals that employing SwAug (swapping-based image augmentation) significantly enhances NAS model generalizability, with an average improvement of over 3 percentage points. Furthermore, combining SwAug with other established countermeasures allows NAS to achieve state-of-the-art results on a diverse range of datasets including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, and Mini-ImageNet. These findings highlight the significant influence of data distribution variations and suggest the effective utilization of data augmentation for mitigating NAS experience degradation and further consolidating its position as a vital component of automated model design. Trustworthiness assessments of translators are crucial, especially for high-stakes purposes such as verifying the original authorship of a document.  A well-known method for making these assessments is the Reverse Register checks developed by Russian linguists, involving a rigorous examination of a translator's ability to replicate the source language's stylistic characteristics.  However, this method has significant drawbacks - it demands substantial time and resources from both the translator and the evaluator - presenting an opportunity for a more efficient approach.  A Bayesian evaluation method is proposed, analyzing a single translated text's linguistic features against a comprehensive database of authentic translations to identify a translator's level of reliability.  The proposed method offers several benefits: it provides a more precise measurement of a translator's trustworthiness, unaffected by a translator's limited repertoire and capable of evaluating a translator's trustworthiness regardless of the translation's field or level of difficulty.  Moreover, this method is simple to implement and efficient, capable of processing even the largest datasets in a relatively short period of time.  The Bayesian method is able to identify a translator's trustworthworth with about the same amount of time and resources required to perform one Reverse Register check.  The proposed method was tested on two groups of translators, each working in different fields, using a database comprising 150 texts and demonstrating superior accuracy in trustworthworth assessments. Convolutional Neural Networks achieve superior results with significantly lower parameters compared to fully connected neural networks. This phenomenon is attributed to the Concept of the Lottery Ticket with the winning ticket being the subset of unimportant weights that enables better performance. Our research investigates whether using Convolutional Neural Networks as the initial baseline or whether trimming a fully connected model can produce a better performing lottery ticket than the one obtained from a convolutional one. Additionally, we explore the concept of Adaptive Pruning, an algorithmic-level trimmer that adapts to individual models, as opposed to Structural Pruning which is baseline-level and typically ignores neural network architecture. Furthermore, we assess the impact of trimmer algorithms and training methods on the performance of lottery tickets and validate our results on two datasets, IMDB and MNIST. Our experiments demonstrate that trimming a fully connected model leads to better performance than using a convolutional network as the baseline and that adapting a prune algorithm to the model architecture yields better results than a fixed method that disregards architecture. This indicates that an optimal trimmer algorithm and training procedures are crucial for finding the best possible lottery ticket regardless of the initial model. For future work, we suggest combining the strengths of different models and trimmers rather than choosing between them. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Abdulaghath/Trimmer. Time-constrained lottery ticket buyers seek to maximize the expected payout, but face uncertainty about the ticket's winning odds, pricing, and total rewards. To overcome this, we develop a model that uses expected value and optimal stopping theory. Our research shows that a strategic buyer should buy tickets until the expected price per win matches the pricing of a ticket, and then uses the derived odds to calculate the expected payout as the sum of the probability of the first win and the expected value of subsequent wins. If the ticket is initially overvalued, the buyer should purchase an additional ticket only if the difference between the expected payout of the current ticket and the expected sum of subsequent wins does not exceed the pricing of an additional win. A numerical example illustrates that the optimal decision-making strategy can be easily computed from publicly available information, and may result in not purchasing any tickets at all if the pricing is unfavorable. To promote ticket sales, sellers could offer initially discounted pricing or establish programs such as lotteries or loyalty rewards. Our analysis also considers the acquisition strategies for magnifying tickets, a concept introduced in the original research. A practical example demonstrates that the optimal decision-making strategy for magnifying tickets can be applied in the case of a winning streak in a game. The theoretical framework we developed assumes that the tickets are unique and purchasing them is an irreversible decision, and it would be best suited for applications in fields such as machine learning, data mining, and economic forecasting where the ticket acquisition process can be effectively applied. In a comparative analysis, we also demonstrate that the proposed optimal decision-making strategy outperforms a choice mechanism in terms of both the expected payout and the variance of the expected payout. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core component is a probability distribution over nearest neighbors in lower dimensions, which is calculated using a Gaussian process and its pairwise interactions. Nearest neighbor probabilities in t-SNE follow a multivariate normal distribution, making it impractical for datasets like spherical data due to its non-constrained support. We introduce the VMF-SNE model, which models t-SNE's probability distribution using a von Mises-Fisher distribution on the sphere's surface. Our proposed model develops a probabilistic framework by imposing a soft constraint on the data points' distribution over the sphere's surface, and in return, we derive an efficient method for learning the lower-dimensional representation. We conduct several experiments using 3D spherical and curved datasets, and the results show that VMF-SNE performs significantly better than regular t-SNE, and also compares favorably to other popular dimensionality reduction methods. We use diagrammatic Monte Carlo to investigate the characteristics of the Fermi polaron in 2D and 3D systems. Diagrammatic Monte Carlo enables the computation of the polaron energy and the ground state of a paired boson system formed within the Fermi sea. From this, we can determine the interaction threshold for polaron formation and the process's zero-temperature threshold in 2D and 3D spaces. Notably, our results show that polaron formation is significantly affected by the spatial dimension, with a more intricate structure of the many-body wave function contributing to this variation. Specifically, our findings in 2D contradict the earlier results of Belkacem et al., who employed the variational Monte Carlo method. We have revised the earlier results by removing errors in the 2D calculation, including an incorrect estimate of the wave function overlap and the omission of the ground-state energy variational theorem. Our results for 3D also resolve a discrepancy with the results of Jankowski et al., who employed the sum-rules method. We have discovered, however, that the sum-rules method overestimates the polaron energy compared to our 3D results. Furthermore, our results for 2D predict that the polaron formation process will be influenced by the nonanalytical correction to the energy due to the change in dimensionality. We have derived the leading nonanalytical term and demonstrate that it can be described by a renormalization group flow. Our work in this area provides new insights into the polaron problem, which has significant implications for the description of superfluidity and ferromagnetism in dilute magnetic systems. Specifically, our 2D results show that a second-order phase transition is suppressed by nonanalytical corrections to the energy, causing a continuous flow to the polaron state at zero coupling. We have also determined the width of the polaron in 3D, which is found to be much smaller than previously estimated and reveals that the polaron has a more complex structure than initially assumed. Finally, our results for 3D demonstrate that the ground-state energy of the polaron converges to the energy of a paired boson system formed within the Fermi sea at strong coupling, providing strong validation of our diagrammatic Monte Carlo results. Our work in this area provides new insights into the description of superfluidity and ferromagnetism in dilute magnetic systems. A cutting-edge approach to quantum computing called the hybrid digital-analog architecture has the potential to access a broader number of quantum states than the classical quantum computing method, primarily due to its ability to process multi-bit states as analog entities. In this study, we simulate a fermionic system composed of Bosonic hardcore bosons, utilizing the analog approach to quantum computing and running it on a 12-qubit superconducting device. By applying a quantum variational algorithm, we've managed to scale up to 12 qubits, calculating the ground state energy of the system to a high degree of precision. Furthermore, we examined the characteristics of the two lowest energy states within the system to gain insights into its quantum properties. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of digital-analog methods in quantum computing and provides proof-of-concept experimentation on a near-term device. This method may hold significant advantages for near-term quantum processing and may offer a crucial gateway to accessing the quantum analog realm in future quantum simulations. This research has been published in the journal Physical Review Applied, volume 7, issue 1, article 014082. A related paper detailing the digital-analog approach and its application to near-term quantum processing can be found at arXiv:2108.00513. Given a finite graph, G, we examine series of polynomials derived from graph invariants, specifically those of chromatic, flow, and tropical vertices. These invariants are also applicable to infinite graphs that exhibit local finiteness. Notably, the identity of a finite graph G is revealed by computing the coefficients of the graph's characteristic polynomial up to its Eulerian polynomial. In contrast, more polynomials are required to identify a graph within a broader class. For instance, utilizing just the Altshuler-Cohen-Zuber polynomials is not enough to uniquely determine a cubic bipartite graph. Additionally, we study linear relationships among these polynomials, also observing similar behavior in selected non-linear invariants. Finally, we explore connections between the chromatic polynomial and the L-function of a graph's covering numbers. Specifically, the coefficients of the chromatic polynomial can be expressed as a finite sum of terms derived from the graph's Eulerian polynomial and the L-functions of its prime-order coverings. This correlation also extends to the alternating graph sign function. Importantly, the chromatic polynomial's convergence properties are directly linked to the graph's order. If the graph is finite, the chromatic polynomial converges absolutely for all complex z not on the negative real axis. In contrast, infinite graphs require a modified domain of convergence, while the alternating graph sign function converges for all real z greater than zero. Nevertheless, the flow polynomials converge for all complex z, as do the tropical vertices invariant polynomials, also sharing a distinct Cauchy integral characterization. Furthermore, the study develops a graph invariants theory for toric tangles and toric links, along with selected properties of the graph's Laplace transform, also revealing a unique relationship between the graph invariants and the cohomology of simplicial complexes. Specifically, the study demonstrates that the graph invariants constitute a cohomology model that is equivalent to the graph's reduced homology theory. The graph invariants also exhibit an analogous relationship to the graph's Euler-Poincare characteristic, also complementing a similar connection between the graph's chromatic polynomial and the graph's orientability characteristic. Lastly, the study provides examples of the graph invariants' practical applications. For instance, the study demonstrates that the graph invariants can be employed to uniquely identify a chordal graph within the broader class of perfect graphs. The widespread adoption of Scrum methodologies in software development projects has led to varied applications among diverse industries and teams. However, the implementation of Scrum often poses challenges, especially with the rise of remote working. Despite an overwhelming need to understand its impact, there is a surprising scarcity of in-depth research. To bridge this knowledge gap, our study aims to examine the influence of remote working on achieving Scrum principles. By collecting data from 177 professionals via a cross-sectional survey and analyzing 31 real-world projects from GitHub, our findings have been validated. The results indicate that remote working has a non-significant effect on most Scrum values, except for the principle of continuous improvement, as revealed by four statistical analysis methods. These include logit, Lasso, decision tree, and random forest algorithms. By using a multi-faceted approach comprising both secondary data analysis and quantitative research, our study offers an extensive understanding of Scrum implementation, emphasizing the need for future studies to incorporate qualitative research and professional experience. The findings can serve as a foundation for organizing remote working practices, informing the development of Scrum best practices, and inspiring future research in related areas. The code used in our study has been made available for researchers and practitioners to replicate and extend our results. The outcomes of our study may help remote teams achieve a smoother implementation of Scrum practices, while inspiring future studies in related software engineering domains. We introduce the concept of persistence within colored alpha-complexes formed from colored points in n-dimensional space. A subset of these points is chosen at each level, creating a convex simplex if the resulting points form one when ordered. We demonstrate that the persistence of colored alpha-complexes can be calculated in a specific time complexity. Furthermore, this concept is applied to the study of colored point sets constrained within convex polygons. It is proven that a set of colored points in 2-dimensional space, placed within a convex polygon, retains the full persistence of its unconstrained counterpart if sufficient space is provided. Nevertheless, sets lacking sufficient empty space around them as dimension changes are identified and their implications are explored. This concept is found to be irrelevant in certain situations of colored points constrained demographically. An efficient algorithm for calculating persistence in colored alpha-complexes is provided, operating in a time complexity of O(N^2K logK) for N points in 2-dimensional space, with an efficient sparse matrix technique employed. An alternative approach with a time complexity of ~O(NK^2) exists using matrix triplads. For colored points in 3-dimensional space, a time complexity of O(N^3K^2) is achieved using similar techniques. Experiments have shown the following execution times: 0.15ms for 2500 points in 2-dimensional space, 15ms for 20000 points in 2-dimensional space, and 4.5s for 50000 points in 3-dimensional space. These findings have been used to study the spatial distribution of galaxies within the PISMA survey. An approach for visually engaging analysis of persistence in 2-dimensional space is also provided. Furthermore, compactness of colored alpha-complexes within colored point sets is theoretically explored, with the understanding that this may have significant implications in their analysis. Finally, the concept is applied to the study of colored point sets demostratively constrained by a convex polygon in a time complexity of O(N^3K^2). An efficient algorithm for calculating compactness in this situation operates in a time complexity of ~O(N^4K^2). An alternative approach with a time complexity of ~O(N^5K^2) exists for unconstrained sets. Experiments have shown the following execution times: 25ms for 2500 points in 2-dimensional space, 900ms for 20000 points in 2-dimensional space, and 15000s for 50000 points in 2-dimensional space. This work sends a communication to the IEEE Information Theory Society's Summer School on Information Theory, where we present a thorough investigation of the general and obtainable directions of degrees of freedom (GDoF) for interference networks involving $K$ users. We start by obtaining the GDoF region under complete network connectivity and show that optimal and binary power regulation strategies converge to the same GDoF region at high values of $K$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an interval, specifically between $K$ and $2\sqrt{K}$, within which the GDoF for binary power regulation methods approaches infinity as $K$ tends to infinity. This implies that for large numbers of users, providing optimal power distribution does not significantly impact the GDoF, especially for large-$K$ values, where the difference between optimal and binary power regulation methods diminishes to nearly zero. We fortify our findings by demonstrating that the discovered bounds are precise and of the same order of magnitude, thus validating the obtained results. Moreover, we show that the GDoF for binary power regulation methods in a donut-shaped network (where intermediate nodes do not transmit) experiences a significant decrease, following the derivation of a new GDoF expression, which may be of independent interest. We finally conclude by synthesizing our findings with existing GDoF expressions found in the literature. While analyzing the GDoF for binary power regulation methods proves to be relatively straightforward, the derivation of optimal power regulation methods involves a level of difficulty not seen in other existing GDoF studies. We therefore decide to communicate our findings on the GDoF for binary power regulation methods first. In a companion paper, we will extend our analysis to derive the GDoF for a special case of tiered interference networks. We will further complement our findings with a thorough investigation of the capacity region under finite $K$ values. This work is part of a larger research project focused on understanding the GDoF for interference networks with $K$ users, which has led to the discovery of various interesting results, most notably the derivation of a concise formula to calculate the GDoF for linear power regulation methods, which may be of independent interest. However, due to character limitations, we can only present our findings in the companion paper. In the case of tiered interference networks, we will demonstrate that the GDoF for linear power regulation methods can be derived by considering a special case of two users. In a final note, we will complement our findings by briefly discussing their connection to recent results

In recent years, there has been a growing need to establish trust and confidence in artificial intelligence (AI) decisions, which has led to the emergence of the explainable AI (XAI) research field. The objective of explainable AI is to provide clear insights into the workings of an algorithm, which can be difficult to achieve in deep neural networks. In this paper, we explore the auditability aspect of XAI and present a novel technique for giving auditors the ability to adjust how an algorithm interprets data based on the importance of individual features or groups of features. The proposed approach uses formal concept analysis and the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence to discover hidden patterns in unstructured data. The suggested method is tested using a dataset from the Enron email corpus. The experiments show that our method can scale up to larger datasets, including human-level language, and our technical solutions can be easily integrated into a web application for a user-friendly experience. The paper also discusses the theoretical limitations of our approach and outlines a potential technical extension to further improve the method. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in providing clear and actionable insights into an algorithm's decision-making process. The technical integration of our approach was implemented using the Python programming language, which is documented in a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/timothyedmiston/Auditable). The repository contains the complete code for reproducing our experimental results, which demonstrates the ability of our method to provide intuitive and actionable insights into an algorithm's decision-making process. Our method achieved an average accuracy of 50.9% (with feature 1) and 64.7% (with feature 9) after applying the FC approach. In contrast, without the FC approach, we obtained an accuracy of 61.4% (with feature 1) and 66.7% (with feature 9). These results highlight the need for further research in XAI. The presented research contributes to the literature by providing new insights into the explainability of machine learning methods and their potential applications in providing clear and actionable insights into an algorithm's decision-making process. Additionally, our method opens up a range of potential applications in providing human-in-the-loop explanations, such as auditing and providing clear and actionable insights into an algorithm's decision-making process during the deployment phase. The research is presented in a structured format, with a clear introduction, background context, methodological framework, experimental design, results, discussion, and potential extensions. The main objective of the current work is to expand the capabilities of the diffusion, interface motion and phase separation models developed within the Strauss method framework, by enabling the production of a state through a combination of processes, facilitated by the stitching technique. This technique allows for the integration of individual model solutions to develop a comprehensive production mechanism. As a demonstration of this concept, a novel production model was created by combining diffusion, interface motion, and phase separation processes within a particle framework. This new model incorporates stitching, interface reduction, and interface growth mechanisms to develop a production mechanism that is comprised of multiple individual model solutions, thus enabling the optimization of production processes and control over the resulting product properties. This new model shares similarities with well-known processes such as oil percolation and sedimentation, and can be used to develop materials with varied structures, such as porous and layered materials, by controlling the stitching mechanisms. Recent advancements in quantum machine learning have shown that quantum computers can outperform their classical counterparts in certain tasks, specifically when dealing with large datasets.  Nevertheless, existing studies have primarily concentrated on generating test samples against a single model, overlooking the potential impact of diverse instances and disturbances on quantum classifiers.  In this research, we investigate the effect of adversarial samples and noise on quantum classifiers, revealing both universal and special instances of these effects that threaten the robustness of quantum classifiers, just like their classical counterparts.  Moreover, we discovered that universal adversarial samples can be generated in both universal and isolated quantum systems, but specific patterns require the use of customized quantum circuits.  Our findings demonstrate that quantum classifiers can be compromised by adversarial samples and noise just like their classical counterparts, and we show that the failure of a quantum classifier can still provide valuable insights for their classical counterparts.  Additionally, we developed a new and efficient method for generating adversarial samples using a quantum circuit mapper, facilitating the creation of customized quantum circuits.  This research holds significant potential for advancing quantum-inspired machine learning applications.  Moreover, we found that the failure of a quantum classifier can still provide valuable insights for their classical counterparts.  In particular, we observed that the quantum classifier's overconfidence in certain classes with complex physics can be attributed to or at least complemented by the performance of their classical counterparts.  These results indicate that diversity in quantum instances and disturbances is a critical concept that should not be overlooked in quantum machine learning.  In order to develop more robust quantum classifiers, we recommend introducing universal and special instances of these effects as an essential part of quantum classifier training.  Our work has also facilitated the creation of customizable quantum circuits.  These results will contribute to advancing quantum-inspired machine learning applications.  In particular, we discovered that the failure of a universal quantum classifier can still provide valuable insights for their classical counterparts by pinpointing the pattern in data that it incorrectly identified.  This result holds significant potential in developing more robust quantum classifiers that can better withstand diverse instances and disturbances.  In particular, we observed that the overconfidence of a universal quantum classifier in its incorrect classification of data with complex physics is an instance of a universal pattern.  This pattern could be a result of introducing diversity in quantum instances and disturbances as an essential part of quantum classifier training, similar to the result obtained for disturbances.  In particular, we recommended an easy and efficient method to introduce this universal pattern by modifying the Pauli matrices, which can complement the performance of classical classifiers. We have developed a concept of alignments that can effectively check the compliance of process traces that are observed from different perspectives. Specifically, when process runs are represented by prefix, infix, and postfix traces, we have shown that the compliance checking problem can be solved in an efficient manner with the following approaches. Firstly, given two traces, we have demonstrated that the problem of determining whether they represent the same process can be solved in cubic time. Secondly, when two traces are given along with a prefix trace, we have shown that the problem of determining whether they represent three different aspects of the same process can be solved in quadratic time. These approaches rely on a special notation called the QNOT operator, which represents a prefix-suffix alignment. In order to provide better understanding, we have defined a set of limitations regarding the usage of such QNOT operators, and we have demonstrated that the problem of checking the compliance of traces, when restricted to prefix-suffix alignments, becomes intractable in terms of efficiency when the number of such operators exceeds a certain limit. Furthermore, in order to facilitate practical applications, we have outlined a steps-based approach that focuses on key instances of the compliance checking problem, and we have discussed its potential in guiding process improvement efforts. A tool called CVF, which supports the infix-based form of compliance checking, is another contribution that has been described in the paper. Specifically, the tool can be used to monitor the evolution of process runs and to determine whether the observed traces represent the expected process behavior. The problem of checking the compliance of prefix-suffix alignments is another functionality that has been implemented in the tool. In order to illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we have described an actual case study involving a real-world bank that used our approach to monitor the evolution of successful transactions made using mobile apps, and in the process, the bank's management was able to take steps to improve the process. Accurate prediction of radio transmission performance is essential for optimizing mobile communications systems. This requires precise models of device antennas and reception under varying practical field conditions. Existing field testing models, although valuable, can be insufficient or inefficient in certain situations such as urban environments with macro base stations. This paper showcases the potential of deep neural networks, specifically in the form of convolutional neural networks, in producing predictive models of radio transmission performance. By training and testing these models on data collected in both rural and urban settings, we demonstrate their capacity to: 1) generate reliable signals even with limited, point-based field measurement data, 2) adapt to unforeseen base station locations and types, 3) account for the complex interactions between multiple devices and base stations, 4) predict radio transmission performance across a broad frequency range, 5) apply universally across various field conditions and make scalable, data-driven predictions without the constraints of laboratory-based measurements. The outcomes of this study indicate that deep neural networks can be utilized to develop data-driven models of radio transmission performance that surpass traditional field testing models in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and versatility. These models can then be employed for a range of purposes, including wireless system design and optimization, field testing planning, and radio link analysis. Potential real-world applications of these models extend beyond mobile communications to other fields like satellite communications and radar systems. This study may also have broader implications for the fields of physics and engineering as they become increasingly intertwined with artificial intelligence and data-driven methodologies. The primary contribution of this research lies in the development of a universal approach for utilizing machine learning algorithms to translate physical space measurements into predictive models of radio transmission performance. By doing so, we significantly accelerate the pace at which researchers can validate their measurement setups, reduce labor and measurement costs, and tailor their models to specific applications, effectively paving the way for data-driven optimization of mobile communications systems. A comprehensive framework for modeling and assessing planning tasks within dynamic environments has been established. A formalization of task execution is provided, along with a rigorous evaluation of the notion of goal achievement. We introduce a strategy for high-confidence verification of goal achievement by leveraging model checking. The proposed approach enables developers to identify insufficiencies in task definitions and ensures goal achievement can be verified for consistent world states. The application of temporal logic enables the accurate definition of task goals and provides a flexible means of limiting the scope of world states to be evaluated. We present an efficient validation method for high-level planning tasks that relies on the application of model checking, supported by a practical implementation using the Z3 SMT solver. The efficiency of our approach allows for the automatic verification of goal achievement for a wide variety of task definitions, including those featuring fluctuating world states and diverse goal definitions. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach to complex planning tasks, including markov decision processes and planning under executive temporal constraints. The integration of an optimal planning engine enables the automatic generation of a plan in response to goal definitions that are confirmed to be realizable. The proposed approach achieves an accurate assessment of goal realizability, plan validity, and goal achievement, thereby filling a critical theoretical gap in planning systems. Extensive testing using a diverse set of synthetic and applied tasks revealed our approach to be fast and efficient, with the validation bottleneck being the model checking process. Notably, most of the model checking time can be mitigated through the application of domain limitations. The resulting tool enables developers to define planning tasks at varying levels of abstraction and accurately validates the generated plans, thereby facilitating the deployment of planning systems in autonomous agents that rely on high-confidence goal achievement for survival. A comprehensive tool integrating the planner, validator, and validation tool is available for public use at https://sites.google.com/view/formal-planning-systems. Our work marks a significant breakthrough in the development of formal planning systems and sets a new standard for the integration of formal verification in planning systems. A related video illustrating the validation of goal achievement in the time alarm task can be found at https://youtu.be/5o4fVwW9Y7M. Furthermore, a detailed formalization of executive temporal logic and model checking has been incorporated into the Lean logical framework and is accessible at https://leanprover.org/view/ formal-executive-temporal-logic-and-model-checking. Multi-factor models that forecast the evolution of energy systems require precise predictions for energy service demand, energy carrier requirement, technology development, and societal factors to hold credibility. This study evaluates the sensitivity of these models by analyzing how changes in input parameters, within statistically acceptable ranges, impact projected energy system outcomes at a global level, particularly in terms of energy system growth. We utilize a basic Energy System Growth model to investigate these variations, conducting two sets of analyses. One assessment alters the lower bounds of specific input parameters, while another applies random fluctuations within range for all parameters. These analyses indicate that model output is particularly sensitive to changes in energy service demand, technology advancement, and energy carrier requirement. We also find that the model is highly susceptible to random fluctuations in almost all parameters, underscoring the need for precise input data. These findings emphasize the importance of precise input data estimation and the necessity for flexible modeling frameworks to account for the dynamic nature of input parameters. This study's findings and analysis provide a foundation for future research to investigate and address these considerations. This research aims to enhance our understanding of global energy models, helping to identify and prioritize topics for further study. We anticipate that these results will be widely applicable to other energy models, not solely those developed in this study. Further research is needed to provide specific recommendations for modeling best practices, but this initial study seeks to lay a foundational framework for this exploration. This work could ultimately contribute to the advancement of more reliable and applicable global energy models, shifting from basic to complex models that account for additional variables and can be applied at a more detailed regional or sectoral level. Such models could be utilized to design, optimize, and evaluate sustainable energy systems that meet the needs of future energy system growth. Furthermore, these models could be applied retroactively to assess past growth outcomes and prospects. This research is currently limited to global modeling, but we intend for it to be expanded to other regions in the future. This study aims to establish a starting point for this future development, contributing to the advancement of modeling best practices. Therefore, we hope this research will open the door for further improvement in global energy system growth modeling and related applications. This property is managed through the application of external vibrations in advanced industrial manufacturing processes. To further understand and manipulate the behavior of these gels at a molecular and particle level, researchers have employed acoustic waves since the 1990s. Moreover, studying the acoustic properties of these gels can help predict their mechanical behavior when subjected to stress. This paper investigates how altering the composition of a colloidal gel impacts its mechanical properties and yield stress when undergoing stress or being vibrated acadically. By changing the thickening agents in a gel from clays to a combination of clays and fibers, researchers discovered a decrease in yield stress and storage modulus. However, utilizing acoustic waves had no effect on the yield stress or storage and loss moduli of these gels. On the other hand, incorporating a small amount of mixtures of clays and fibers, known as TEMs in a gel of primary fibers, allows for the manipulation of both stress and storage moduli through the application of acoustic waves. This results in a decrease in storage and loss moduli when the frequency of the waves is decreased from its initial high point to a lower setting. Ultimately, these discoveries demonstrate the potential for modifying the flow characteristics of these gels and increasing their versatility through the utilization of acoustic waves. Possible areas for further research on the topic are also explored. Analysis of these discoveries was made possible by an original model for describing how alterations to a gel impact its mechanical characteristics and yield stress when subjected to stress or vibration. This model was developed by drawing from established research methods in the scientific community and incorporating the results of these specific studies into its design. This model is intended to be a starting point for further research into the topic, and its relevance to industrial manufacturing processes is also briefly discussed. The Collatz Conjecture, also known as the 3x+1 Problem, is a mathematical hypothesis that has withstood all efforts to disprove it thus far, despite over eighty years of attempts. This simple-seeming conjecture concerns a sequence of numbers starting with a positive integer $n_0$, which is governed by a specific transformation rule ($3x+1$ if the number is odd, $3x+2$ if the number is even). A key claim of the conjecture is that regardless of the initial value $n_0$, this sequence of numbers must eventually reach zero. This article will provide a comprehensive overview of the conjecture, examining its history, theoretical foundations, and notable results, as well as highlighting some of the many open questions surrounding this enduring puzzle. Furthermore, the article will share some insights from an authorial perspective, highlighting potential avenues of research meritworthy of exploration. Ultimately, the article will offer a reflection on the significance of the Collatz Conjecture and the broader $\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{NP}$ problem in the realm of modern computing and mathematical theory. This essay is intended for an interdisciplinary audience, with the goal of inspiring younger researchers and seasoned professionals to delve deeper into this fascinating topic. A related GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/barakmichal/Collatz-Conjecture. This essay won the First Place prize in the Student Research Paper Category at the 2021 IEEE Congress on Intelligent Systems. A related project is hosted at https://collatz-conjecture.net. To achieve automated document categorization in STEM fields, experts typically manually examines and categorizes a set of documents within a particular domain. However, the conventional method of categorizing by abstracts loses effectiveness when handling complex multi-thematic papers common in STEM, as it cannot penetrate to a detailed level. On the other hand, employing pre-existing knowledge graphs to leverage domain-specific information doesn't provide notable improvements, since STEM documents often cover diverse ground. In contrast, we introduce a novel approach to document categorization utilizing a newly developed knowledge graph of fundamental mathematical entities and their relationships. The results show that incorporating this graph, specifically through a task-focused subgraph, enhances categorization accuracy and provides systemized reasoning. Additionally, we provide categorization performance benchmarks and offer open-source documentation for the graph so other researchers can build upon this work. The combination of high categorization accuracy and transparent, interpretable reasoning holds significant potential for improving both document categorization and STEM fields' expert-level workflow. Our findings also motivate further investigation into utilizing these graphs for reasoning about STEM documents' intricate multi-thematic nature. Ultimately, we plan to make this system accessible to researchers and practitioners within the STEM community. Self-referential rankings in situations involving double auctions without direct observations of others' valuations pose challenges for making strategic decisions. The problem of identifying a mutually beneficial matching between a buyer and seller is particularly complex when coupled with a limited budget constraint, as seen in the well-studied stable marriage problem. This paper explores two specific problems: the reliable matching problem and the reliable offer problem. In the first, a buyer aims to identify a trustworthy matching while minimizing the likelihood of being matched with a low-value partner. Meanwhile, in the second, a buyer is given a set of pre-negotiated matches and aims to optimize the outcomes by deciding which, if any, previously made matches to cancel. Both problems involve identifying an optimal'match selection' among a large set of potential matchings. To tackle these challenges, this paper introduces three simple algorithms: random search, proportionality-based evaluation, and hybrid evaluation. These algorithms serve as effective solutions to the reliable matching and reliable offer problems. Furthermore, this paper provides an in-depth analysis of how to implement these solutions efficiently using algorithms based on large numbers and cryptology. The proposed solutions are universally applicable and do not rely on specific characteristics of the value functions used in rankings. Instead, they provide strategic guidance based on the buyer's and seller's relative rankings. To validate these solutions, this paper conducts extensive numerical experiments in various artificial scenarios as well as real-world applications, such as renewable energy and human organ donation. The experimental results provide valuable insights into the effective use of reliable offer algorithms in various practical situations. Finally, this paper demonstrates how to extend the proposed solutions to more complex situations, such as when buyers and sellers have different levels of bargaining power. The approach of using a large number, also known as the Coulomb coupling, is particularly useful in handling interactions between multiple levels of bargaining power. The method enables efficient solutions to various problems, including buyer auction, combinatorial auctions, and general many-to-many matching problems, while minimizing unfair outcomes. The use of large numbers has far-reaching implications and is not limited to these specific challenges once properly understood. The approach provides new avenues for tackling a wide range of complex decision-making problems involving double auctions. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates the potential for organ donation through large numbers and is currently being applied in various real-world implementations, including energy cooperatives. The approach can potentially save lives in organ donation by providing more accurate and efficient matching solutions. Existing assessment metrics for summarization models are plagued by issues: (1) They rely on static evidence about human summarization preferences that fails to account for variations in quality across different domains, (2) They are unable to capture nuanced aspects of summaries due to their reliance on simplified quantitative values and (3) They do not provide valuable feedback for improvement as they often focus on exceptional rather than typical summaries. To address these limitations, we introduce SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation framework that leverages cross Encoder architecture and static BERT-based models to accurately capture human preferences in diverse environments and encode complex summary attributes, respectively. By integrating these components, SummScore offers a wide range of evaluation metrics for various types of summaries and training data to help related tasks, as demonstrated by its successful applications on ABC, SummEval, and SummLink datasets, encompassing extended summarization with diverse summary types including indirect evidence and argumentative writing. Our results indicate that SummScore surpasses existing benchmarks on all datasets while providing insights for enhancing system performance from the extensive human evaluation conducted in English and Arabic languages. The implementation of SummScore along with the training data and human evaluations are publicly available. Our work is also extended by a related paper on ARSumm: Grounding Summarization Models with Arabic Abstractive Machine Translation. The recovery of a complex signal with abstract form s = a * P (f) is investigated, where 'a' represents an arbitrary scalar coefficient and P (f) represents a complex polynomial function of higher than a certain degree (denoted as d + 1) in a finite-dimensional complex vector space. The signal s is observed via a quadratic transformation, resulting in a complex vector b = b0 + b1, where bo and b1 are respectively a dual pair of linear and linear-affine functionals in the same space. The goal of the problem is to determine if and at what rate a linear mapping (b → s) is stable, specifically to imply that s has a unique representation as a function of b. The research is achieved by first establishing recovery methods for individual parameters (a and the polynomial coefficient) and subsequently generalizing these findings to the entire signal s, with the results showing that s can be recovered up to poly(d) precision with number of sample observations in the order of poly(d)^2, thus significantly improving on the previous known results of recovering d-dimensional signals. The experimental findings for the specific case of a complex vector space is also provided. The theoretical efficiency of the new approach is further demonstrated in the specific case of a 2-dimensional complex vector space by first showing that the dual functionals b0 and b1 for the transformed signal b have an intrinsic non-linear correlation that limits their linear relationship, resulting in the recovery of the signal s being highly computationally demanding via a semidefinite programming problem. An alternative method of efficiently recovering the signal s is thus developed by first showing that the signal s can be represented as a function of a quadratic polynomial in a subspace of a complex vector space with dimension closely related to the degree of the polynomial (denoted as d'), resulting in the recovery of the signal s being highly efficient via a quadratic programming problem in the specific case of a 2-dimensional complex vector space with very high dimensional complexity (in the order of d'^4), thus far surpassing the known results of recovering d-dimensional signals. The experimental findings for the specific case of a 2-dimensional complex vector space is also provided. The theoretical efficiency of the new approach is further demonstrated in the specific case of a d-dimensional complex vector space by first showing that the signal s can be represented as a function of a quadratic polynomial in a sub-space of a complex vector space with dimension closely related to the higher dimensional complexity of the signal s (denoted as d' = O(d^2)). The development of autonomous vehicles hinges heavily on 3D perception capabilities for navigating various environmental obstacles. Currently, beam representation-based LiDAR 3D perception methods have achieved notable success and excel in many areas. However, they often struggle with encoding vibrant visual cues and fail to enhance other sensors' perceptions. This paper presents a novel LiDAR-Camera integration framework called BEVFusion, which seamlessly incorporates the strengths of both sensors through a unified feature fusion architecture. By representing scenes with beam-based 3D vertices and pixel-based 2D images, BEVFusion's unified feature map enables direct fusion and extraction of meaningful features. Furthermore, its cross-attention layer enables cross-sensor interactions and feature fusion. Evaluations using the NuScenes dataset and benchmarking with top LiDAR-based 3D object detection methods have shown that BEVFusion's performance enhancements through camera integration, with a notable 2.5% mAP gain, are particularly robust in the presence of distractors and for large objects. Moreover, its resilience is further demonstrated by its ability to function accurately even in environments with degraded LiDAR data. The code and related data has been made publicly available on the code repository 'bevfusion'. We propose that the turbulent flow in the dissipation range of liquids is driven by thermal fluctuations that create localized disturbances, causing the fluid to move erratically. These disturbances lead to a turbulent dynamics characterized by the interaction between the resulting temporal disorder and the structural organization of the fluid, based on its thermal equilibrium state. This hypothesis allows for the prediction of an energy spectrum following the Kolmogorov power-law and justifications for supporting experimental and numerical findings. The phenomenon of laser-induced thermal gradient diffraction in a liquid has produced a range of seemingly complex interference patterns, from concentric rings to arrays, due to variations in observation angles. Our key discovery is that these patterns can be attributed to a universal cause - the circular liquid surface acting as a diverging phase plate. We developed a numerical model simulating the process and observed the following main results: (1) The numerical model can be used to determine the laser pulse energy by analyzing around the second-order spot and (2) the energy dissipated by the laser is primarily responsible for the observed patterns through thermal gradients. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding and reproducing various liquid-based optical structures. These results have been experimentally validated. Our numerical model and the recognition of laser energy as the dominant influencing factor enable researchers to (1) predict interference patterns, (2) modify and generate novel structures, and (3) develop new techniques for analyzing and measuring laser pulse energy. Our study presents a unified interpretation of previous numerical model results in chronological order. Our work is expected to contribute to the development of various laser structures and serve as a resource for numerical model applications in the future. The numerical code and all associated data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/wenhuihuangphd/Laser-induced-thermal-gradient-diffraction. Developing software requirements through conversations is an effective approach used by both professionals and non-experts, yet it poses challenges to automating the process as it often lacks structure and clarity. To help with cross-functional requirements gathering, we're exploring ways to apply design conversations among developers with non-technical stakeholders towards more effective communication. In pursuing this goal, we've compiled a dataset from conversations with non-experts, annotated it, and trained models using the Pretrained Transformer architecture, specifically Goose and Alberi, to evaluate their performance in summarizing conversation notes in a manner understandable by developers and non-experts alike. Our study, however, also uncovered significant variability in model output consistency, indicating a need for further refinement and consideration of design conversations' inherent variability when replicating our results in practice. Furthermore, we observed that, despite consistency issues, non-expert participants were able to provide feedback and improve the models, leading us to believe that this interaction could be a crucial factor in utilizing AI-assisted design conversations for software development in the future. As a result, we recommend incorporating AI-assisted design conversations more deeply into software development protocols and using it as an integral part of cross-functional requirements gathering. Our paper is accessible at https://arxiv.org/assistant-and-contributions. Additionally, the code used for our study is available at https://github.com/danielaovs/csd_conversational_notes. The study findings can also be found at https://danielaovs.github.io/conversational_notes. To facilitate future studies, we're providing access to the study participants' feedback and the annotated dataset via https://c8r.github.io. Furthermore, we're listing the study participants' information at https://c8r.github.io/StudyParticipants. In the future, we intend to replicate our findings through user studies set in realistic development settings, with both professionals and non-experts, and to continue refining the AI-assisted design conversations framework to maximize its potential. Ultimately, our long-term goal is to integrate AI-assisted design conversations into mainstream software development protocols. The ability to continuously process changing data is becoming increasingly essential due to the rising influx of data in numerous application domains.  Current systems, though capable of handling data streams, typically either handle single data streams or rely on data storage methods (like databases and key-value stores) that impede stream-based processing, thus creating a gap between data flow and storage approaches.  In this paper, a fully functional system, called H-STREAM, is introduced that bridges this gap by integrating stream processing with data recording capabilities for enhanced flexibility and utility.  By combining the Reservoir sampling concept, a probabilistic approach is developed to project a data stream into a finite dataset.  Furthermore, a major system component, a graphical interface, is designed to assemble analysis pipelines from data processing operators, allowing these datasets to be created for in-depth, interactive exploration and analysis.  By incorporating these concepts, the system offers users the capability to simultaneously process data streams and create datasets for comprehensive, interactive exploration and analysis.  By means of a data analysis example, the utility of H-STREAM is demonstrated and its capabilities are compared with a data recording system, called Apache Cassandra.  Through extensive experimentation, the H-STREAM performance is evaluated and benchmarked against these criteria.  Our results validate the effectiveness of H-STREAM in addressing data analysis challenges and provide valuable insights for its future enhancement and development.  H-STREAM, a major system innovation, fills an important gap between data processing and storage technologies, creating a new paradigm that opens up opportunities for data analysis applications.  By projecting data streams into datasets, the system enables interactive exploration and offers a unique feature among data processing and storage tools.  By allowing the assembly of analysis pipelines from operators, the system enables flexible composition of processing and storage layers for data analysis applications.  Consequently, the system has a wide range of potential applications in various data analysis areas, opening up new opportunities and use cases for data analysis and processing libraries and systems.  As such, the H-STREAM architecture and design can inspire the creation and development of more innovative data analysis libraries and processing and storage technologies.  Furthermore, the H-STREAM utility and benefits can be extended to other technologies and systems, enhancing their capabilities and providing new features and uses.  For instance, the H-STREAM utility and benefits can be leveraged in other data analysis libraries and processing and storage technologies, as well as data streaming and storage technologies, and is expected to be a subject of future research. In a theory where a new, heavy particle decays into a top quark and a bottom quark, researchers have investigated final states containing two top quarks, a top quark and an anti-top quark, and a bottom quark and an anti-bottom quark. Initial analysis via the standard Effective Field Theory framework revealed a particular diagram that significantly contributes to the signal. However, in this paper, the full phase space was explored and it was found that the standard Effective Field Theory description is insufficient, particularly in cases where the top and bottom quarks' momentum distributions differ. As a result, the standard Effective Field Theory predictions do not accurately represent the actual cross-sections. Therefore, it is recommended that the analysis be revised by taking into account the complete momentum distributions across a range of energy scales for both two-top and one-top-one-bottom final states. A new method has been proposed, known as the Singular Production Topology (SPT). It has been applied to the two-top and one-top-one-bottom final states and provides results that can be used for data interpretation. It has also been found that the SPT provides a more detailed understanding of the cross-sections compared to the standard Effective Field Theory. It has been applied to the one-top-one-bottom final state and provides new insight into its properties. It has also been compared with the standard Effective Field Theory and found that the difference in results is more pronounced in cases with higher transverse momentum. As for the phenomenological results, it has been applied to the CMS search for a new physics model, a phenomenological interpretation of the associated top production has been performed using CMS data from 13 TeV LHC dataset. It has been compared with the existing CMS analysis and found that the SPT provides stronger limits on the parameters. It has also been able to establish the mass of the new physics particle for certain ranges of its coupling. It has also been found that the analysis has limited sensitivity to the new physics parameter for certain ranges of the coupling. Based on these results, it is recommended that the analysis be revised by taking into account the complete momentum distributions across a range of energy scales for both two-top and one-top-one-bottom final states. It is also recommended that the analysis be applied to the associated top production in various search for a new physics models. Finally, the results of the SPT have been found to provide a more detailed and systematic understanding of the cross-sections and interpretation of the search results. In the last few years, significant interest has been directed toward translating English into English using SPARQL as an intermediate step, which facilitates conveying queries that typically can't be translated directly. This innovative idea builds upon the foundation of SPARQL and machine translation, and researchers have established a framework for studying SPARQL machine translation by using knowledge base components that are accessed via API calls. Nevertheless, the methods employed for managing these components, which consist of graphs, lists, and data types, have not been universally defined, leading to inconsistencies in the implementation. This paper presents an easily reproducible mechanism that leverages Python for managing components and provides a template structure that can be used in SPARQL machine translation. It incorporates a dataset with knowledge base access methods, which has been made publicly available on GitHub. This template and dataset aim to facilitate SPARQL machine translation replication and promote standardized practices, much like the templates provided by GLUE for evaluating masked word-scoring models. Furthermore, we intend to establish a replication challenge to evaluate the new replication mechanism, which will provide participants with access to the necessary code, data, and detailed instructions. The results of the challenge will be shared at EMSWICT 2022. This work is an extension of a research paper that was presented at EMSWICT 2022, where we explored the new replication mechanism conceptually. Both the replication code and data are available at: https://github.com/sofia-rl/SparqlMTReproduction. The domain-specific knowledge base, which is used to train the models described in the paper, can be found at: https://github.com/sofia-rl/DBpedia-RG-Batch. The knowledge base API used in this work is available at: https://github.com/sofia-rl/DB-API. The results of this project will be submitted to a replication challenge, which requires participants to use the new replication code and data. The challenge results will be shared at EMSWICT 2022.
