Building on the success of the vast dataset of over 87 million research papers indexed by the DOAJ, a comprehensive dataset of research outcomes is developed, comprising over 1.5 million conferences. A novel suite of tools, known as VIGOR, is engineered to optimize the processing and analysis capabilities of this dataset, enabling the evaluation of a wide variety of research venues in an unbiased manner. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of VIGOR's applications, covering aspects such as detecting publishing scams, analyzing the impact of scientific journals, and detecting research and research institutions engaged in ethical malpractices. Given its capacity to expand to new domains at will, VIGOR enables the creation of a powerful tool for continuous discovery and research. Furthermore, to distinguish it from other metrics, VIGOR's methods are labeled as Venue Insights, implying a more detailed and informed approach that surpasses traditional citation-based metrics. For instance, Venue Insights can automatically flag self-publishing conferences as suspect, and subsequently reveal the extent of unethical behavior among these conferences, highlighting the need for researchers and the scientific community to exercise caution in their publication policies. Moreover, Venue Insights can provide accurate estimates of the average citation rates for top scientific journals, thus exposing the significant discrepancies between estimated performance and actual behavior among these outlets. The development of VIGOR by Corbett and colleagues showcases the value of large-scale human computation in academic research, and the resulting work illuminates the need for sustained human involvement in automated systems. The resource, known as VIGOR-CLI, is made available to the public at https://github.com/jycn/vigor. Additionally, the data collected from the analysis of research outcomes is available at https://github.com/jycn/vigor-data. The current capabilities of VIGOR do not extend to the evaluation of research impact beyond that of citation analysis, a gap that remains to be bridged in future developments. Notably, to guarantee the integrity of research outcomes, VIGOR's methods detect ethical malpractices such as multiple submissions and duplicate publications, highlighting the need for researchers and the scientific community to exercise greater caution in their publication policies. The results of VIGOR's analysis suggest that nearly 14% of conferences engage in unethical behavior, and the average citation rate for research published in these outlets trails significantly behind that of their ethical counterparts. The increased reliance of system performance on neural networks in industry has raised serious concerns among economists, lawyers, and engineers regarding their inherent unpredictability and lack of explainability. In this study, we examine the current state of validation methods for neural networks within current regulatory frameworks. We then suggest a framework for qualifying and regulating neural networks, which we demonstrate can effectively evaluate supervised neural networks in systems by leveraging standard metrics. We also address potential limitations of our approach and outline further research needed in this field. This study aims to initiate a conversation between the legal and technical communities to develop novel methodologies for validating neural networks. As these artificial intelligence tools become ubiquitous in critical infrastructure, a thorough examination of their validation is essential to ensure they meet the required standards, especially in fields where malfunction can lead to substantial harm. Therefore, this study offers a crucial contribution, not only to the scientific community but also to regulators and industry practitioners.

Furthermore, functorial clustering is capable of handling overlapping clusters, a feature that is not typically encountered in traditional clustering scenarios. We have applied this method to a variety of scientific domains, including a set of breast cancer data. It is demonstrated that a Nichols algebra over a traditional Weyl group possesses the properties of a cleft object or a Bruhat interval ring if its given generator $x$'s degree is 2 or less. Our results build upon work initially published in arXiv:1809.05821. In addition, examples illustrating Bruhat interval subrings of odd degrees are provided. Furthermore, an unknown upper bound of the degree of a Bruhat interval subring is established. In specific cases, it is shown that a Nichols algebra over the algebraic closure of the rational numbers of degree 6 or less cannot serve as a Bruhat interval subring. This information is then used to establish that a specific Bruhat interval subring of degree 7 over the Bruhat interval subring with index 2 does not exist. Lastly, a specific case of an infinite series of graded coalgebras over the rational numbers whose $G$-action characteristics enable the construction of graded $G$-modules is also presented. A new avatar representation is proposed, utilizing a highly compact representation called Articulated Neural Representation (ANR), specifically tailored for virtual human models, which is both versatile and efficient to render. Unlike conventional methods, ANR is trained end-to-end and is composed of two main components - a standard neural image representation (NeRf) adapted for skeletons and textureless objects, and a compact neural function that integrates point coordinates to local object coordinates. The proposed method does not only apply to characters with rigid exteriors and rationally arranged skeletons but also extends to character types with complex and irregular structures such as robots and creatures with intricate details. Furthermore, ANR is capable of supporting real-time interactions, such as manipulation and also facilitates quick switching between different views, which is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the viewer's perspective changes rapidly. In addition to these advantages, ANR is simple to implement, and only requires a single static image of the avatar, without needing to access other relevant information, making it an efficient and effective solution for creating and rendering virtual avatars from a single image vision only. The results of our experiments show the ANR's rendering performance far surpasses that of previous thin-shell models in terms of image quality, and the similarity between generated images produced by ANR and those taken from the object's virtual camera, and the integration of ANR and real-time collision detection technology has resulted in the creation of a new efficient framework for interactive character rendering and manipulation. The source code of our project, and the related figures and 3D videos have been made available online for further review and analysis. To determine whether individuals and artificial intelligence equally rely on image nuances or can be guided by contextual understanding, we analyzed extreme variations in visual inputs by creating radically altered but semantically linked images. Both human observers and a visual recognition model, Deep Neural Network, made distinct decisions about the images. While the Deep Neural Network primarily bases its judgments on minute visual differences, human observers took a more comprehensive view, considering the images' underlying context. These results show that artificial intelligence may not replicate natural intelligence's ability to be guided by nuanced semantic information in visual tasks. Moreover, machine vision shares some similarities with human vision but exhibits some key differences in visual perception. It is assumed that future visual AI systems following the same principles as Deep Neural Networks will behave similarly, but this might limit their ability to outperform humans in complex semantic tasks. In order to bridge this gap, we suggest an artificial intelligence framework capable of making more informed decisions based on the underlying meaning of visual information and evaluate its effectiveness through two experiments. When trained with modified high-level visual inputs that reflect changing real-world conditions, the semantic-guided framework led to significant improvements in a vehicle classification task. Additionally, the framework enabled artificial intelligence to detect subtle image manipulations more accurately that the Deep Neural Network. These achievements pave the way for developing artificial intelligence that accurately interprets the underlying meaning of visual information just like humans do. A family of materials called Y$_{2}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ has been studied due to its unique properties stemming from frustrated triangular clusters linked by shared vertices. The inter-cluster connections in Ru$^{4+}$ are very weak, resulting in an expanse of unexplored parameter spaces containing long-range exchange, anisotropy, and Zeeman interactions. Our study focuses on a theoretical investigation of the two-dimensional, weakly-labeled triangular clusters comprising Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}^{4-}$ without inter-cluster interactions, employing ab initio calculations to determine the ground state and low-lying excited states. Our findings, derived from Monte Carlo simulations at zero temperature, reveal the presence of three distinct phases: a small impurity state for the isolated cluster, a tri-frustration dimerization state for adjacent clusters linked by strong exchanges, and a two-dimensional spin-1/2 liquid state for the entire material. Our proposed phase diagram encompasses these states and suggests a stable two-dimensional state for Y$_{2}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$. Lastly, possible experimental observations are discussed including NMR, transport, and magnetic susceptibility measurements. Our measurements indicate a significant decrease in magnetic susceptibility at low temperatures, accompanied by a characteristic temperature proportional to the exchange constant, as well as an increase in low-temperature Jones ratios and quantum critical points resulting from the substitution of tri-hedral clusters. Our findings enhance our understanding of the recently identified materials from the Y$_{2}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ family and open up novel pathways for investigating two-dimensional materials featuring fragile, tri-frustrated triangles. These pathways may also be effective in other materials exhibiting closely-linked triangular structures at the atomic level. For instance, 1T-A$_{2}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{5}$ chloride and its related hydrogen analogs have been found to exhibit analogous behavior to NMR, transport, and magnetic susceptibility measurements. Our measurements reveal the presence of two-dimensional characteristics that can be destroyed by inter-layer coupling. Our findings, derived from the combination of computational and experimental tools, provide new insights into the recently identified materials from the Y$_{2}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ family and other Pd/CD materials. Our work encourages the utilization of quantum materials comprising triangular structures that are triangular in shape and offers promising avenues for the investigation of two-dimensional materials featuring shared vertices. Recent breakthroughs in Zero-shot Natural Language Inference (Zs-NLI) from large-scale, publicly available pre-trained language models (PLMs) have highlighted the potential for next-generation artificial intelligence to underpin education. These advances have led to the development of various applications outside of Zs-NLI, such as educational question-answering and detection of off-topic responses in discussions. However, the internal logic behind Zs-NLI models is somewhat opaque, particularly with regard to the interplay between the datasets and prompts. Furthermore, enhancing these models for new tasks is a time-consuming and artfully constructed process, involving complex hyperparameter adjustments. This study investigates the interrelations between the datasets and prompts utilized in Zs-NLI models, and demonstrates that combining subsets of NLI datasets and crafting novel prompts can significantly boost model performance on unseen benchmarks. This finding opens up new avenues for leveraging Zs-NLI models in educational tasks and informs the meta-tuning process, which is shown to be applicable to all the examined benchmarks. Consequently, such meta-tuning is not task-specific and is likely to accelerate future improvements in the field. Our findings are implemented in a new repository called Assemblage, located at https://github.com/hitzke/dataset_and_prompt_assemblages. This project is built upon the existing source code of ZS-MLM, accessible via https://github.com/dfried/zero-shot. We anticipate that our research will stimulate further growth in the field of language technology for education. Ultimately, the key insights and conclusions from our work are distilled into four takeaways, presented in the conclusion section. They represent crucial guidelines to follow when utilizing Zs-NLI models in educational settings and training the underlying PLMs, which is crucial for developing AI solutions that can successfully underpin future educational applications. Additionally, the performance of the model variants on the benchmark analysis dataset has been incorporated into the paper's conclusions for added context. This study investigates the disrupted symmetry states and liquid states in low-dimensional quantum magnets. We provide a theoretical model describing the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model's low-energy dynamics on the triangular lattice for small $J_2$ values. Our analysis, in conjunction with existing Monte Carlo data, reveals distinct low-energy excitations for triangular lattice antiferromagnets and honeycomb systems, supporting recent findings that the honeycomb ferromagnetic Heisenberg model exhibits a unique state known as a valence bond liquid. We also identify two distinct liquid states in the triangular system. One state bears a resemblance to the valence bond liquid in the honeycomb system, while the other lacks a direct analogy. We propose that the latter could potentially correspond to a proposed state in the pyrochlore lattice, referred to as a fragile spin liquid. We demonstrate that our findings are a natural consequence of the low energy dynamics generated by a chiral Higgs mechanism. We further show that significant "accidental symmetry" is responsible for the emergence of the symmetric spin liquid in the honeycomb model. Our analysis highlights an important concept: symmetry may play a crucial role in the formation of spin liquids, and breaking this symmetry may facilitate the emergence of such states. Additionally, by controlling the ratio of $J_1$ and $J_2$, it might be possible to transition between the two distinct liquid states in the triangular system. If this is indeed the case, it may be possible to realize both states in an experimentally realizable system. We discuss a possible pathway to achieve this in certain materials. Finally, by establishing a low-energy model for broken symmetry states in low-dimensional quantum magnets, our study sets the stage for a potential realization of spin liquids in triangular lattice antiferromagnets through quantum control in systems such as Y$_2$Ru$_2$Si$_2$O$_9$, Y$_2Ir$_2$_2$O$_9$, and Na$_2$Cu$_2$TeO$_3$. Natural language processing aims to comprehend the meaning of text by evaluating the context-specific interpretations of words, much like human learning. Unfortunately, current methods often rely on pre-trained models that learn interpretations through statistical analysis rather than contextual understanding. By modifying the RoBERTa model to prioritize semantic consistency, our proposed approach successfully trains interpreters with limited text input. In a study involving three languages, our results indicate that this modified model can learn word meanings across a wider range of contexts than the pre-trained model. Moreover, our technical enhancements enable the model to learn word meanings with just one example per word, showcasing effective zero-shot learning capabilities. These findings demonstrate the potential for naturalized interpreters to truly 'learn' language understanding in the same way that humans do. Moreover, our research reveals that semantic inconsistency can significantly hinder interpreter performance, often resulting in flawed output even with extensive training data. By investigating the effects of data scarcity, we found that critical input data can substantially improve interpreter performance, particularly when it directly addresses common misunderstandings. These performance enhancements, based on training with 'difficult' examples, result in interpreters that are both accurate and adaptable. Importantly, our results show that naturalized interpreters can actually improve their understanding of language challenges over time, something that statistical models cannot achieve. By opening the 'black box' of how RoBERTa models process language, we discovered that naturalized models tend to avoid making premature assumptions and instead carefully balance context and semantic information when making interpretations. These findings imply that naturalized models have the potential to outperform their statistical counterparts, offering a critical step towards true natural language understanding. Ultimately, our research makes several key contributions, including suggesting new methods for training interpreters with naturalized models, providing a new framework for evaluating semantic consistency, and demonstrating the effectiveness of naturalized models in zero-shot learning and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer tasks. A related demonstration can be found at: https://interpreters-demo.vercel.app/

A federated learning method known as Offline Federated Learning (OffFLL) allows a model to be trained on a model sharing platform without the need for continuous model updates on the central server. This paper explores the use of OffFLL for nonlinear regression tasks. Since real-time data communication is not possible, the model and its parameters are initially synchronized before training on the client devices. However, the model's convergence is hindered by periodic model uploads and downloads. To overcome this limitation, OffFLL aims to achieve convergence using only the client devices. A key challenge with OffFLL is achieving convergence, as the solution space is non-compact. To address this challenge, OffFLL utilizes a local data fitting method, which effectively establishes upper bounds for fitting losses on the client devices. Furthermore, the model design ensures that the empirical and theoretical risks are accurately representative. A key aspect of OffFLL's success is the sequential regression method used for model selection. A unified mathematical framework has been developed to establish the single-layer Neural-Network's (NN) continuous-risk-minimization (CRM) property under nonlinear regression tasks. A novel technique has been developed to create deep silicon atomic vapor chambers. By utilizing a photothermal method and incorporating a microstructured silicon device, we can produce a 2.8 mm deep silicon n-type silicon wafer chamber capable of containing rubidium gas at atmospheric pressure. Even though the silicon atomic vapor density is significantly reduced, we can still achieve a rubidium optomagnetostatic trap with a 1 millisecond lifetime. This new method offers an affordable and robust alternative to conventional materials, including those made from high-quality silicon, allowing for widespread applications in optical lattice clocks and other research applications. Additionally, we can also utilize this technology to create more sophisticated multi-layered silicon structures capable of containing multiple gases. Possible applications in optical clock ensemble and multi-species laser cooling have also been explored. Furthermore, we can also enhance the trap capture probability by improving the light power and chamber depth. However, current limitations of the silicon material itself need to be addressed such as improving the quality of the silicon crystal, reducing the surface roughness, and minimizing the etched silicon structure to further optimize the chamber performance. Future work will also involve optimizing the etching process to achieve a smoother surface, reducing the feature size to further increase the trap lifetime, incorporating autocalibration systems to increase stability, and designing a maintenance-free vacuum-free solution by utilizing a rubidium droplet trap to further reduce the system's thermal conductivity. Such an advancement will allow the silicon deep atomic vapor chamber to approach the state-of-the-art performance. A related technology has also been developed to create a silicon structure with a 1.7 mm deep and 1.5 mm wide multi-channel silicon region. By utilizing a laser beam to heat the silicon structure, we can create a multi-component silicon wafer chamber that contains rubidium and other alkali metals at atmospheric pressure. Although the reduced silicon atomic density still enables the rubidium optomagnetostatic trap to function effectively, we can further optimize the silicon structure to achieve a deeper chamber depth with existing technology. By employing a multi-layered silicon structure, we can trap rubidium, strontium, and calcium vapors simultaneously, demonstrating a considerable enhancement in the system's capture probability. These silicon-based multi-component gas chambers can function effectively with current technology and hold considerable promise for future optimizations to further reduce the feature size and increase the feature density. A deeper understanding of the silicon material's limitations and advancements in the etching process are necessary to fully unlock the silicon-based atomic vapor technology's potential.

Reinforcement learning agents regularly encounter unsafe actions dictated by an optimal policy, which may cause harm to themselves or others. Directly optimizing the long-term return is insufficient because the optimal policy often produces risky outcomes. Our research focuses on modeling the system's risk level, measured by expected losses, using a mathematical representation. This enables us to modify a reinforcement learning agent to be risk-aware by optimizing a combined objective of long-term returns and risk levels. Our framework allows for various risk measures and different formulations of the combined objective. Initial experiments were conducted in two environments where the agent's risk level is affected by its actions, showcasing the modified agent's ability to reduce risk while maintaining long-term performance. Our results indicate that the agents we developed achieved significant risk reduction, with up to 93.6% fewer hazardous states visited. The associated code and implementation details are available on our website at the provided link. Furthermore, we extended Bellman optimality to model various measures of suboptimal loss and developed a dynamic programming method for calculating expected loss in Markov decision processes. This enables us to directly evaluate the combined objective of long-term returns and risk levels, and find optimal parameter values using dynamic programming. Our method uses expected loss as a representative risk measure and was employed to obtain joint return and risk optimisation results in environments where the agent's risk level is affected by its actions. The expected loss values demonstrated variability in relation to the return values, indicating that higher long-term returns were often associated with greater risk. Our experimental findings showed that the agents we developed achieved balanced returns and risk performance compared to the results of our theoretical model. The expected loss values were found to be lower than the actual loss experienced by the reinforcement learning agents, with up to 27.8% less loss. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for modeling, and mitigating risk in Markov decision processes. The expected loss values may serve as a measure of task automation proficiency, with higher expected loss values indicating less automation. Our experimental results suggest that the agents we developed could be more fully automated in the future. Our research enables the systematic modelling of the system's risk level using expected loss, and the simultaneous optimisation of the long-term return and risk levels in automation systems. The properties of the unique soluble form of the double confluent Heun equation and its symmetric unfolding have been examined. Through identification of a Sturmian chain corresponding to a specific monodromy matrix, we determine the basis for the solution space of the equation in terms of a Frobenius-like basis, composed of a generalized eta-function and a modified eta-function. Furthermore, employing a linear-foliation approach, we derive the invariant manifolds of the unfolding, demonstrating that it has a two-dimensional invariant lattice near a particular, globally regularized singular point and providing a geometric framework for understanding its properties. Additionally, we qualify the invariant lattice to be a cyclide of Poincar-Bendixson type and confirm that it accurately describes a singular, separable two-dimensional differential equation. Our analysis also extends to encompass the properties of a general, Fuchsian form of the double confluent Heun equation. However, we find that the invariant lattice of the latter fails the cyclide criterion due to the presence of a limit cycle. Consequently, we suggest that the cyclide property serves as a reliable indicator of a singular, separable equation, while a presence of a limit cycle would imply a universally non-solvable equation. Our findings are supported by a table listing various forms of the double confluent Heun equation and their properties, as well as a diagram illustrating the configuration of the cyclide. By comparing the original Max-Type statistic to a group-wise weighted version, we find that only the latter can produce meaningful results. Additionally, we demonstrate that a group-wise heterogeneous rMAX test is optimal in terms of power, but its critical regions are partially occupied by the original rMAX test. A new group-wise heterogeneous rMAX test is proposed, which maintains high power while providing additional theoretical guarantees. We also create standardized weights to establish a more reliable test. Furthermore, this research develops a group-wise heterogeneous maxima-based test, which possesses the highest possible power among all group-wise heterogeneous maxima-based tests. We conduct numerical experiments to evaluate the performance of these group-wise heterogeneous tests under realistic data assumptions, supporting our theoretical findings. Ultimately, this research addresses a pressing economic issue by applying our results to a joint test of the ZD and FZT, which are key parameters in a stochastic differential equation used to model a primary commodity price. Specifically, we apply our findings to data on US soybean oil prices. Our results suggest that, based on the test's power and statistical significance, there is evidence supporting the presence of jump components, mean-reversion, and FZT, but the absence of multi-scale multiplicative corruption and heteroscedasticity. We also observed that accounting for potential group-wise heterogeneity does not affect our overall model. A related R code is included in the online repository. In current research, channel-state information is often assumed known or estimated. This paper focuses on a different approach for multi-channel networks, where only the output signal and channel order are known. Diverging from conventional centralized regulation methods, a distributed, decentralized solution is presented, maintaining the network's low-dimensional structure. As a result, information need only be exchanged between adjacent nodes, reducing communication complexity. Furthermore, to expand the network's capabilities, additional nodes can be integrated at any inter-node connection point, leading to enhanced channel estimation and regulation performance. As a proof of concept, a distributed regulation method for a 10-channel network is tested and compared across multiple simulation scenarios. For large-scale networks, an efficient information exchange strategy based on cluster grouping is developed, along with a novel distributed estimation algorithm that eliminates the network's low-dimensional structure bias. Through theoretical and experimental analysis, the proposed solutions' advantages are demonstrated. Lastly, a comprehensive evaluation reveals these solutions' efficacy across a range of parameter values. As an added benefit, the network's stability is ensured through absolute Robinson consistency in channel estimates and mean-square convergence in estimation and regulation processes. As a result, the network's capacity for channel estimation and regulation is significantly enhanced. This represents a significant achievement, surpassing previous research peers. The novel COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in the loss of countless lives across the globe, with the majority of countries imposing strict lockdowns to contain its spread. As the disease continues to afflict millions, the global community remains preoccupied with understanding its nature. Physicians and researchers are working tirelessly to gather knowledge on COVID-19's causes, its varying levels of severity, and how to mitigate its deadly consequences. A new method has been developed to categorize COVID-19 into two phases based on symptoms such as fever, sore throat, and respiratory issues. This study uses two models, one based on BERT attributes and another grounded in sequential algorithms, to classify patients into either High-Risk or Low-Risk categories based on their symptoms and health attributes. When tested with real-world COVID-19 datasets and controlled variables, the BERT model exhibited superior accuracy, precision, and F1-score metrics compared to the sequential model. A comparative assessment with existing baselines further underscored the BERT model's performance advantages. A web tool has been created for users to make predictions using the BERT model. This study offers a practical solution for healthcare professionals to identify patients at high risk of COVID-19 complications and potentially severe outcomes, while also advancing the understanding of the disease's multiple facets. As the global community continues to grapple with the pandemic, the proposed model serves as an essential tool for healthcare workers in distinguishing between Low-Risk and High-Risk cases. This distinction is crucial not only for patients' individual well-being but also for broader community safety concerns. For example, in determining whether an individual should be isolated, whether they pose a threat to others, or whether they should be eligible for priority vaccine consideration. A subsequent paper has been published as reference \cite{rahman2022covid19} to explore additional COVID-19 classification categories in conjunction with the BERT model, while yielding superior performance compared to the sequential model and numerous baseline classifiers. A tool for making predictions using the BERT model has been created at the following URL: https://covid19risk-assessor.herokuapp.com/. Moreover, the proposed model has been developed with the aim of facilitating quicker model predictions, with plans for future model enhancements including multiclassification, as well as additional features such as the automatic detection of lung infection complications via the integration of relevant medical images. Ultimately, this project seeks to contribute meaningfully to the global fight against the devastating effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. A demonstration video of the tool can be found at https://youtu.be/yU4ie

To deepen the relationship between deep ecological and evolutionary dynamics, we suggest modifying eco-evolution models to incorporate elements of memory, similar to models used in financial systems. This memory effect is controlled by a maximum time period, known as the duration, and can either remain constant or fluctuate. In addition to memory, we introduce an information factor that influences the rate at which eco-evolutionary dynamics change over time. Our research, consisting of various numerical simulations, reveals that the rate of eco-evolutionary change is mostly influenced by the average duration and rate regulator combination, and that the rate of change in the shortest-duration population is consistently less than that of the longest-duration population. Furthermore, we observe that using an average duration can lead to unexpected and sudden shifts in eco-evolutionary dynamics, and that incorporating memory into eco-evolutionary models accelerates the rate of change and promotes population differentiation. These findings can be applied to both ancient and modern eco-evolutionary dynamics, and potentially resolve discrepancies in the observation of accelerated evolution in the present day compared to expectations based on genetic variability. The simulations presented here represent a new and significant step towards synthesizing deep ecological and evolutionary models into a unified theoretical framework. Furthermore, both websites offer the option for users to run and customize their own simulations, promoting user-involvement and citizen science in the field of eco-evolutionary dynamics and citizen science in the field of science. Research on using self-supervised learning for speech education has shown significant progress in reducing the need for labeled data, but little is known about how two systems, labeled and unlabeled sources, interact during the learning process simultaneously. In particular, there are two main challenges: labeled data falling short or overfitting, and the trade-offs in exploiting vast amounts of unlabeled data. This issue can be compared to the balance of counting on expert instructors or exploration by children in a learning environment. We propose introducing "asymmetric competition" as a training technique to promote the development of skills through interactions between two contrasting learning methods. By combining the two methods, the model is encouraged to improve its existing skills in speech representation learning by identifying areas where it falls short or overlaps with each other. We investigate the technique's effectiveness by conducting the models' competitive learning process using a variety of datasets, and observe a notable improvement in the models' skill levels, specifically in edge cases not well represented in the labeled data, without adding any extra complex components, making the technique straightforward to implement and utilize. This study sheds light on the antagonistic education process in the models' skill development, and provides key design choices for training and dataset design. Ultimately, the technique opens up new possibilities for using vast amounts of unlabeled data to enhance speech representation learning and related applications. Human evaluation reveals that the models' skills are beneficial for a range of speech processing tasks and applications, and could potentially be expanded to other domains. Digital currency initial adopters were initially attracted to decentralized cryptocurrencies as a means to mitigate centralized power abuses. Nonetheless, the trading of digital currencies through decentralized platforms poses a significant technical challenge. To fill this gap, decentralized blockchain-based exchanges have emerged, offering a viable alternative to conventional digital currency trading platforms. Despite their potential, decentralized blockchain-based exchanges present unique difficulties, particularly in trading efficiency, a challenge addressed in this dissertation. The researcher, acknowledging these limitations, has devised a decentralized blockchain-based exchange solution, focusing on scalability and minimizing the significant proof-of-work issues associated with conventional blockchain systems. A detailed analysis of this solution's features and merits is presented in this dissertation, including an empirical assessment of its capabilities using a D7 blockchain network. The researcher also conducts a comparative study with existing decentralized blockchain-based exchanges, highlighting both the advantages and disadvantages of this solution in relation to its peers. Ultimately, this dissertation aims to contribute to the ongoing digital currency research agenda while empowering readers to make informed decisions regarding the application of decentralized blockchain-based exchanges in digital currency trading. A comprehensive evaluation framework has been developed to facilitate digital currency trading platform selection, including a detailed checklist, available at [https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/19H4p5F2L2L1P/fo/formResponse]. A new approach, established upon the evidence value E, is developed to assess the findings of unobserved studies. The original E-value protocol is designed to provide upper limits on how much unobserved study results could deviate, potentially turning null findings into statistically significant ones. Following the introduction of the E-value, various unobserved study scenarios have been addressed; however, no clear framework was presented for determining the credible bounds of unobserved study results. This study presents a Bayesian framework, similar to E-values, to assess the range of unobserved study results in four distinct scenarios. The Bayesian framework uses normal priors and Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to establish a distribution of unobserved study results. The method provides a complete range of unobserved study results and enables the calculation of upper and lower bounds similar to E-values. The Bayesian framework offers flexibility, as the priors can be adjusted based on prior knowledge. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method using unobserved study results on the association between fine particle air pollution and stroke mortality in Hong Kong. The findings show that the credible intervals of unobserved study results include null values in some scenarios, while the upper and lower bounds of unobserved study results can be established for all scenarios. The Bayesian framework facilitates the evaluation of the original E-value by sampling the odds ratio at the extreme values within the bounds, resulting in comparable results. The use of the Bayesian framework enables the generation of a prior distribution for unobserved study results, which can be utilized for parameter estimation when incorporating unobserved study results in Bayesian meta-analysis. The study contributes to the development of a framework for assessing unobserved study results with absent data, which can be extended with the inclusion of mixed-effects models, prior data, and other considerations. The generated code and plots are publicly available on the repository https://github.com/hisanndy/Bayesian-absent-data. The study provides a framework for assessing unobserved study results with absent data; however, it does not address the simulation study. A separate study addresses the simulation study in https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.24.19. The newly established framework facilitates the generation of a prior distribution for unobserved study results, which can be utilized for parameter estimation when incorporating unobserved study results in Bayesian meta-analysis. The integration of the original E-value and the new framework enables the calculation of upper and lower bounds of unobserved study results using both traditional and Bayesian approaches. This research focuses on the quantum plane $\mathbb{Q}_q^2$ as studied in the context of the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ quantum group. We utilize the method of Laurent expansion to investigate the properties and representations of $\mathbb{Q}_q^2$. By applying this approach, we can analyze the existing relationships between the elements of the quantum plane. Our study provides a comprehensive listing of representations driven by $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ symmetry. These representations are categorized based on their corresponding conjugate-momentum subspaces and associated momentum values. This research aims to offer a pioneering and potentially influential outcome in the fields of quantum mechanics and the study of classical systems, leveraging modern mathematical tools. Furthermore, our findings on the representation categories of $\mathbb{Q}_q^2$ and the characteristics of the subspaces within can serve as essential references for understanding the broader family of quasiclassical systems of order two. As such, they may also be applicable and useful in the study of higher-order quasiclassical systems. In addition, our conclusions are further substantiated by the illustrative example of a system based on the harmonic oscillator. We use this example to demonstrate the essential role of coherent states in the context of $\mathbb{Q}_q^2$-representations, particularly in the application of fundamental ideas originating from the correspondence principle. Lastly, in the appendices, we provide a detailed review of the relevant mathematical foundations used throughout this study, including the method of Laurent expansion and the construction of coherent states, as well as an overview of the conventional formulation of the study of quasiclassical systems of order two, for the reader's convenience. Additionally, the study offers a unique perspective on the concept of a classical system by reinterpreting it as a special case of a quasiclassical system, thus providing a novel means of viewing classical mechanics. This study is part of a larger series on quasiclassical systems of order two, initiated by the publication in Annals of Physics, 2020, 413: 165224. The present work serves as an independent continuation of that study, as well as a comprehensive exploration of the fundamental mathematical and physical properties inherent to the quantum plane $\mathbb{Q}_q^2$ as an essential component of the family of quasiclassical systems of order two. The LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider has measured the production of beauty and charm mesons, together with their underlying physical characteristics such as transverse momentum and rapidity, in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV energy. These measurements were based on data collected from the experiment lasting 6 years, spanning a large range of prompt and non-prompt B mesons and direct and semi-leptonic D mesons. Moreover, the experiment assessed the physical properties of beauty and charm mesons, including their fragmentation properties, as well as the effects of elastic scattering with the surrounding matter at various rapidities. These findings expand on a similar study conducted at the Tevatron with pp collisions at 1.96 TeV and demonstrate a significant decrease in matter-induced fragmentation shifts of around 20% for beauty mesons in the forward rapdity range. Additionally, the experiment compared these effects to various theoretical models. These research results will help inform calculations of in-medium effects across various collision processes and aid in gauging fragmentation function variations. These findings were also compared to a simulation of a scenario with no matter interaction and a simulation of a theoretical model predicting energy loss based on radiative energy transfer. These comparisons revealed that, in the forward rapdity range, beauty and charm fragmentation show a variation of around 5% and 10% respectively when compared to no matter interaction simulation. Furthermore, the experiment compared these findings to a theoretical model called SPS. These research results and findings will be presented in two separate papers. Achieving reliable quantum computations requires safeguarding delicate superpositions from external disruptions.  Currently, the most advanced cold storage systems cannot fully isolate quantum information from ambient fluctuations.  Consequently, specialized cold storage facilities are being developed to prioritize preserving millikelvin temperatures.  Our work describes the design of a 27 square meter cold room at Fermilab dedicated to supporting quantum information processing, with a focus on integrating it with the Laboratory's existing infrastructure.  We outline the electrical systems, temperature management, and magnetic shielding strategies within this facility.  Additionally, we present our plans to utilize a substructure to build the storage room and refine the refrigeration system for enhanced efficiency and stability.  Notably, the development of this storage room marks the first time a quantum-related system is incorporated into Fermilab's formal laboratory setup, marking the beginning of the Laboratory's foray into support of quantum information processing.  Our storage room will serve as both a testing ground for novel quantum systems and a prototype facility representing Fermilab's entry into the developing field of quantum information processing.  The information presented in this article is based on the documentation from the Laboratory's Review and Approval Process.  Our facility is intended to support a range of quantum systems, including superconducting qubit-based systems like those utilized by the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center, as well as other emerging quantum technologies.  Our initial research will concentrate on quantum computing utilizing unconventional superconducting systems, with the goal of performing real-world demonstrations and experiments that can eventually be transitioned to the research programs within the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center.  Our storage room will also become a hub for collaboration between the superconducting center and other quantum research programs, facilitating the development of new quantum systems and cutting-edge demonstrations.  Similarly structured storage rooms are being developed at National Laboratories, including Brookhaven National Laboratory's quantum incubator, for application to diverse quantum information processing applications, with the Brookhaven facility specifically targeted at integrated photonic systems.  Our work represents the first detailed public accounting of the development of a laboratory-capable, National Laboratory-funded, state-of-the-art quantum computing infrastructure, and the first public disclosure of a planned shipment of a prototype superconducting system for experimental purposes, in advance of the shipment.  Our storage room and the research programs it will support are made possible by the funding and support of the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center and the Fermilab Director's Office, in partnership with the Laboratory's Administration and Infrastructure teams. Previous research indicates that developers' lack of expertise in security causes most issues in Python cryptocurrency programs, with many imperfections visible on public platforms. To understand errors in Python cryptocurrency software, we analyzed 189 widely used libraries by randomly selecting and scrutinizing 30 of them, which involved examining the code and testing the security of the libraries' APIs. We discovered that nearly 25% of the examined libraries have insecure password storage issues. We found six distinct ways developers improperly utilize password storage APIs, five distinct ways to improperly validate addresses, four distinct ways to improperly validate block heights or hashes, and three distinct ways to improperly validate op return data. Additionally, we found multiple vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, race conditions, and insecure use of deserializing data without validation. We found that only a few libraries follow best security practices in Python cryptocurrency software, which is significantly less than in Java cryptocurrency software. Just like our prior research on Java cryptocurrency software, this study once again confirms that "there is no expertise in security." It is highly likely that similar findings would emerge if a similar analysis were conducted for other domains outside of cryptocurrency software. Furthermore, such errors have already led to several cryptocurrency heists. 

Based on our analysis, we provide recommendations to improve security for Python cryptocurrency software developers.

The proliferation of sensors in modern urban environments has created a wealth of data that can be leveraged to build enhanced, high-resolution city maps. These maps go beyond conventional boundaries, encompassing not only geographical spaces but also the digital presence and the rapidly evolving shared infrastructure of urban networks. This study focuses on constructing such digital city maps through an unsupervised approach to data extraction, which utilizes the diversity of urban structures across various dimensions. By merging data from different sectors, we can reveal hidden patterns and trends within the city's spatial and social frameworks. The proposed framework enables the automatic segmentation of data streams from networks of urban sensors, including networks of IoT devices, by applying a unified framework for feature development and clustering. This method uses polling-based data sampling within the city's digital network to identify and group related structures efficiently. As a demonstration of its capabilities, the framework was tested on a network of over 200,000 digital anchors deployed across 700 square kilometers of a large Italian city, resulting in the identification of structure types across the city's network. The performance of the framework was evaluated using comprehensive metrics, including a baseline estimation method, clustering metrics, and a human validation process involving IoT device reset, showing an 83% recovery rate. The output of the framework provides the city's digital network presence and facilitates the efficient organization and management of the shared urban infrastructure. This research offers methods for building digital city models through urban sensor networks and can serve as a foundation for related topics, such as urban planning, infrastructure management, and network optimization. Additionally, the framework's implementation is freely accessible to the public, and our team actively welcomes user contributions and collaboration. The study has been successfully applied in real-world environments, including cities like Aarhus and Trieste, and has also inspired similar initiatives in Copenhagen and Melbourne as well as multiple universities in the US, Europe, Asia, and other parts of the world. The study's influence extends globally, spanning countries such as the US, Italy, Sweden, Australia, and Singapore. The value of the idea has been recognized internationally, receiving funding from prestigious organizations like the US NSF. We introduce a general sparse learning approach based on a pre-defined convolutional network (SPAN), and a pre-trained version of SPAN (NuSPAN) specifically tailored for seismic reflectivity recovery. We derive the expression for learning SPAN, and for the first time, it is presented in a mathematical framework compatible with its convolutional network structure. We also investigate under what conditions learned SPAN or NuSPAN can minimize a specific optimisation problem while maintaining convexity. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the learned NuSPAN (as well as its inverse model) is more efficient than the conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) in recovering seismic reflectivity from trace data. The reason behind this is that the sparsity of the problem is better explored in the context of the learned models. By using the same learned NuSPAN across different seismic traces, it requires less model parameters than the conventional CNN. The results also show that the learned NuSPAN (as well as its inverse model) is able to handle the irregular sparse patterns encountered in seismic reflectivity better than the conventional CNN. Finally, the performance of the learned NuSPAN (as well as its inverse model) is also evaluated in a seismic synthetic data set from Western Greenland. The results indicate that the learned NuSPAN is capable of reducing the rank of the convolutional network by at least an order of magnitude. As a result of its ability to explore the sparsity of the problem at a lower model parameter cost, the learned NuSPAN is capable of achieving significantly better results compared to the conventional CNN. The learned NuSPAN is also capable of being used as input to other learning methods such as iterative sparse recovery and alternating direction methods of optimization in a hybrid approach. The results from the hybrid approach indicate that the learned NuSPAN is capable of achieving a 3 dB improvement in terms of root mean square error compared to the conventional CNN. The learned NuSPAN is also capable of being used as input to other learning methods such as least square optimization and deep learning as an architecture component to further enhance the accuracy of seismic reflectivity recovery in future research studies. The integration of the learned NuSPAN into other learning methods has the potential to significantly reduce the size of the models by at least an order of magnitude. The results from the integration indicate that the learned NuSPAN is capable of achieving a 2 dB improvement in terms of root mean square error compared to the conventional CNN. The integration of the learned NuSPAN into other learning methods is also capable of reducing the number of parameters required to achieve comparable results in seismic reflectency recovery.

We introduce a multivariate spatial model for the peaks of extreme values in multi-dimensional data, focusing on particular challenges posed by extreme marine data. The natural spatial significant factors often fail to capture the extreme events' characteristics, which are often influenced by complex environmental and climatic factors. The self-exciting nature of extreme events enables a dynamic approach based on past events' intensity. However, this technique has limitations in dimensions higher than two and is not suitable for finite samples due to the necessity of treating events as point processes. To address these challenges, we developed a spatial conditional peak model as an alternative to the self-exciting method. The model enables the use of extreme events' properties in a higher-dimensional space and employs a Gaussian process to represent spatial relationships among extreme events' characteristics. The model's estimation is based on a weighted approach, utilizing a non-parametric kernel density to avoid multi-dimensional singular integral problems. Extensive empirical analysis confirms the model's effectiveness in a critical environmental context, specifically in forecasting extreme events' strong winds in the North Sea. The findings show that spatial relationships are significant for 50-75% of extreme events, while using wind speed as a proxy fails to account for significant spatial links. The model's practical applications in a predictive setting using Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate its effectiveness, while its limitations mainly stem from the requirement to treat events as point processes, which may lead to lost information due to the threshold selection issue. To overcome this shortcoming, research should focus on a new method that does not necessitate treating events as processes. Additionally, the model could be improved by incorporating an alternative spatial model that does not require complex mathematical integration, which would enhance its computational efficiency, specifically in a real-time predictive context. A critical next step could be to expand the model's use beyond wind speed and explore its potential in a broader range of environmental and climatic sciences. Furthermore, the model could be easily adapted for use in a Bayesian framework with informative priors as an alternative method for updating parameters based on additional information. Finally, the model's potential could be leveraged through the creation of an open-source software package that facilitates its adoption across various fields of application. The model's utility and next steps will become clear once results from a limited spatial extent experiment, currently in progress, are analyzed and the model's potential beyond extreme marine data is assessed. Currently, the largest advancements in vision-language models benefit from multi-modal pre-training with vast datasets like CLIP. However, this approach encounters challenges in understanding subtle relationships between images and text due to the diverse nature of potential correlations. To overcome these limitations, our technique integrates pre-training with a direction mechanism, enabling vision-directed text learning and simultaneous text-directed vision learning. This method is developed using a unified encoder for cross-modal learning, and we've created the VT-CLIP loss function to measure learning performance. Evaluations conducted on FLIC, Conceptual Captions, and Flickr30k datasets reveal significant enhancements of 3.0%, 2.2%, and 2.1% over the top-performing models, with our technique achieved zero-shot results comparable to fine-tuned results. Furthermore, our technique demonstrates improved generalizability across 21 additional datasets. Overall, our technique delivers enhanced performance across various vision-language benchmarks and exhibits better cross-modal learning robustness and generalizability. The source code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/whwu604/VT-CLIP.

The precise calculation of noisy interactions in complex biological networks faces a collaborative data scarcity challenge due to limited accessible data across various scales. To efficiently calculate noisy intensity distributions in such systems, we developed the universal operator switching formula. This formula expands the existing matrix product state renormalization method, offering a versatile and efficient solution that can be applied to noisy systems with or without symmetries. Notably, our proposed formula demonstrates superior scalability and computational efficiency when compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we validated the intrinsic symmetry of the formula itself using a mathematical proof. Through our findings, we demonstrate the utility of the universal operator switching formula in tackling complex problems in statistical physics, biology, and related fields. Specifically, we apply this formula to analyze the effects of noisy environmental factors on rhodopsin in the human retina, revealing new molecular properties. Our research and calculations indicate that subtle external factor interactions may play a significant role in biological processes, emphasizing the need for accurate calculations of interaction mechanisms in medicine and biology. Finally, we outline potential future research directions for tackling noisy systems in general and calculate operator switching in particular. Given a Noetherian local ring with a prime characteristic, we establish a key duality concerning artinian local rings that are formally invertible. Specifically, we show that the compact Hilbert function of such a ring is solely determined by the ring's Frobenius action on the local coordinate ring. Furthermore, this duality holds true for rings possessing a monomial order due to the direct relationship between the compact Hilbert function and the Frobenius action in such cases. As a direct application, we demonstrate that the ring's formal singularity and F-regularity are equivalent characteristics. We also derive a self-contained proof of a previously proposed conjecture regarding artinian local rings with a prime characteristic. Lastly, we show that the ring's regularity is solely determined by the ring's Frobenius action for certain types of rings, including those of codimension three or rings modeled after power series over the two-dimensional affine line. This specific fact provides a theoretical underpinning to explicit calculations recently performed by Li-Zhang in their study on three-dimensional local Fermat rings. Those calculations notably revealed that every local Fermat ring with a codimension of three possesses a regularity of six. As an additional note, the ring's formal singularity and F-regularity were previously established by Ulrich-Valla in their study on three-dimensional locally complete intersection rings. The current authors' findings, however, offer a novel and independent proof of that earlier result. The present paper's key contributions were initially presented at the January 2020 IMS Workshops on Commutative Algebra held in Baltimore. A related finding by the authors, regarding duality's implications for locally free modules of rank one over non-local Noetherian rings with a prime characteristic, was presented at the January 2018 Commutative Algebra and Algebraic Geometry conference held in Mumbai. We derive a surface expression for the Einstein-Hilbert action's variation using a suitable general concept of a manifold with boundaries, combining both differential forms and metrics. By linking this result to the Noether charge, we show that the Virasoro algebra's central extension is driven by the boundary terms of the Einstein-Hilbert action. Furthermore, combining these Noether charges leads to a previously unknown relationship between entropies from holography and from the Jackiw-Teitelboim model. We also explore the general form of the gravitational surface action, examine alternative approaches to deriving the Noether charge, and discuss the role of the boundary Lagrangian's variation in this context. Finally, we provide evidence that the surface Einstein-Hilbert action's variation satisfies the holographic entanglement entropy conjecture even when the manifold has multiple boundaries. The calculations in this work are expressed through the formal language of differential forms and their integrations on manifolds with boundaries. As a result, this work offers a comprehensive view of the topic, emphasizing the role of the Noether charge in linking the Virasoro algebra's central extension and two types of entropies from holography and from the Jackiw-Teitelboim model. The approach in this paper may be extended to other topics in the context of AdS/CFT correspondence. Using results from this paper and its prequel, we have presented three talks about the connection between Noether charges, Virasoro algebra's central extension and entropies from holography and from the Jackiw-Teitelboim model, which were held at an online conference on the integration of differential forms in November 2021. Additionally, this paper was completed with figures illustrating key mathematical concepts and their relationships. We have utilized the description of the manifold with boundaries from the book by's and the Noether charge from the paper by. The central extension of the Virasoro algebra was first established by Polyakov. The concept of entanglement entropy was introduced into conformal field theory by 't Hooft. In preprints, both Ba\~nados and Brown-Henneaux independently derived the Noether charge for the boundary of an anti-de Sitter gravity in three dimensions. In this paper and its preprint, we have extended the domain of this Noether charge to any dimension. In the evolving field of genomics, representing DNA sequences through visualization is becoming increasingly crucial for discovering hidden patterns within genomic data and efficiently analyzing it. Due to the rapidly increasing pace at which genomic data is gathered, establishing efficient techniques for representing and understanding these sequences becomes significantly more important. One promising approach to representing sequences is by utilizing dimensionality reduction methods, similar to those commonly applied in text analysis. However, the success of these methods depends on substantial amounts of labeled data, a resource that is expensive and time-consuming to obtain in the field of genomics. Consequently, novel research aims to automatically acquire comprehensive knowledge about genomic data from large-scale unlabelled datasets. This paper focuses on introducing an innovative DNA sequence embedding technique, known as SpEcTrU, which is an unsupervised method that reduces sequence complexity. By employing our approach, notable improvements have been discovered in representing and visualizing long DNA sequences, particularly in representing bacterial and viral genomes, yielding results that significantly outperform established techniques in a comparative study. This study proposes orientation-aware convolutional neural network architectures for image identification tasks, which account for the rotational influence of image content on classification. The framework's versatility allows for seamless integration with existing models, both with and without orientation representation modules. Our model's key features include a globally averaged orientation representation that simplifies integration with existing models, and a compact sub-pilaster representation that contrasts with global spatially-averaged approaches. Furthermore, the framework's components enhance model robustness and reduce hallucinations, particularly in scenarios where image content distribution varies by orientation. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through our enhanced CNNs' superior performance on the CUB-200-2011 bird dataset, where our model's shadow variation reduction maximally augmented benefit potential. Our source code is available at a publicly accessible GitHub repository. To facilitate model comparison, we have created an interactive tool that replicates our results, along with a benchmarking repository with pre-trained models and datasets for ease of use. Our main contribution is threefold: new insights on image content distribution variation by orientation, a method for reducing texture variation by orientation, and a set of best practices for identifying images through orientation-aware deep learning models. Our research reveals that an orientation representation that is too sophisticated can actually diminish a model's ability to distinguish between classes, especially when the class distribution varies by orientation, a phenomenon we term 'orientation overfitting.' Our results also show that an orientation-aware model can learn to accurately distinguish between classes with significantly less training, a form of sample efficiency. This suggests that an orientation-aware model can successfully classify a larger set of classes or train on a dataset with more variables. Additionally, our research shows that an orientation-aware model can be used to automatically label datasets and fill gaps in existing ones, providing a method for filling missing images in the CARS200 dataset. Our model's success is a step towards developing general image classification models that can successfully classify images across different orientations and are more resilient to changes in orientation, a crucial requirement for working with raw image data from cameras without any processing. Our work is a significant advancement towards automatically removing the bias introduced by image orientation in the results of classification models. Our research is a starting point for a line of future research on automatically removing the bias introduced by other factors in the results of classification models. The concept of intervals with a spatial curvature offers a more dynamic understanding than straight lines. Building upon this, a generalized version of the trace equation is proposed for curved linear intervals. Its utility is demonstrated through the application to Fibonacci curves and a generalization of the Fibonacci sequence. Additionally, a theory for Gaussian curves and curves defined by the Langevin equation is developed, which is consistent with the established framework of Brownian and reversible Brownian curves. A novel equation is derived for true self-similar curves, enabling the identification of newly discovered families such as Fibonacci-Goldberg curves. These families are found to possess positive Fuss-Catalan numbers and the curves are found to be stochastically stable. Moreover, a generalization of the Catalan numbers to n-dimensional spaces is proposed. We outline the potential expansion of this work, including applications to other types of curves. Finally, a connection is made between the trace equation and a generalized version of the Polya equation for curved intervals. It is proposed that the Polya equation can be utilized to construct suitable wavefunctions for curves that exhibit symmetry. The proposed framework has the potential to lead to novel functional invariants for curved intervals in general. It is suggested that this and similar equations may hold a key to understanding integral transforms for curved intervals in the future. Currently employed COVID-19 detection methods rely on pulmonary CT scans taken at least eight hours after infection, often accompanied by lung density analysis. For faster results, researchers have turned to quantitative measures derived from pulmonary HRCT images. However, since some COVID-19 patients may not exhibit visible symptoms on HRCT, a more sensitive detection method is needed. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of a two-stage capsule network for detecting COVID-19 from low-dose CT scans, revealing superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, a time-distributed capsule network is introduced, enabling the model to adapt to varying data sizes and efficiently utilize GPU resources. This approach enables the detection of COVID-19 and normal/control cases from imbalanced datasets. Our study utilizes three datasets: Wuhan, China-based patients with pulmonary issues, COVID-19 patients with chest HRCT images, and normal/control cases from CT scans. Due to the time-consuming process of labeling data with medical expertise, only a small normal/control dataset is available. A data augmentation strategy is employed to expand the dataset and create a more comprehensive training corpus. The model's accuracy and robustness are evaluated using the entire training set in a semi-supervised manner. This approach outperforms existing methods, with particularly strong results for the Wuhan and normal/control datasets. For the COVID-19 dataset, the F1 score is reported as 0.86 due to the model's slight imbalance in predicting true positives over false positives. This research contributes to the development of a sensitive detection method for COVID-19 and normal/control cases from low-quality CT images, with potential expanded applications to other visual classification tasks. As the use of machine learning techniques in good and bad decisions grows, it highlights the need for making their processes more transparent and explainable to users, especially in critical domains like the online shopping and law industries. Explainable AI (XAI) is now a high priority in research, with the development of new methods to provide clear and understandable interpretations for machine learning models. Among these methods, LIME is a popular technique used for providing understandable interpretations. A variation of this technique known as LIME-RS aims to improve the interpretability of machine learning models by leveraging the structure of data. In this study, we evaluated the effectiveness of LIME-RS in providing transparent explanations for recommendation models compared to traditional LIME. The results showed that LIME-RS provides localizable and comprehensible interpretations in a set of datasets, outperforming the traditional approach. Moreover, we found that the complexity of data affects the accuracy and consistency of interpretations provided by LIME-RS. These findings open up new avenues for enhancing the transparency of machine learning models used in recommendation systems. The development of these techniques could eventually lead to the creation of explainable recommendation systems that meet legal requirements, providing users with the transparency needed to make informed decisions. Interestingly, the study revealed a distinction between the accuracy of interpretations provided by LIME-RS (local interpretability) and the stability of these interpretations (global interpretability). While the accuracy of interpretations was affected by dataset complexity, the stability of these interpretations was found to be influenced by the consistency of training datasets. These findings are expected to facilitate the development of explainable machine learning models used in recommendation systems. The code used in this study has been made available for others to build upon. A pre-recorded video of this study's findings is also shared for the community. The study is expected to inspire future research in making machine learning models used in recommendation systems more transparent. In particular, the study is expected to inspire research into providing globalizable interpretations, improving the transparency of machine learning models used in recommendation systems. By applying a continuity correction, a bias-adjusted PCR estimate is obtained. Just like conventional PCR, this metric ranges from 0 to 1 and can be employed for both observed and predicted data. Traditional approaches fail to produce realistic 360-degree views directly due to the complexity of natural scenes. Recently, neural rendering-based methods have made progress in this area by leveraging pre-existing 360-degree datasets and separating scene and view information using neural radiance fields. We've developed a new framework that uses input-output data from complex systems to predict their future behavior, optimize their performance, and ensure smooth operation. Our methodology is model-independent, adaptation-free, and requires minimal structural information. It utilizes advanced black-box methods, including dynamic mode decomposition and optimization, to identify and refine performance limitations and the best settings for system parameters. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on a network-based epidemiological model, yielding better outcomes compared to traditional control methods in a comparative study. This method showcases the significant potential of data-driven strategies in complex system management. Our accompanying code has been made available to facilitate widespread adoption. This work presents an innovative pathway for tackling the challenges associated with modeling and optimizing intricate, multi-scale systems driven by nonlinear processes. Its applications extend beyond the forecasting and enhancement of networked epidemic models to a broad array of dynamic network management and optimization tasks. Moreover, the framework can be adapted for the analysis of time-series data in fields such as neuroscience, neuroscience-inspired systems, and liquid-based communication systems. Our investigation also contributes to the ongoing debate regarding the trade-offs between model-based and data-driven approaches as well as the emerging field of machine learning in system analysis and optimization. It is anticipated that the insights presented here will foster future research in machine learning and system modeling. Our study's findings can inspire the development of new computational tools and algorithms for system analysis and optimization, ultimately advancing the intersection of machine learning and system dynamics. Our accompanying code can serve as a valuable resource and starting point for future research in this area. In the broader context of system analysis and optimization, the insights presented here can initiate a paradigm shift from traditional adaptation-based to fixed, data-driven approaches, to mitigate the ongoing challenges associated with modeling and adaptation in system dynamics. This study is part of a larger body of work, the summary of which can be found at arXiv:2202.00973. Our research has significant implications for a variety of fields, including the analysis of liquid-based communication systems, neuronal systems, epidemiological models, and other multi-scale systems. In the near future, the community may move towards a framework that integrates data-driven and model-based approaches to system analysis and optimization, based on the system's available information and the trade-offs between the two methods. Our accompanying code can start the starting point for future research in system analysis and optimization.
