Simulations of a black hole's shadow can serve as conclusive evidence for the presence of exotic matter surrounding a supermassive black hole in the center of a galaxy. To conduct these simulations in the future, we suggest modeling the matter using PopSyCLE, a flexible framework designed for (1) developing algorithms that naturally distribute matter, and (2) accurately simulating systems with phasar interactions, including general relativity. Our project involves multiple scenarios, such as various types of matter, multiple forms of interaction, and the presence of a plane of collisional matter. PopSyCLE allows us to (1) create simple, natural distributions of matter, and (2) model matter that is not spherically symmetric. These simulations enhance our understanding of a black hole's environment and serve as a foundation for developing scenarios that naturally include exotic matter. Furthermore, by using the concept of a natural distribution, we can perform the actual optimization of algorithms designed to simulate matter distributions that resemble those predicted by cosmological models. To this end, we have identified several objectives that mimic the characteristics of cosmic structure and primordial black holes in order to (1) develop algorithms that naturally distribute matter, and (2) accurately simulate systems with phasar interactions, including general relativity. Our work is foundational in nature and serves as a stepping stone for technological advancements in modeling black hole environments in the presence of exotic matter. Language model pre-training has been successfully applied to various downstream tasks through direct and indirect decoupling methods. However, pre-trained models often contain many adjustable parameters, making decoupling expensive. To tackle this issue, we developed an efficient framework for decoupling, which incorporates Unique Token Adaptation with early stopping. This approach adjusts only the relevant model components for each task and introduces task-specific unique tokens to distinguish them from the general knowledge embedded in the pre-trained model. We implemented and evaluated our framework on six text-related tasks, including two classification and four generation tasks. Compared to the traditional PLM fine-tuning method, our framework yielded comparable or superior results, but with a significant reduction in the number of adjustable parameters, specifically 2.25 times fewer. Furthermore, we successfully adapted our framework to zero-shot settings, which resulted in a satisfactory performance with a accuracy of 0.2446 on the evaluation metrics. Our results suggest that Unique Token Adaptation is an efficient and effective decoupling strategy. We released the framework's open-source implementation on GitHub at https://github.com/atenxia/UTA. Our experiments provide valuable insights into the usage of pre-trained models and how to efficiently fine-tune them according to specific tasks and resource constraints. What's more, our framework is flexible and can be extended to support a variety of text-related tasks including natural language inference and machine translation. We hope that our work contributes to the development of efficient model architecture and provides inspiration for future research. We are pleased to release our framework as a resource to the NLP community. This research has been supported by the Grant No. U1831101 from the National Natural Science Foundation of China. To the best of our knowledge, our framework is the first to successfully apply early stopping to pre-trained models for various text processing tasks. We have thoroughly documented our research and released our framework as an open-source contribution to the NLP community, which we hope will spark future research. Our framework's main differentiating feature is the innovative application of Unique Token Adaptation with early stopping, a technique that efficiently fine-tunes only the relevant model components for each task and introduces task-specific unique tokens to distinguish them from the general knowledge embedded in the pre-trained model. To the best of our knowledge, this technique has not been proposed in previous research, which we hope will spark future research. This study introduces a method for calculating the Kontsevich weights of graphs related to symplectic Poisson systems and their curvature graphs, a specific type of elliptic partial differential equation. By employing this technique, we demonstrate that the primary variables and their interactions in the Hamiltonian formulation remain under algebraic control. Additionally, we show that the symmetry inherent in the symplectic structure prevents a similar explosion of variables in the curvature graphs, thus yielding simple, solvable ODEs for any stationary Hamiltonian structure. Consequently, when solving the Hamilton-Duffing equations, which arise from a canonical symplectic structure combined with a quadratic potential, we derive a single first-order ordinary differential equation along with two nonlinear second-order equations. Similarly, for linear coupling in the time-harmonic case, we obtain a first-order equation along with two second-order equations that involve only quadratic nonlinearities. Notably, this formulation provides an explicit solution expressed through elliptic arcsine functions. A similar approach yields similar simplifications for the curvatures in systems featuring non-degenerate quadratic Poisson structures. However, for degenerate Poisson structures, the situation is more complex due to the presence of boundary terms that may require special treatment. On the other hand, when dealing with elliptic PDEs derived from degenerate quadratic Poisson structures, the boundary terms can often be omitted by adopting a suitable 'physical space' approach to interpretation. Moreover, when handling linear coupling of elliptic PDEs, the system can be reduced to a set of first-order linear equations whose solutions are readily obtained via well-known methods. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of superintegrability of elliptic PDEs, which we demonstrate in the case of linear coupling. A collection of related mathematical notes and software is available online at the website https://tanpop92.github.io/math/. The software utilizes the Xarray package for numerical computing and the BrownGraphs package for graph theory, both of which offer simplified functionality not typically found in the standard Python NumPy and PyTorch implementations. An alternative implementation without external dependencies can be found in the TANPOP repository. Although we have focused on the context of Poisson structures, the underlying methods hold more broad significance. In fact, a key advantage of our approach lies in its potential for easy adaptation and application to a wide range of dynamical systems, as illustrated by the accompanying example of a mechanical system featuring conservative coupling, which has been generated using the provided code at https://github.com/TANPOP92/mechanical_

In a recent publication, Huang et al. (2021) developed a comprehensive framework for pricing Asian options using a stochastic factor. We aim to prove that this approach is inherently too restrictive and we will provide an alternative, more general method. Specifically, we will show that one-dimensional projective products of ergodic Markov chains cannot simultaneously meet two critical criteria as outlined by Huang et al. for four specific paths. By analyzing the necessary conditions for pricing perfection in two specific cases, we will derive upper bounds on the possible values for c and d. We will also introduce an alternative structure for pricing Asian options and provide numerical methods to determine its parameters. Finally, we will compare the performance of our proposed structure, referred to as the eCPAF, with the original model from Huang et al. by applying both to a range of typical Asian options featuring a Brownian motion, mean-reverting, or market model. The results will show that eCPAF outperforms h4F in nearly all instances, with a notable improvement in terms of the number of regime-switching variables, and eCPAF exhibits a more orderly transition between regimes. What's more, eCPAF incurs a level of computational complexity similar to or less than that of Huang et al.'s model, thereby allowing it to efficiently facilitate an online pricing service for a wide variety of Asian options. Such a platform would be very useful in a real-world setting. The source code for our numerical methods has been made available at https://github.com/jayc9/CPAF. As an added note, while our eCPAF model is still somewhat restrictive, it still offers a level of flexibility not seen in previous single-factor models and we hope to build upon this in future work. The proof of correctness for Huang et al.'s findings, by providing upper bounds for the values of c and d, marks an important step in the literature and we plan to explore the reverse problem (deriving lower bounds) in a future publication. Furthermore, we intend to develop efficient multivariate extensions of eCPAF. In terms of future work on numerical methods, we aim to create faster, non-linear solvers for eCPAF. As for applications, we would like to integrate our model with a machine learning-based option pricing system. Ultimately, our goal is to develop a precision-level online pricing service for a wide range of derivatives, including a real-time platform for pricing Asian options across multiple markets. The integration of eCPAF with such systems holds significant potential as a key component.

We conduct an in-depth quantitative examination of cosmic collider phenomena, specifically the production of massive particles with significantly differing masses, in contrast to conventional high-energy colliders. We identify the primary production mechanism as the double scattering of quantum fluctuations from quantum inflation, a process distinct from the commonly observed production of particles with similar masses via resonant states. Calculations of cross-sectional areas and average multiplication factors are performed for various particle configurations. Furthermore, we demonstrate how recent theoretical constraints on primordial features, derived from mild non-Gaussianity and gravitational wave spectra, can be combined with observations of large scale structure data to set stringent lower bounds on the production rates of the lightest possible cosmic colliders, specifically particles with masses greater than approximately 1 TeV, with production rates ranging from a few orders of magnitude greater than those predicted by tree level diagrams alone. We also show that observations of the cosmic microwave background data, specifically its lack of noticeable non-Gaussianity, serve as a strong lower limit on the production rates of extremely light cosmic colliders, specifically particles with masses less than approximately 1 MeV, with production rates ranging from a few orders of magnitude greater than those predicted by tree level diagrams alone. All of these results can be effectively understood through simplified models that quantify the magnitude factor by which an initially smooth quantum fluctuations landscape has been modulated and amplified. This simplification model has the added benefit of being compatible with various distinct cosmic collider configurations, specifically particle configurations with either significantly differing masses or similar masses. Moreover, in the context of the magnitude factor model, theoretical constraints on primordial features can be seamlessly reinterpreted as limits on the efficient production rates of particles with arbitrarily large or small masses. Finally, in the interest of promoting future research, we note that experiments involving cosmic collider phenomena, specifically particle production in the early universe, can be effectively distinguished from standard high-energy particle physics experiments by incorporating analytical models describing the early universe's unique cosmological settings and conditions. This distinction can be achieved through a straightforward extension of existing simulation software and algorithms used in high-energy particle physics experiments. Such a separation between these two classes of phenomena can be viewed as being confirmed at two distinct levels, a purely theoretical level and an experimental testing level. In this work, we have explicitly detailed and implemented the experimental testing level case. In contrast, the confirmation of the separation based on theoretical considerations is addressed in a companion paper. Together, these two separate but comprehensive analyses effectively validate the distinction between cosmic collider phenomena and standard high energy particle physics experiments. By taking the risk aversion parameter r greater than or equal to 0, and the parameter gamma greater than or equal to 0, we develop a model where the logging of the ratio of financial wealth to a benchmark or the logarithm of 1 plus the ratio of financial wealth to a benchmark is applied. This results in a HARA-type absolute and a CARA-ARLITA-type relative power utility function, both of which are homogenous of 1 - gamma. By assuming complete and infinite market dynamics, we find an analytical solution for the optimal portfolio in the form of a strategy tree and derive an equation for the value of the optimal portfolio. This is the first time such an optimal portfolio has been found for a relative profit function. The complete RAG framework consists of two components: a retrieval module that extracts relevant documents from a given query, followed by a generation module that synthesizes responses based on the retrieved documents. The proposed frameworks were evaluated on data sets including our own, generated through human-like questioning and responding, and showed superior performance and coherence compared to the original RAG framework. Microtasks, such as those distributed via Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform, are gaining traction in various fields of NLP research. Although participating workers have demonstrated a wide range of writing abilities, from being relatively unskilled to being proficient in summarizing content, selecting an experienced writer for a specific task can be a challenge. In our study, we aimed to identify Mechanical Turk workers with strong summarization capabilities. To achieve this, we created a comprehensive evaluation that combines high-level skills with straightforward comprehension. By analyzing the results of this evaluation, we discovered a substantial gap in skills held by Mechanical Turk workers, ranging from basic comprehension to experienced writers with graduate-level proficiency. In contrast to less skilled workers, expert writers exhibit significantly higher performance in key aspects of task comprehension. Due to their superior skills, these workers complete tasks much faster. In our experiments with a live MTurk population, we developed an algorithm that leverages performance and response time to identify top-tier authors. Our focus is on text-text retrieval, specifically the text-clip retrieval (TCR) branch of text-vision, where incoming text and vision features from a particular location or scene must be matched. Current TCR approaches rely on a pre-trained visual language model (VLM) that takes text and vision features, often from specific points or regions within a clip, and performs cross-modal attention to match query and candidate features. Since these features may not always sufficiently capture the overall meaning of the input text or the scene's visual content, we propose an enhanced Transformer model. This new model, called TS2-Net, is based on Token Shift and Selection (TSS), which allows the selection of relevant tokens from the input text and the shifting of tokens from the vision feature map to create new, semantically rich features. This paper introduces the concept of a sweeping procedure that incorporates integral conditions. We redefine the motion of a body based on its interaction with and response to the forces and torques applied across specified areas or surfaces. The applied forces and torques are described by distribution-valued functions, and our goal is to elucidate their effect on the motion of the body. To address this challenge, we develop a comprehensive mathematical model that describes the motion of the body and its associated flow for all positive time, leveraging properties of measures and distributions. The resulting model and its associated solution regime are validated through various existence and uniqueness analyses, including primary results demonstrating the existence of solutions to the modified sweeping procedure and a detailed mapping diagram that illustrates the long-term behavior of solutions. The long-term behavior of solutions is characterized by two distinct sets, and our analysis demonstrates that the solution flow maps are weakly continuous with respect to time. The solution mapping also exhibits the invariance of a closed, positively invariant subset of the cone condition, and we identify specific scenarios in which these solutions are uniquely determined. The logical structure of our solution mapping is examined in the context of two main cases: the case in which the integral conditions are absent, resulting in a standard sweeping procedure, and the case in which these conditions are present, resulting in a more complex, integral sweeping procedure. The application of these cases is illustrated through two examples, including a scenario in which a body is subject to a force applied across its entire surface and a more complex scenario in which a body is subject to forces applied across disjoint, bounded regions of its surface. The solution flow maps for these cases are analyzed and described in detail. The integrity of our solution mapping is further demonstrated in the context of a unique scenario in which these solutions are globally attractive. The solution mapping also satisfies a key system property: the solution flow maps are locally Lipschitz, and this result is essential for establishing the local uniqueness of solutions to the modified integral sweeping procedure. The solution mapping also satisfies a key system property: the solution flow maps are semilocal, and this result is essential for establishing the semilocal uniqueness of solutions to the modified integral sweeping procedure. The system properties of our solution mapping are the basis for a range of open problems, including the challenge of proving the global uniqueness of solutions to the modified integral sweeping procedure, an open problem that remains active in the context of the standard sweeping procedure, where solutions may be globally defined. In the realm of networks, nodes and edges play distinct roles, with some being more central than others, as seen in various real-world applications including social media, chemical compounds, traffic patterns, and email exchanges. The task of measuring node importance has been extensively researched, but when a network's structure evolves over time, as with growing social media platforms or increasing city road systems, traditional measures can be overly conservative and fail to account for the changing importance landscape. This study draws inspiration from the concept of embedding objects in low-dimensional spaces to develop a framework for evolving graphs. This framework enables us to represent each node as a point in a low-dimensional space and update it dynamically as the graph evolves over time. Multiple embedding algorithms can be used, and the framework is evaluated by applying various centrality measures to multiple graphs, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing the evolving importance of nodes. Furthermore, a discussion on the limitations of existing centrality measures and the effectiveness of the embedding framework is provided along with a comprehensive analysis of the results. The benefit of using this framework is illustrated by demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying key nodes for monitoring in the case of an attack on a network and the optimal nodes for investment when faced with an attack or a spread of a disease or virus. The presented method is also validated by applying it to various synthetic and real-world networks, confirming its effectiveness in capturing the evolving importance of nodes. The complete code used in this study is available for review on the linked repository. The importance of updating node embeddings in low-dimensional space is graphically illustrated by providing a physical analogy, as seen in the added appendix. Calculating the ground-state properties of this configuration using the $^3$H-4n Gaussian overlap approximation, we derive the $^7$H separation energy with considerable precision, predicting it to be around 23 MeV, in close agreement with the 20.5 MeV estimated in an earlier experimental study. Additionally, our calculations reveal a significant error in a 2012 theoretical assessment, which attributed the $^7$H ground state's negative separation energy to an erroneous estimate of the $^7$H ground state's binding energy, corrected here in light of our findings as a resonance of $^3$H and 4 neutrons. As a result, our work suggests that these isotopes should be producible using an $^3$H+4n fusion using a $^4$He beam. Consequently, our recommendations aim to guide future experimental projects focused on the $^7$H resonance series. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that this theoretical resonance has the potential to be a key elementary building block for the island of stability consisting of neutron-rich hydrogen-like isotopes. approaches, including the autoencoder. The standard method for measuring the
distance between images is the mean squared error, which has been shown to be
insufficient for learning optimal representations. This paper introduces a new
method for measuring distance between images, based on the Wasserstein distance,
to tackle this issue. The Wasserstein distance is known to be effective in preserving
the underlying structure of data, especially in its modified form known as the
Sinkhorn distance. However, calculating Sinkhorn distances is computationally
expensive, which has previously limited its use in machine learning algorithms.
This paper demonstrates that it is feasible to efficiently use Sinkhorn distances
in training autoencoders through batch optimization techniques. The resulting
autoencoders can be applied more broadly in semi-supervised learning and
reconstruction-based adversarial training. The computational complexity of
calculating Sinkhorn distances is shown to be O(N^2), where N is the number of
data points, and this cost can be reduced to O(N) using batch optimization.
Furthermore, our approach enables the use of Gaussian covariance and Laplacian
matrices, leading to state-of-the-art results in semi-supervised learning. The
method achieves an accuracy of 99.5% on the MNIST dataset and 7.2% on the CIFAR10
dataset, outperforming previous methods. The source code for our approach can be
found at https://github.com/andrebarba/representations. Our results demonstrate
that unsupervised deep neural networks, trained with Sinkhorn distances, can
captivate and manipulate visual data, which has implications for various tasks

One notable effect observed was the reduced efficacy of contact tracing in the North West region compared to the South West, raising questions about the effectiveness of regional tracing efforts. Our study aims to assess the return on the investment of resources for each regional tracing collaboration. These findings have far-reaching implications and can be seamlessly transitioned to the analysis of other infectious disease outbreaks. A crucial factor in many manufacturing automation systems is an eye-in-hand camera for analyzing workpieces. Nonetheless, calibrating these cameras poses a significant challenge due to the numerous possible orientations and poses of workpieces and cameras. Prior studies have focused on calculating a camera's position and orientation based on three key poses: a fundamental position, a pose showing the front and back sides, and a third pose for determining rotation. Nevertheless, when only the front and back sides of a workpiece are visible in the third pose, the calculated camera position often results in an unfeasible orientation. Consequently, direct application of previous methods is not always possible in practical scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose introducing a trainable convolutional neural network to predict adjustments to a camera's orientation. Our approach involves generating simulated images based on hypothetical camera poses and training the convolutional neural network to calculate necessary adjustments based on these images. We also employ a novel front-to-back image translation technique that enables reliable calculation of camera poses even when only the front and back sides are visible. Our algorithm's effectiveness is validated through experiments on multiple models manufactured via 3D printing and a 2008 PR2 Robot Challenge workpiece model, with our method outperforming previous fundamental pose-based methods. Furthermore, our algorithm can be executed in as little as 0.5 seconds on a mobile device, making it highly suitable for real-world manufacturing applications. Lastly, our study demonstrates the potential for combining our method with prior approaches to achieve even more accurate results. We address the inverse reinforcement learning problem where a complementary agent mimics the behavior of an expert player by learning their policy using observed behavior and a learner-memory system. The latter serves as a simplified version of the growing neural network used in most existing approaches. We demonstrate that this simplified model is sufficient and offer proof that it generates a unique optimal estimator for the expert's policy. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of its computational aspects and compare its performance in a player of chess. We also explore the practical benefits of this approach by applying it to the problem of imitating the behavior of a state-of-the-art Atari game player using a neural network policy. The resulting model enables the transfer of knowledge from a master model to a more compact system, resulting in a lightweight agent that mimics the expert's behavior. Such an agent can be deployed on devices with limited resources, opening up possibilities for real-time online learning and complementary gameplay. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through a comparison of its performance with that of existing inverse reinforcement learning methods on a variety of tasks. Furthermore, we showcase the applications of our model by demonstrating its ability to seamlessly integrate with off-the-shelf reinforcement learning methods, such as Deep Reinforcement Learning, without compromising either learning process. As a result, our approach enables the creation of a cohesive and harmonious system of complementary agents that work in unison with existing learning algorithms, ultimately leading to a synergistic effect. We validate the practical utility of our model by successfully mimicking the behavior of a state-of-the-art Atari game player using a neural network policy. Extended versions of this research are publicly available on the companion websites: https://publications.ai/dadabecb/ and https://publications.ai/6cda9d6c/. Additional information can also be found at the following repositories: https://github.com/jayelzes/irl-differentiable-learner and https://github.com/jayelzes/ild. The derived code has been openly sourced for other researchers to build upon, with support and collaborative modifications encouraged through the adoption of the Governance Participation Recognition License (GPRL). We have explicitly included our model's design and development limitations and hope that this research sparks the creation of additional iterations and advancements, ultimately contributing to a more robust and reliable reinforcement learning ecosystem. Moreover, a playable version of the model's behavior can be accessed at https://rtfeldman.github.io/Iluminati. The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the Milky Way galaxy by studying approximately 1 billion small to medium-sized stars over a period of at least 10 years. This report will provide an in-depth overview of the mission, covering its scientific objectives, instrumentation, data analysis processes, operational framework, testing phases, and key characteristics associated with the spacecraft and ground-based processing systems. Additionally, the report will offer an update on the current status of the mission and outline future plans, taking into account any lessons learned or difficulties encountered so far. A comprehensive overview of the mission will be presented, focusing on aspects involving the spacecraft and ground-based components, as well as the scientific aspects and operational aspects of the mission. This report will also explore the potential applications and considerations of using the Gaia mission for various astronomical observations, such as astrophysics, planetary science, and astrobiology. However, this topic will not be the primary focus of the report. Once the mission is operational and data collection begins, a follow-up report will be written to share lessons learned, potential difficulties encountered, and additional information on the Gaia mission. This follow-up report is set to be issued approximately two years after the completion of the initial data collection period, providing an update on the processing of the data, testing of the data analysis processes, and initial findings of the Gaia mission. A presentation based on this report was initially presented at the 2005 Astrobiology Science Conference, and the findings from the Gaia mission are set to be presented at the 2009 conference, offering an update on the current status of the mission. The present document will provide an in-depth overview of the mission, but it is anticipated that the information may need to be revised once the data analysis processes are implemented and the results of the Gaia mission are known. For determining the treewidth of a graph, which is a crucial structural property defining optimal parameterized complexity, researchers have been exploring efficient (under the PTAS), NP-approximation algorithms since the 80s. A key obstacle in treewidth approximation stems from the necessity of maintaining adjoiny structures to enable vertex removal evaluations. Our innovation involves the introduction of'space-effective vertex dividers', allowing us to freely apply them without necessitating the maintenance of adjointy, thus significantly reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, we propose a polynomial-time approximation solution utilizing a new vertex cutter technique. Additionally, we illustrate the applicability of our approach to approximate clique-width and genus within bounded-degree graphs. Furthermore, we propose an iterative version of our method, providing a universal tool for dealing with treewidth approximation and showing its potential in achieving PTAS without the need for expensive structures. Furthermore, we show that our method has a specific limit in its approximation capacity. Ontologies provide organized frameworks for modeling interconnected knowledge and have a wide range of applications in diverse domains, including artificial intelligence, biomedical research, and computer science courses. Visualizations that showcase the organizational structure of ontologies can enhance teaching methodologies and facilitate understanding, especially among students. However, graph visualizations that represent class relationships as nodes and relationships as edges often fail to offer a comprehensive understanding of ontologies due to several limitations, such as not being able to visualize cycles, hiding relationships, and inadequate support for large-scale networks. In response to these limitations, we have developed OntoPlot, a novel visualization approach designed to provide intuitive insights into ontologies through an innovative, non-hierarchical graph structure. Building on Sankey diagrams, OntoPlot visualizes multiple relationships of individual classes and their distributions, enabling users to identify patterns such as redundant relationships, overlapping domains, and hierarchical incoherencies. In addition, OntoPlot's interactive features allow for enhanced user experience by seamlessly zooming out and zooming in, as well as accessing enriched information with a simple click. In order to demonstrate the capabilities of our ontology visualization method, we have applied OntoPlot to a computer science course ontology and a biomedical ontology focused on Cancer Biology. In this study, we showcase the value of interactive visualizations in discovering ontology limitations and present various use cases that can be further extended to more complex knowledge engineering applications and beyond. In order to easily implement OntoPlot for educators and researchers, we have made the source code accessible through our public GitHub repository at https://github.com/AndreaCimino/OntoPlot. As a result, this tool can be freely utilized for visualizing and sharing large-scale ontologies with non-hierarchical relationships at https://onto.pl, our public OntoPlot server. In conclusion, OntoPlot represents an innovative visualization approach that provides a new perspective on ontologies through data-driven and interactive visualizations. In the future, we plan to further develop OntoPlot and explore additional use cases that involve sharing and visualizing large ontologies with non-hierarchical relationships. In addition, we believe that OntoPlot's innovative visualization layout is a promising candidate for being incorporated into other taxonomy engineering libraries, such as Wikipedia. In order to further improve OntoPlot's interactive features, we also aim to optimize its performance by identifying and addressing potential scalability limitations. In particular, we have already identified an optimization opportunity related to edge duplication in Wikipedia's taxonomy network, which we plan to explore in a related journal article. Moreover, with our approach, the required voice restoration model does not need to be retrained, and it also enhances the speech clarity without affecting speaker identity. All our research findings are publicly available on our GitHub repository.

Traditional computer vision models are often ineffectively applied in modern deep neural networks due to their potential to create labeled noise during training. Consequently, researchers have been exploring ways to circumvent this issue by developing methods for automatically eliminating false positives. In this study, a novel technique called box reordering is introduced for the task of pedestrian detection. Box reordering is a straightforward approach that assigns a score to each bounding box based on the classification confidence and Inception score, and then truncates the distribution above a set threshold. Comprehensive evaluations were conducted on a plethora of pedestrian datasets, revealing that box reordering is particularly effective in large-scale pedestrian detection tasks across public datasets and showcasing its merit of noise suppression in both offline and online settings. Furthermore, box reordering is effectively applied to domain adaptive pedestrian detection using label-free techniques. Our findings also highlight its superior performance in reducing false positives without compromising localization accuracy. The source code for box reordering is available for public use on the GitHub repository 'Box Reordering'. 

In detail, our paper's key contributions are threefold:
- Box reordering is introduced as a cost-free method for eliminating false positives in object detection tasks.
- Extensive evaluations were conducted on a plethora of pedestrian detection datasets.
- Box reordering is successfully applied to domain adaptive pedestrian detection using label-free techniques. 

Our findings also show that box reordering can be combined with existing object detection models, such as Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet, to significantly improve their robustness and efficiency in pedestrian detection tasks across challenging scenarios. Lastly, the source code for box reordering has been made accessible to the research community and will hopefully inspire the development of similar techniques to tackle unsupervised object detection tasks. The potential benefits of using generative adversarial networks (GANs) for music generation are still being explored. A significant obstacle in the development of music generation algorithms arises from the need to significantly increase the complexity of output data without providing corresponding labels. This challenge is similar to that encountered in the process of image upscaling. A music generation model, based on multi-scale autoencoders combined with GANs, is proposed to overcome this difficulty. By leveraging a large, pre-trained automatic transcriber and converting music into a pulse rate wave (PWC) representation, the model enables the generation of labeled multi-scale annotations, which are then used to reconstruct the audio. Notably, when compared to existing methods, the proposed model produces more coherent and sustained outcomes. Moreover, the integration of the automatic transcriber and PWC conversion allows for a direct relationship between the model's internal representations and the well-established field of music information retrieval. The model's capabilities can also be expanded through the use of additional GAN trainers, providing an efficient and flexible framework for music generation. Visual comparisons and objective evaluations demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over state-of-the-art approaches. Relevant source code and demonstration videos can be found at the provided website. Keywords: music generation,GANs,multi-scale architecture, automatic transcriber,PWC representation. In virtual environments, the effectiveness of a game controller's interaction can be manipulated by the designer. However, some misleading visual feedback may sometimes be provided to users, disrupting their normal game interactions. Our research focuses on the impact of errant throwing movements in virtual games with visual realism. Through a survey of existing studies and initial user tests, we uncovered the throwing movements (such as overarm or underarm throws) expected by users in both casual and sports games. Additionally, we found that user performance deteriorates when the point of release viewed on a head-mounted display does not match the actual throw technique employed. Our findings suggest that incorrect throwing movements result in reduced accuracy and increased frustration for users. Ultimately, we recommend transparent and consistent visual feedback of the virtual object's trajectory. Since this requires a unified understanding of user expectations, we propose a framework for determining expected throwing movements based on game type. This framework can aid designers in determining the initial and target positions of the virtual object and the throwing technique involved. Our study offers guidelines for optimizing the interaction in both casual and sports games. These guidelines also encourage designers to maintain transparent and consistent user feedback. Finally, we outline methods for determining the expected throwing movements of users and suggest that game designers implement user training to tailor the virtual object's trajectory. This can be achieved by adjusting the point of release based on various throwing techniques such as overarm or underarm throws and taking into account the physical properties of objects being simulated. Our study resulting findings are applicable to a wide variety of games involving virtual objects such as bowling, archery, or tennis. In summary, our study results provide essential insights for designers to enhance the user experience by understanding the impacts of erroneous point of release in throwing movements. This research investigates the impacts of errors on virtual games that involve simulations. While simulations provide a means to create a more immersive user experience, the effects of logical errances on user behaviour in these games are not well understood. In order to ensure that users are not hindered by erroneous visual feedback, designers should strive to provide accurate and logical visual feedback. Our study initially evaluated the impacts of errors on the fauf throw on both arm movements and impact points in both tennis and bowling games. By representing sentence structures as trees and assigning linguistic significance to tree branches, the translation process can be viewed as traversing a syntactic network. However, conventional methods that link sentences to tree structures have a limitation in accounting for the inherent linguistic connections within the sentences themselves. In response to this constraint, our study proposes an innovative method that builds upon the translation process by assigning meaning to the tree branches using syntactic links. Additionally, we develop an interpretive tool that provides detailed, step-by-step analysis of the translation process, giving us a deeper understanding of the translation system's language use. The results of our experiments show that this method significantly improves the accuracy of the translation system and provides valuable insights into its language generation patterns. In comparison to the existing methods, our approach yields more reliable and detailed interpretation results. Examples of our interpretation tool's output are presented alongside the relevant tree structures and syntactic links in the paper. In particular, our interpretation reveals the translation system's preference for the word "novel" in situations where there are multiple possible word choices. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the translation system's use of the word "well" is often conditioned by the grammatical context. In addition to the interpretation results, our analysis demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving the highest ever reported scores on the WMT19 parser benchmark. In particular, our method achieves an impressive performance with a labeled tree parsing accuracy of 66.9%. We're seeing great achievement in the multiplicative stochastic model proposed by Ge and Ma (Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and Applications, 2019, 532, 1238). This model represents particle growth through a multiplicative process. We offer comprehensive analyses of both theoretical execution and numerical tests. Due to specific requirements of practical applications, we also develop a model variant, where the lower limit of a sample-specific distribution is tied to the previous time step's sample value. This allows us to handle scenarios where growth cannot yield negative values, thus enhancing model applicability. Our variant's efficacy in simulating particle-particle interactions is demonstrated. We also explore using MMSMs as a foundation for learning multiplicative models from empirical data, and an example application demonstrates the capability of our method to distinguish monofractal and multifractal time series. Our studies also include measurements of characteristic indices and their practical meaning, as well as a comparison of MMSMs with special lower limit (MMSM-L) and traditional distribution models. Numerical simulations show that MMSMs and MMSM-L possess identical fractal properties as measured by the capacity dimension, an energy density measure. This, and other results, reveal that MMSMs and MMSM-L produce highly symmetric probability distributions for growth increments and initial values, as well as absolute differences between consecutive growth values. Furthermore, our variant and traditional models exhibit equal scalability properties. Finally, our work includes an application of MMSMs and numerical analyses on real-world datasets. We hope our research contributes to ongoing and future multiplicative stochastic model studies. It offers theoretical and numerical foundations, as well as practical applications and a new method for learning monofractal and multifractal time series from data. We used pandemic-related social distancing measures to maintain low risk levels for our research team. The study was completed in a timely fashion. We look forward to continuing our research in this field. This breakthrough is facilitated by the concept of eigenvalue spectra and our development of spectral shades, which are akin to quantum circuits but with fixed eigenvalue spectra instead of circuits. We've discovered that these shallow shades can serve as indicators for projection circuits through the application of the Spectral Shades Appraisal oracle. This use of shades represents a significant step towards addressing the challenges associated with validation in quantum development. Unlike the integrable square-everywhere potential scenario, solutions typically exhibit a large-k limit where the system displays a distinct reflexive behavior. Interestingly, the reflexive behavior can be attributed to the interaction between a soliton-like solution and a particular form of bound state. By applying a new approach inspired by a recently developed sum rule, we have demonstrated a specific asymptotic behavior for the reflection coefficient, showing a dense range of values as compared to a square profile, with implications that may be observed in the long-distance behavior of the solution's properties. We have explicitly shown the method applies to a specific case where a soliton-like solution and a dark hole waveform interact, resulting in a solution with a large-k limit reflexive behavior. In the realm of machine learning, self-improvement methods allow systems to enhance their performance on a variety of tasks through minimal supervision. Our study focuses on developing meta-learning algorithms capable of exploiting task relationships in both proprietary and open-source settings. It is common for systems to form inaccurate connections between tasks, resulting in suboptimal performance on unknown tasks. To address this issue, we introduce two novel algorithms. The first method prevents systems from learning task-specific patterns that may lead to overfitting. The second approach utilizes a constraint to limit the model's parameter set when processing unseen tasks, ensuring consistent results across all tasks. Our experiments with real-world data sets confirm the efficacy of our algorithms in achieving superior performance on unknown tasks. Additionally, we conduct a thorough investigation into the theoretical boundaries of our algorithms, with a primary finding that optimally training on two unknown tasks under specific constraints yields comparable performance to the best possible outcomes in a self-improvement setting. Our work also provides a foundational understanding of meta-learning and its application in model robustness analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the value of open-source settings in self-improvement methods by developing and validating general linear representations of data using only input-output examples, with results including precise count of linear representation dimensions and the derivation of an optimal algorithm among all possible methods, with our algorithm providing comparable performance to the best possible outcomes in a self-improvement setting. Finally, we show the effectiveness of our algorithms in a series of real-world data set experiments, with our results highlighting the practical advantages of using meta-learning and constraint optimization techniques in a self-improvement setting. The code for our algorithms can be found at https://github.com/locheneg/dml. Our related work is discussed in Section Section 9.4. Our work has been validated through extensive experiments and theoretical analysis, and we hope that our research may lead to a range of future investigations. Language models have become a cornerstone of modern NLP frameworks. Despite their success, large language models are computationally expensive, hindering their application to lower-resource devices. In this study, teachers-students frameworks such as distillation and teacher-student quantization have been explored as means to create lightweight NLP models for deployment on edge devices. These methods alleviate the memory and computation burdens of these models, allowing them to be run on smaller hardware. However, the teachers-students frameworks themselves are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that compromise model accuracy, which this paper seeks to investigate. The paper evaluates the robustness of distillation and teacher-student quantization against adversarial modifications in teacher models and their corresponding students. In the context of low-resource machine translation, this study's findings reveal that teacher-student quantization outperforms distillation, achieving better performance even when the teachers-students frameworks are exposed to adversarial attacks. In addition, this research applies backdoor attacks to investigate the vulnerability of these methods, which could have significant implications for their application in security-sensitive domains. These results suggest that while these methods facilitate the creation of lightweight NLP models, their reliability and accuracy rely heavily on the models themselves, making them susceptible to attacks that compromise model integrity. This challenge highlights the need for developing more robust teachers-students frameworks that enable the creation of accurate and lightweight NLP models, especially in the face of potential security threats. Potential solutions to mitigate these threats are also discussed in the conclusion. A thorough analysis in this study aims to provide a more accurate depiction of these methods' applicability to low-resource MT domains, taking into account their susceptibility to attacks that affect model accuracy. This research aims to contribute to the development of more reliable and accurate techniques for creating lightweight NLP models, especially in the presence of potential security risks. Such attacks on these methods can have far-reaching consequences on their application in security-sensitive fields, which this study's findings and analysis aim to explore in the context of low-resource machine translation models. The research also aims to contribute to the development of more robust teachers-students frameworks and/or transfer learning methods that enable the creation of accurate and lightweight NLP models, especially in the presence of potential security threats. These methods for creating lightweight NLP models, such as teacher-student quantization, have the potential to create models that are resilient to attacks that compromise model accuracy, which this study's findings and analysis aim to explore in the context of low-resource machine translation. Consider a hypergraph consisting of n vertices and 2n edges, where interaction edges have sizes two and one, arranged in a specific order. For such a hypergraph, determining the minimum possible energy for a given potential function becomes straightforward, specifically for functions f i (j) = e^(2aj) where a > 0. However, when edge sizes j vary from 1 to 2n, determining the minimum energy becomes a complex task and in fact, no fully determined solution exists yet. Nevertheless, for a particular potential function, where the minimum and the maximum values of the exponential function overlap, an unsolvable equation is presented. This equation has an inconsistent and logically unsolvable solution, indicating the non-existence of a definitive formula. Interestingly, this solution is remarkably close to the minimum energy solution of another type of hypergraph, the parabolic x^2 hypergraph. Furthermore, for another set of potential functions, where the exponential function's intermediate values are as low as possible, a approximate formula is presented. This approximate formula is surprisingly accurate, considering it differs from the minimum energy solution by a factor of at most CN^(-1/2), where C is a constant. In the following sections, the extended versions of this solution and the extended version of the approximate formula are also provided. These extended versions are applicable to more complex hypergraphs with three or more interaction edges of various sizes. Moreover, for a potential function with a variable k > 0, a formula is presented in the generalized version, where the minimum energy is equal to the (2n + 1)/((2 + k)^((2n + 1)/2) partition function of a certain type of Ising model, a well-known equation in the field. Interestingly, for a potential function with a variable a > 0, a formula is presented in the approximate version, where the minimum energy is equal to the (1/(a pi))^(1/2) partition function of a certain type of XY spin chain model. Both of these formulas were previously proposed in the studies by the same authors. To conclude, for a potential function with a variable m > 0, a formula is presented in the extended approximate version, where the minimum energy is equal to the (1/m) partition function of a certain type of Heisenberg magnet. Once more, this formula was previously proposed in the studies by the same authors. Ultimately, for a potential function with a variable n > 0, a formula is presented in the extended approximate version

The detection and analysis of infections like COVID-19, particularly in lung CT scans, poses significant challenges. One complication is detecting lung infections from image batches with varying levels of noise. Noisy input data can hinder the accuracy of segmentation models used in pneumonia detection. We found that noise affects the performance of segmentation models as much as the underlying disease. Therefore, it's crucial to remove the influence of noise before the models process the data. We evaluated several image enhancement techniques - including filter methods (filtering the entire image) and point filters (filtering specific points) - to determine which was more effective at removing noise for the task at hand. Our experiments showed that using entire-image filters increased the model's precision in identifying genuine cases from fake ones by up to 6%, and its precision in identifying fake cases from genuine ones by up to 12%, when compared to unprocessed data. Furthermore, it was discovered that incorporating information about the location of pneumonia within images allowed the entire-image filters to perform similarly to point filters, without the added complexity. This study demonstrates the potential for leveraging image enhancement techniques to mitigate the consequences of noisy data and human annotation discrepancies in medical image analysis. Our code for performing these image enhancements and evaluating their effects is written in TensorFlow and is publicly accessible at https://github.com/miguelapalencia/image-enhancement-for-pneumonia-segmentation. Our 3D segmentation model is publicly accessible at https://github.com/miguelapalencia/covid19-3d-segmentation-model. For both the code and the model to download, please scroll to the bottom of the page. Additionally, our related paper for the model can be found here: Apalencia et al., 2021. Decreasing Sensitivity to Noise for Segmentation Models through Image Enhancement, in Proceedings of the 2021 IEEE 27th International Conference on Image Processing, Scottsdale, AZ, USA, 2021.

Deep neural network models' ability to interpret visual data primarily relies on large collections of labeled images. Nevertheless, they often produce confusing or off-topic descriptions when asked to summarize images in their own words, as evidenced by the significant errors in some benchmark tests. Our study presents an alternative approach that enables more controlled output through the use of prompts that dictate the specific content and tone of the descriptions. This technique allows for descriptions containing any number of words and can be learned using the same datasets commonly used for pre-trained visual models. Our results demonstrate that visually grounded language models significantly outperform their non-visual counterparts and show promising results on a range of benchmark tests, including the VGG-Text, COCO Captioning, and Conceptual Captions datasets. Additionally, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the prompts that help guide the models' behavior and discovered that, using the MS-COCO train split, fully trainable models can create accurate, human-readable image descriptions without requiring human-labeled data. This breakthrough has significant potential for transforming a wide variety of computer vision tasks into natural language interaction applications. A new code repository called promptit is available for other researchers to share in this vision. Finally, our study highlights some exciting future research opportunities inspired by this study, including the potential for leveraging automated prompts to mitigate biases in existing visual datasets. For example, existing datasets like ImAgENet contain descriptions that reflect a limited range of perspectives, but our study shows that these biases can potentially be mitigated through the use of prompts developed using natural language models. This breakthrough could have a significant impact on future research and real-world applications of visual recognition techniques. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the significant progress that can be achieved by leveraging the capabilities of large language models in a multi-modal learning setting. One key example of this is our development of a model called LMS, which integrates the capabilities of a 8B parameter language model with 45M image features from a high-performance efficient neural network. When tested on the challenging COCO Captioning dataset, our model (in its standard form) achieved a remarkable 64.8 mean average precision, which is a new record among fully trainable models. This breakthrough in multi-modal interaction capabilities is all the more impressive considering that our model was trained on a relatively small dataset, namely the MS-COCO train split, without requiring any human-labeled data. Machine learning models can be compromised by model damages, intentionally created to trigger failures in the model's prediction process. Research has focused on detecting damages by measuring how predictions vary with input parameters, but this approach has limitations. In contrast, we investigated damages from a causal perspective and found that with certain data properties, the effect of a damage can be identified without knowledge of the damaged model. By utilizing causal inference techniques on training data, it is possible to isolate and quantify the impact of a damage. Our method does not rely on knowledge of the model or its training process, making it a suitable approach for testing machine learning models. Through both theoretical analysis and experimental testing, our results confirm the effectiveness of this approach in identifying damages and demonstrate robustness across various input properties and model types. Furthermore, the efficiency of the algorithm makes it a suitable approach even for complex machine learning models. In summary, our method does not rely on the model itself but rather leverages causal information present in the training data, thereby providing valuable insights into the model's behavior. Experimental testing of binary models, probability models, and deep neural networks revealed that the approach is highly versatile and can be applied across diverse model architectures. Additionally, the results suggest that the complexity of the model does not affect the computational time required to perform the causal analysis. Importantly, the causal efficacy of a damage provides accurate and reliable information about the model's behavior, making it a valuable tool for testing machine learning models. Moreover, the results suggest a number of promising research directions, including the use of adversarial attacks to test robustness, the extension of the approach to multi-dimensional models, and the application of transfer learning to improve the efficacy of damages. This study showcases how to use MMLSpark, a open-source Spark library, for building a end-to-end machine learning platform that integrates Python and Java within Azure Data Factory.  Firstly, we investigate the advantages of using Python versus Java in Azure DataFactory and Spark environments.  Subsequently, we provide a comprehensive guide on developing a machine learning pipeline in Azure DataFactory, coupled with an illustrative example highlighting the functionality of each stage within the pipeline.  Ultimately, this knowledge can be applied and expanded to other algorithms from open-source Spark libraries, including Spark ML and Deep Learning libraries.  The primary restriction of this work lies in the limitations of supporting only Python and Java within Azure DataFactory, as well as the constraints imposed by the execution of pipelines in standalone environment, an aspect that could be further investigated in the future.  The future developments could also involve integrating other Spark libraries such as Spark ML and scikit-learn, and exploring support for Scala within Azure DataFactory.  The result of this research provides data scientists with a foundation to build adaptable and expandable machine learning pipelines in Azure DataFactory, developed on top of MMLSpark. Voice command systems are popular for their ability to be easily operated hands-free, but they are often limited in understanding the intent behind the commands. The emerging field of voice interpretation is focused on filling this gap by revealing the thoughts and emotions expressed through voice, enabling more intricate interactions. Currently, voice interpretation is generally limited to a pre-defined scope, such as analyzing a person's emotional state, but doesn't require an understanding of their language usage. We propose a new challenge for voice interpretation to involve extensive, unlabelled analyses, uncovering a wider range of insights beyond emotions. We developed an approach that leverages pre-trained speech and language models to uncover new voice interpretation applications without needing labelled data, thereby expanding the scope to include topics such as a person's level of engagement, their identity, or even their personal preferences. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to speech from various sources, such as online forums, podcasts, or voice messages. Our technique unlocks more subtle insights than existing emotion detection models and opens up new possibilities for using voice as a source of in-depth, context-specific knowledge. The developed model and associated evaluation guidelines are available for further research purposes. We also present four innovative use cases showcasing the potential of voice interpretation in areas such as mental health, sales, technology development, and marketing research, thereby paving the way for more natural human-machine interactions. Determining the amount of electricity consumed by specific areas of a grid on specific days is an essential task that becomes increasingly challenging due to the complex nature of consumption patterns. In our research, we investigated daily consumption predictions and analyzed the limitations of predicting hourly consumption. Our analysis is based on a large dataset from the UK's low voltage grid, which we used in two distinct approaches: (1) Demands from different time intervals were predicted and then combined to form consumption forecasts for specific areas of the grid; (2) A unique characteristic of consumption patterns in the grid, involving daily peak values and time-of-day variations, was identified and incorporated into a corresponding prediction model. Our study demonstrates that by considering the variability of daily peak values, the accuracy of combined predictions can be improved by as much as 15%, significantly surpassing the performance of standard forecast methods. Furthermore, we found that peak prediction is particularly challenging, resulting in considerable prediction errors. Consequently, reducing these errors can have a substantial impact on the overall accuracy of combined predictions, which could lead to improvements of up to 50%. In order to facilitate further research in this area, we publicly release our code and make our pre-trained models available through a Tensorflow dataset. These findings are expected to be relevant not only for low voltage grids in the UK but also for similar grids in other countries, including countries such as Spain, Italy, and Greece, which experience similar consumption patterns. Extraordinary consumption peaks that occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic provide a unique research opportunity to investigate the impact of similar unexpected events on consumption patterns and related market dynamics. In particular, our analysis indicates that a sudden pandemic-induced price surge occurred in the UK grid, resulting from inaccurately predicted peak values and resulting losses of up to $\$6.5$M per day for consumers. Accurate vertebra recognition in CT scans is crucial for both emergency response planning and detailed spinal examination. The main obstacle in this process is the initial vertebral alignment, which significantly affects the efficiency of recognition. Existing research in this field, however, has mainly focused on perfect vertebra positioning, failing to account for variations in posture that are common in daily life and often result in misaligned spinal tracts. As such, a critical need exists for a solution that not only recognizes vertebrae but also correctly positions them within the body. Our proposed method integrates vertebral recognition and positioning in a unified framework, utilizing rectification to normalize spinal tracks and enforce anatomical alignment when recognizing vertebrae. Evaluations conducted on public CT datasets have demonstrated that our approach outperforms the standard U-Net in terms of recognition accuracy, and also effectively normalizes spinal tracks. Furthermore, the positioned vertebrae detected by our framework showed 100% accuracy in identifying 12 vertebral bodies and the endpoints of the spinal process in the lumbar vertebra region. These findings suggest that our spine positioning method is generalizable and effective across different spinal regions. Our method has been successfully applied in emergency response cases, resulting in significant time savings and accuracy improvements. In particular, the standard U-Net was replaced by our integrated framework, resulting in a reduction of the manual annotation time from 2.5 hours to 8 minutes in one instance. We introduce a suitable task space formulation for such systems and develop a data-driven method to design an optimal control law. Our approach involves initially guiding the system through a series of pre-defined motions, and from the resulting data, identifying a control pattern that achieves the desired performance. When executed in real-time, this control pattern enables the system to dynamically determine the most suitable action for each instance, thus simulating intentional control. We demonstrate this learning technique on a simulated quadruped robot equipped with actuator springs and dampers. Compared to standard PID control, our approach exhibits better dynamic capabilities, specifically leading to enhanced stability, speed, and romping gait patterns, with the potential to further improve through more complex learning methods. Moreover, we show that the newly acquired control pattern can be seamlessly transferred to a differently modeled quadruped robot, highlighting the strategy's flexibility. The ultimate goal of the Fashion Image Retrieval - Semisupervised challenge is to develop the most effective algorithm to link images of the same outfit. This program is part of the 2019 NTAt workshop, led by Data Science and the French AI Hub. The dataset, provided by Fashionista, comprises 260,000 images and 50,000 key items of clothing. We introduced a novel algorithm, Semi-supervised Feature-level Trait Exchange (SeFTEE), to identify similarities between images. By treating articles of clothing as nodes and outfits as edges, we optimized a graph-based model to distinguish outfits from non-related image combinations. We trained our algorithm using a combination of a self-training technique and multiple iteration refinement. This process, coupled with soft-label assignment and multiple representation exploration, enabled our algorithm to achieve state-of-the-art results. Specifically, from a random start, our algorithm achieved an average precision of 0.4886 over the entire evaluation dataset, exceeding baseline precision by 0.0586. Similarly, from a 1% labeled dataset, our algorithm achieved an average precision of 0.4101, exceeding baseline precision by 0.0481. We've proposed a novel theory of gravity that deviates from conventional Riemannian-based theories. In this alternative, the 3D metric gij and a scalar field φ with non-zero constant β are the fundamental variables. The associated metric tensor δφ has a unique relationship, linking it to β and gij. The resulting action is comprised of three distinct parts, which may be broken down into two physically equivalent theories. The first corresponds to an action-driven, dynamical process governed by a modified Einstein equation. To improve the performance of existing WiFi networks, including dual-band equipment that supports the IEEE 802.11k/v standards, we propose an optimization technique that optimizes the configuration of WiFi access points and extenders within a network. By using the IEEE 802.11k/v standards, we can dynamically collect information about the WiFi channels used by each device and allocate only the most load-efficient configuration of WiFi access points and extenders. Since choosing the optimal configuration is an NP-hard problem due to its exponential number of channels and devices, we developed several heuristics for efficient optimization. According to simulations using real-world networks, our method leads to a significant 60% reduction in interference between channels, outperforming a baseline method that randomly selects channels. As a result, the overall WiFi network speed is increased by up to 50% in some cases. Furthermore, we have developed and tested a compact information model reflecting the performance of WiFi channels and devices, validated through experiments at 95% accuracy. This information model is essential for efficient optimization. Further optimization possibilities are discussed, including the integration of our method with other optimization techniques. Possible extensions of the method proposed in this paper are presented. One possible extension is the integration of our method with existing optimization algorithms for WiFi networks, as well as the simultaneous optimization of WiFi channels and device positions, for example by using the IEEE 802.11s standard. Moreover, the method can be extended to identify the optimal configuration of WiFi channels not only for coexistence but also for maximizing the performance of WiFi devices within a network. However, not all possible configurations are feasible due to constraints, for example, some devices may need to be connected to the same access point or need to use the same WiFi channel. Taking into account these constraints, we have reformulated the problem of choosing the optimal configuration as an integer programming task and proposed several heuristics for efficient solutions. In particular, we have developed in collaboration with the mobile operator Vodafone a method for channel load efficiency by leveraging the information provided by the IEEE 802.11k standard. This method is realized through a device called WiFi Analyzer which is a free, commercial app available for Android and iOS.
